p.seg: Chapter One: Inquiry into the Way
The virtue of literature is truly great!
How could it not be coexistent with Heaven and Earth?
For black and yellow are intermingled in color,
square and round are distinguished in form,
the sun and moon overlap like jade disks,
thereby displaying the image of resplendence in the sky;
mountains and rivers gleam like brocade,
thereby arranging the form of order on the earth;
these are indeed the patterns of the Dào.
Looking up, one sees radiance emitted;
looking down, one observes potential contained.
High and low are fixed in their positions,
thus the two realms (Heaven and Earth) came into being.
Only humans participate in this,
endowed with concentrated spiritual intelligence,
and are thus called the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity).
They are the excellence of the Five Elements,
and truly the heart of Heaven and Earth.
From the heart arises speech,
from speech arises civilization,
which is the natural way.
Extending to the myriad things,
both moving and growing things possess pattern.
Dragons and phoenixes display auspiciousness with colorful patterns,
tigers and leopards exhibit elegance with bright markings;
clouds and mist are sculpted in color,
surpassing the skill of painters;
grasses and trees are adorned with blossoms,
requiring no marvelous craftsmanship of brocade artisans;
how could these be external decorations?
They are naturally so.
As for the sounds of the forest forming harmonies,
they are as attuned as the *yú* flute and *sè* zither;
the springs and rocks create rhythms as they collide,
harmonizing like the *qiú* jade and *huáng* bell.
Therefore, when form is established, pattern is complete;
when sound is uttered, literature is born.
If even insentient things
abundantly possess color,
how can beings with minds
be without pattern?
The origin of humanistic pattern
begins with the Tài Jí (Great Ultimate).
To praise silently the spirits and deities,
the *Yì* (Book of Changes) images came first.
Páo Xī (Fú Xī) drew their beginning,
Zhòng Ní (Kǒng Zǐ) elaborated on their end.
And the two positions of Qián (Heaven) and Kūn (Earth)
uniquely created the "Wén Yán" (Commentary on the Words).
The pattern of words,
is the heart of Heaven and Earth!
As for the Hé Tú (Yellow River Chart) containing the Eight Trigrams,
and the Luò Shū (Luò River Writing) encompassing the Nine Categories,
the reality of jade tablets engraved with gold,
the splendor of cinnabar script on green slips,
who is in charge of them?
It is merely divine principle.
Since bird tracks replaced knotted cords,
writing began to shine forth.
The lost deeds of Yán Hào (Yán Dì and Tài Hào)
are recorded in the *Sān Fén* (Three Tombs),
but the years and ages are distant,
and their sounds and colors are untraceable.
The literature of the Táng (Yáo) and Yú (Shùn) periods
then began to flourish brilliantly.
The sovereign led the singing,
thereby expressing the intent of poetry;
Yì and Jì presented their plans,
also establishing the style of memorials and reports.
When the Xià dynasty arose,
its achievements were lofty and its merits great,
the Nine Odes were sung exclusively,
and its meritorious virtue was all the more elaborate.
Reaching the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties,
literature surpassed substance.
Wherever the *Yǎ* (Odes) and *Sòng* (Hymns) reached,
the beautiful blossoms renewed daily.
Wén Wáng suffered anxieties,
the *Yáo Cí* (Line Statements) shone brightly,
with talismans and colors both overt and hidden,
and profound meaning firm and deep.
Further, with Gōng Dàn's (Zhōu Gōng) many talents,
he promoted their magnificent brilliance,
edited the *Shī* (Odes) and compiled the *Sòng* (Hymns),
polishing the language of all.
As for Fū Zǐ (Kǒng Zǐ) succeeding the sages,
he stood out uniquely among the former wise men,
refining the *Liù Jīng* (Six Classics) in his crucible,
surely with the sound of metal and the resonance of jade.
He sculpted the emotions and nature,
and organized phrases and words.
When the wooden-tongued bell was rung, it resonated a thousand *lǐ*;
when treasured jewels were passed on, they echoed for myriad generations.
He depicted the shining glory of Heaven and Earth,
and enlightened the ears and eyes of the people.
From the Fēng lineage,
up to the Kǒng lineage,
the profound sages created the canon,
and the uncrowned king (Kǒng Zǐ) narrated its teachings.
None did not base their words on the mind of the Dào,
study divine principles to establish teachings,
draw images from the Hé (Yellow River) and Luò (Luò River),
inquire into numbers from the milfoil stalks and tortoise shells,
observe celestial patterns to exhaust change,
and examine human patterns to complete transformation;
only then could they manage territories,
encompass the constant principles,
develop enterprises,
and illuminate the meaning of words.
Therefore, one knows that the Dào is transmitted through the sages by means of literature,
and the sages illuminate the Dào by means of literature,
connecting broadly without limit,
used daily without exhaustion.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"That which stirs all under Heaven is based on words."
The reason why words can stir all under Heaven
is none other than the pattern of the Dào.
Eulogy:
The mind of the Dào is subtle and elusive;
divine principles establish teachings.
The brilliance of the profound sages
illuminates benevolence and filial piety.
The dragon chart presents its form;
the tortoise writing displays its appearance.
Celestial patterns are thus observed;
the people all follow the example.
Chapter Two: Evidence of Sagehood
Those who create are called sages;
those who transmit are called enlightened.
To mold and cast temperament and feelings,
accomplishment lies with the highest sages.
The writings of Fū Zǐ (Kǒng Zǐ)
can be heard,
thus the feelings of the sage
are seen in his words.
The teachings of the former kings
are spread in books and records;
the demeanor of Fū Zǐ (Kǒng Zǐ)
overflows in his maxims.
Therefore, in praising the Táng (Yáo) era from afar,
it was brilliantly prosperous;
in commending the Zhōu dynasty from nearby,
it was richly worth following.
This is evidence that political transformation values literature.
When Zhèng Bó (Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng) entered Chén,
he regarded skillful wording as success;
when Sòng placed the arranged meats,
they valued abundant wording to perform the rites.
This is evidence that events valued literature.
When praising Zǐ Chǎn,
it was said, "Words are sufficient to express the will,
and literature is sufficient to express the words";
when discussing gentlemen generally,
it was said, "Emotions should be sincere,
and words should be skillful."
This is evidence that self-cultivation values literature.
Therefore, when the will is sufficient and the words are patterned,
and the emotions are sincere and the words are skillful,
they are the jade tablets containing potential,
and the golden standards upholding pattern.
To use Zhōu to mirror the sun and moon,
is to reach the extremity of the spirit of the machine;
to complete pattern and measure,
is to think in accord with a talisman.
Sometimes one uses concise words to convey meaning,
or extensive writing to encompass emotions,
or clarifies principles to establish structure,
or hides meaning to conceal function.
Therefore, the *Chūn Qiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) uses a single word for praise and blame,
and the *Sāng Fú* (Mourning Garments) uses lightness to encompass heaviness;
this is using concise words to convey meaning.
The *Bīn Shī* (Odes of Bīn) connects chapters to accumulate phrases,
and the *Rú Xíng* (Conduct of the Scholars) uses elaborate explanation with profuse words;
this is using extensive writing to encompass emotions.
Legal documents use decisiveness to symbolize *Guài* (the breakthrough hexagram),
and writing uses clarity to emulate *Lí* (the radiance hexagram);
this is clarifying principles to establish structure.
The *Sì Xiàng* (Four Symbols) use refined meaning to hide deviously,
and the *Wǔ Lì* (Five Examples) use subtle language to be gently obscure;
this is hiding meaning to conceal function.
Thus, one knows that proliferation and brevity have different forms,
obscurity and clarity have different techniques,
suppressing and drawing out follow the times,
and change and communication adapt to the occasion.
Examining it through Zhōu Gōng and Kǒng Zǐ,
then literature has a teacher.
Therefore, when writing essays, one must seek evidence from the sages;
to understand the sages, one must take the classics as the foundation.
The *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) says, “Discriminating things and rectifying speech,
decisions are then complete”;
the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) says, “Speeches should value substance and brevity,
not only valuing novelty.”
Thus, we know that correct speech is the means to establish discrimination,
substance and brevity are the means to complete an expression;
once expression is complete, there will be no fault of valuing novelty,
once discrimination is established, there will be the beauty of conclusive decisions.
Even if the profound meanings are subtly hidden,
it does not harm its correct speech;
even if the subtle expressions are tactfully obscure,
it does not impair its substance and brevity.
Substance and brevity and subtle expression proceed together,
correct speech and profound meanings are used in conjunction;
the sages’ compositions
can be seen thus.
Yán Hé 顏闔 thought that Zhòng Ní 仲尼 (Confucius) decorated with feathers and painted,
merely engaging in flowery language.
Even if he wanted to criticize the sage,
he could not succeed.
Thus, the elegance and beauty of the sage's writing
indeed holds flowers in its mouth and wears substance on its belt.
The way of Heaven is difficult to hear,
yet some still drill and look up to it;
writings are visible,
so how can one not think about them?
If one seeks evidence from the sages to establish one's words,
then writing will be close to perfection.
The eulogy says:
The ultimate of subtlety produces wisdom,
sagacity and intelligence are the only rulers.
Profound principles become the writing,
outstanding energy becomes the brilliance.
The mirror hangs like the sun and moon,
the language is as rich as mountains and seas.
A hundred years of shadow pass quickly,
a thousand years of heart remains.
Chapter Three: Taking the Classics as the Foundation
The three ultimate, constant teachings,
the books of which are called *Jīng* 經 (Classics).
The *Jīng*,
are the eternal and ultimate Way,
the imperishable great teachings.
Thus, they imitate Heaven and Earth,
emulate ghosts and spirits,
coordinate the order of things,
establish the norms for humans,
penetrate the obscure regions of spiritual nature,
and exhaust the marrow of writing.
The *Sān Fén* 三墳 of the imperial age,
the *Wǔ Diǎn* 五典 of the emperor dynasties,
augmented by the *Bā Suǒ* 八索,
extended by the *Jiǔ Qiū* 九丘,
over ages of misty obscurity,
their branches and streams became numerous and confused,
until Fūzǐ 夫子 (Confucius) edited and narrated them,
and then the great treasures all shone.
Thus, the *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) displays the *Shí Yì* 十翼 (Ten Wings),
the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) marks the seven observations,
the *Shī* 詩 (Book of Odes) lists the four beginnings,
the *Lǐ* 禮 (Book of Rites) rectifies the *Wǔ Jīng* 五經 (Five Classics),
and the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) has five examples.
The meaning is thus molded by human nature and emotion,
and the language is crafted by literary principles,
therefore they can open learning and nourish righteousness,
brightly illuminating with harmony.
However, the mind of the Way is subtle,
the plans of the sages are outstanding and unique,
the walls and courtyard are heavily layered,
inhaling and exhaling is naturally deep.
It is like a ten-thousand *jūn* 鈞 (unit of weight) great bell,
without any small ringing sounds.
The *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) only discusses Heaven,
entering the spiritual and achieving practical application.
Thus, the *Xì* 繫 (Commentary) states that its meaning is far-reaching and its language elegant,
its words hit the mark and its affairs are hidden;
the leather straps were broken three times,
indeed it is the abyss of the black dragon for the wise.
The *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) truly records speeches,
but its commentaries and explanations are vast and obscure;
if one understands the *Ěryǎ* 爾雅 (Approaching Correctness),
then the meaning of the text becomes clear.
Thus, Zǐxià 子夏 (a disciple of Confucius) praised the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents),
shining like the alternating brightness of the sun and moon,
distinct like the scattered movements of the stars,
meaning it is brightly illuminating.
The *Shī* 詩 (Book of Odes) mainly expresses intentions,
its commentaries and explanations are the same as the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents),
spreading wind-like influence and expressing sentiments,
ornate language and surprising metaphors,
gentle and mild in recitation,
daring to most closely attach to deep feelings.
The *Lǐ* 禮 (Book of Rites) establishes the forms,
based on events, it carves out the norms,
its chapters and sections are delicate and intricate,
only after grasping it does it become manifest,
gathering and arranging fragmented words,
nothing is not a treasure.
The *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) discriminates principles,
a single character reveals a meaning,
five *shí* 石 (units of weight) and six *yì* 鷁 (boats),
using detail and omission to form the writing;
*zhìmén* 雉門 (city gate) with two watchtowers,
using sequence to make the intent clear;
its tactful chapters conceal the will,
truly it is profound.
With the *Shàngshū* 尚書 (Book of Documents), browsing the text feels misleading,
but seeking the principle is straightforward;
with the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals), observing the language immediately understands,
but inquiring into the meaning is obscure.
These are the special qualities of the sage’s writing,
the different forms of exterior and interior.
As for the roots being deep and firm,
the branches and leaves being tall and lush,
the language being concise but the meaning abundant,
the events being near but the metaphors being far,
therefore what has passed is old,
but the remaining taste is new every day,
later scholars pursue and acquire it, yet are not late,
earlier scholars have long used it, yet are not first,
it can be said to be Mt. Tài 泰 (mountain) raining everywhere,
and the river irrigating a thousand *lǐ* 里 (unit of distance).
Therefore, for discussions, explanations, prefaces,
the *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) commands the lead;
for imperial edicts, pronouncements, memorials,
the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) initiates the source;
for *fù* 賦 (rhapsodies), *sòng* 頌 (eulogies), *gē* 謌 (songs), and *zàn* 讚 (praises),
the *Shī* 詩 (Book of Odes) establishes the foundation;
for *míng* 銘 (inscriptions), *lěi* 誄 (dirges), *zhēn* 箴 (admonitions), and *zhù* 祝 (invocations),
the *Lǐ* 禮 (Book of Rites) governs the beginning;
for historical accounts, biographies, alliances, and proclamations,
the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) is the root;
together, they exhaust height to set up the markers,
exhaust distance to open up the boundaries,
therefore the hundred schools leap forward,
ultimately entering within the circle.
If one receives the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) to make the models,
draws from the *Yǎ* 雅 (elegant) to enrich the words,
it is like using a mountain to cast bronze,
and boiling the sea to make salt.
Therefore, if the writing can take the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) as the foundation,
the style will have six meanings:
first, the emotion is deep and not perverse,
second, the air is pure and not mixed,
third, the events are trustworthy and not exaggerated,
fourth, the meaning is steadfast and does not turn back,
fifth, the style is concise and not uncultivated,
sixth, the writing is beautiful and not lewd.
Yángzǐ 楊子 (Yang Xiong) compared carving jade to make a vessel,
to the *Wǔ Jīng* 五經 (Five Classics) containing writing.
Writing is established through conduct,
conduct is transmitted through writing,
the four teachings come first,
form and substance complement each other,
advancing virtue and establishing reputation,
nothing does not take the sages as a teacher;
but establishing words and cultivating language,
few can take the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) as the foundation.
Therefore, the Chu 楚 (state) is flamboyant and the Han 漢 (dynasty) is extravagant,
the bad habits flow and do not return,
rectifying the end and returning to the root,
would that not be excellent!
The eulogy says:
The three ultimate, constant Way,
the teachings are deep and examine antiquity.
Achieving transformation and returning to one,
dividing the teachings into five.
Molding the spiritual nature,
the profound storehouse of writing.
How deep, how melting,
the ancestor of all words.
Chapter Four: Orthodox and Apocryphal
The divine way explains the obscure,
the mandate of Heaven is subtly revealed,
the dragon-horse appeared and the *Dà Yì* 大易 (Great Book of Changes) arose,
the divine turtle appeared and the *Hóng Fàn* 洪範 (Great Plan) shone.
Thus, the *Xìcí* 繫辭 (Appended Remarks) says, “The river emitted a chart,
the Luo 洛 (river) emitted a text,
the sages patterned themselves after them,”
this is what it means.
But the world is far and the writing is hidden,
people like to create falsehoods and exaggerations,
though the true still exists,
the false also relies on it.
The *Liù Jīng* 六經 (Six Classics) are clearly displayed,
while the *Wěi Hòu* 緯候 (Apocryphal Texts) are densely layered;
the *Xiào* 孝 (Classic of Filial Piety) and *Lún* 論 (Analects) are brilliantly clear,
while the *Gōu Chèn* 鉤讖 (Occult Prophecies) are luxuriant;
examining the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) and verifying with the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha),
their falsity is fourfold:
that the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) complete the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
is like weaving,
where silk and hemp are not mixed,
and cloth is then made;
now the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) are correct and the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) are strange,
differing by thousands of *lǐ* 里,
that is the first falsity.
The *Jīng* 經 (Classics) are manifest,
they are the teachings of the sages;
the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) are hidden,
they are divine instruction;
the teachings of the sages should be broad,
divine instruction should be concise;
but now the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) are more numerous than the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
and divine principles are even more complex,
that is the second falsity.
If commands come from Heaven,
they are then called *fú chèn* 符讖 (tallies and prophecies),
but the eighty-one sections,
are all attributed to Kǒngzǐ 孔子;
this is like Yáo 堯 creating the Green Chart,
and Chāng 昌 making the Red Book,
that is the third falsity.
Before the Shāng 商 and Zhōu 周 dynasties,
charts and records were frequently seen,
at the end of the Chūnqiū 春秋 (Spring and Autumn period),
the various *Jīng* 經 (Classics) were finally complete;
*Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) first, then *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
the structure deviates from weaving,
that is the fourth falsity.
Since the falsities are greatly different,
then the differing meanings are self-evident,
the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) are sufficient for instruction,
what do the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) add?
Tracing the origin of the appearance of charts and records,
they are the glorious mandate of vast Heaven,
events that correspond with sages,
their meaning is not to be paired with the *Jīng* 經 (Classics).
Therefore, when the Hé 河 (Yellow River) did not produce a chart,
Fūzǐ 夫子 (Confucius) sighed,
if they could be created,
there would be no need for lamentation.
In the past, Kāng Wáng 康王 (King Kang) displayed the Hé Tú 河圖 (Yellow River Chart),
in the Eastern Hall,
so we know that the tallies of previous generations,
were treasured and passed down through the ages,
that Zhòngní 仲尼 (Confucius) compiled,
were merely prefaces and records.
Then, those skilled in techniques,
attached them with deceptive arts,
some explaining Yīnyáng 陰陽 (yin and yang),
some describing disasters and anomalies,
like birds chirping resembling speech,
and insects and leaves forming characters,
the clauses and sections grew luxuriantly,
and they all borrowed the name of the Kǒng 孔 (Confucius) family,
a learned scholar investigated,
and said the forgeries began in the Ài 哀 (Ai) and Píng 平 (Ping) reigns,
the secret treasures of the Eastern Hall,
were confused by official robes of purple and vermillion.
As for the time of Guāngwǔ 光武 (Emperor Guangwu),
he sincerely believed in these arts.
The customs were influenced,
and scholars gathered shoulder to shoulder,
Pèi Xiàn 沛獻 (Pei Xian) collected *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) to understand the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
and Cáo Bāo 曹褒 (Cao Bao) compiled *chèn* 讖 (prophecies) to establish rites,
deviating from the Way and mistaking the Classics,
was already excessive.
Therefore, Huán Tán 桓譚 (Huan Tan) criticized their falsehood,
Yǐn Mǐn 尹敏 (Yin Min) mocked their deep flaws,
Zhāng Héng 張衡 (Zhang Heng) exposed their biased errors,
and Xún Yuè 荀悅 (Xun Yue) clarified their deceitful absurdities,
these four worthies were broadly skilled,
and their discussions were precise.
As for the origins of Xī Nóng 羲農 (Xi Nong), Xuān Hào 軒皞 (Xuan Hao),
the essentials of mountains and rivers, and the pitch pipes,
the tallies of white fish and red crows,
and the omens of yellow silver and purple jade,
the events are abundant and wonderful,
and the language is rich and fertile,
they do not benefit the Classics, but they do assist literature.
Therefore, later writers,
gathered up the excellent blossoms,
Píngzǐ 平子 (Zhang Heng) feared they would mislead learning,
and submitted a memorial to prohibit and cut them off;
Zhòngyù 仲豫 (Xun Yue) regretted their mixture with truth,
and did not allow them to be burned;
the previous generations paired them with the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
therefore they are discussed in detail.
Eulogy:
The Róng 榮 (Rong) River and the Wēn 溫 (Wen) River,
are where charts and *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) were conceived.
The divine treasures are hidden in use,
the principles are obscure and the language is valued.
Through the two Hàn 漢 dynasties,
vermillion and purple rose and fell.
Weed out the cunning and strange,
and select their elegant carvings.
Discussing *Sāo* 騷 (Lament) Fifth
Discussing *Sāo* 騷 (Lament) Fifth
Since the sounds of *Fēng* 風 (Airs) and *Yǎ* 雅 (Odes) have ceased,
no one has been able to extract their threads,
and extraordinary literature has flourished,
with the *Lí Sāo* 離騷 (The Lament)!
It has already soared beyond the poets of the past,
and energetically flown before the writers of *cí* 辭 (rhapsody),
could it be that we are not far from the sages,
and that the people of Chǔ 楚 are exceptionally talented?
In the past, Hàn Wǔ 漢武 (Emperor Wu of Han) loved the *Sāo* 騷 (Lament),
and Huáinán 淮南 (Prince of Huainan) wrote a commentary,
saying, "*Guófēng* 國風 (Airs of the States) is fond of beauty but not licentious,
*Xiǎoyǎ* 小雅 (Little Odes) expresses resentment and criticism without disorder,
as for *Lí Sāo* 離騷 (The Lament),
it can be said to combine both.
It sheds its skin from within filth and turbidity,
and floats beyond dust and grime,
it is purely white though stained without becoming black,
it can contend with the sun and moon for glory."
Bān Gù 班固 (Ban Gu) said, "It exposes talent and flaunts self,
with resentment it drowns in the river;
Yì 羿 (Yi) and Jiāo 澆 (Jiao), and the two Yáo 姚 (Yao) sisters,
do not agree with the *Zuǒ Shì* 左氏 (Zuo Tradition);
Kūnlún 崑崙 (Kunlun) and Xuánpǔ 懸圃 (Hanging Garden),
are not recorded in the meaning of the *Jīng* 經 (Classics);
but its language is beautiful and elegant,
it is the ancestor of *cí fù* 詞賦 (lyrical prose),
though not wise,
it can be called wondrous talent."
Wáng Yì 王逸 (Wang Yi) said, "The poets remonstrate by pulling ears,
Qū Yuán 屈原 (Qu Yuan) is gentle and compliant,
the writing of the *Lí Sāo* 離騷 (The Lament),
relies on the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) to establish its meaning,
riding four dragons with a screen of feathers,
is like riding six dragons at the proper time;
Kūnlún 崑崙 (Kunlun) and the quicksand,
are where *Yǔ Gòng* 禹貢 (Tribute of Yu) surveyed the land;
the *cí fù* 詞賦 (lyrical prose) of famous scholars,
all imitate its appearance,
it can be called gold and jade,
unparalleled for a hundred generations."
And Hàn Xuān 漢宣 (Emperor Xuan of Han) praised it,
saying it all accords with the arts of the *Jīng* 經 (Classics);
Yáng Xióng 揚雄 (Yang Xiong) savored and tasted it,
and also said its form is the same as the *Shī* 詩 (Odes) and *Yǎ* 雅 (Odes).
These four families cite it as comparable to the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
but Mèngjiān 孟堅 (Ban Gu) said it does not accord with the *Zhuàn* 傳 (Traditions),
praising and criticizing at will,
