Conclusion:
Writing reality and pursuing emptiness,
the stele and the *lěi* (誄) are established.
Recording virtue and compiling conduct,
literary embellishments are appropriately gathered.
Observing customs is like seeing a face,
and hearing words is like weeping.
Stone and ink engrave brilliance;
how can the declining shadow be suppressed?
Chapter Thirteen: Dirges and Laments
As for bestowing the posthumous title of Xiàn (憲),
"to die young is called Āi (哀)."
Āi (哀),
means "to rely on."
Grief truly relies on the heart,
therefore it is called Āi (哀).
Using words to express grief,
is generally a lament for those of lower status,
thus it is not used for the elderly,
but certainly applied to those who die young.
In the past, when the three good men died for Qín (秦),
even a hundred men could not redeem them.
The circumstances were equally premature and tragic,
and the "Huáng Niǎo" (黃鳥) expressed grief.
Indeed, it was a poet’s expression of grief!
When Hàn Wǔ (漢武) performed the fēngshàn (封禪) ceremony,
and Huò Shàn (霍嬗) died suddenly,
the emperor was saddened and composed a poem,
which was also a type of eulogy.
Coming down to the Later Hàn (後漢),
when the Rǔyáng (汝陽) Prince died,
Cuī Yuán’s (崔瑗) eulogy
began to change the previous style.
However, "stepping into the gate of ghosts"
is strange and not eloquent;
"riding dragons and clouds"
is immortal and not sorrowful.
Moreover, the concluding chapter in five-character lines
somewhat resembles a ballad,
and also vaguely resembles Hàn Wǔ (漢武).
As for Sū Shùn (蘇順) and Zhāng Shēng (張升),
both wrote eulogies,
and although they expressed their literary talents,
they did not fully express their heartfelt sincerity.
Among the Jian'an (建安) eulogies,
only Wèi Cháng (偉長) was relatively good.
The "Xíng Nǚ" (行女) piece
sometimes has a sense of sorrow.
When Pān Yuè (潘岳) continued to write,
he truly embodied its beauty.
Observing his thoughtful considerations and varied diction,
his poignant emotions and sorrowful bitterness,
his narration of events like biographies,
and his concluding words imitating poetry,
with concise four-character verses,
there are few relaxed sentences.
Thus, he could achieve righteousness and gentleness in his writing,
adhering to the old form while embracing new ideas.
"Jīn Lù" (金鹿) and "Zé Lán" (澤蘭)
have no successors.
The main theme of eulogies in general
is that emotion centers on pain and grief,
and the words exhaust the feelings of cherishing.
Because the young have not achieved virtue,
praise is limited to discerning intelligence;
because the weak are not capable of handling affairs,
lamentations are added to their physical appearance.
Concealing one’s feelings and composing the text makes the matter appropriate,
while observing the text and attaching one’s heart to it makes the style extravagant.
An extravagant style of writing
may be beautiful, but it is not sorrowful;
it must make the emotions meet with grief,
and the words draw tears,
then it is valuable.
Diào (弔) means "to arrive."
The *Shī* (詩) says,
"The spirits have come to offer condolences."
It means the spirits have arrived.
When a noble person determines the posthumous title at the end of life,
the matter is most extreme, the reason most sorrowful,
therefore, the guest's consolation to the host
is expressed by saying "to arrive."
To be overwhelmed by water or to violate the proper way
are reasons not to offer condolences.
Also, the water disaster in Sòng (宋) and the fire in Zhèng (鄭),
where messengers conveyed condolences,
were national disasters that caused the death of the people,
so everyone offered condolences.
When Jìn (晉) built the Tái (臺) Tower,
and Qí (齊) attacked Yān (燕) city,
Shǐ Zhào (史趙) and Sū Qín (蘇秦)
turned congratulations into condolences,
oppressing the people and creating enemies
are also ways to ruin.
All such examples
are situations where condolences are appropriate.
Sometimes, people die from arrogance and nobility,
or from narrow-minded anger and violating the proper way,
or having aspirations but lacking opportunity,
or possessing talent but burdened with difficulties;
to remember and console them
are all called diào (弔).
Since Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) floated on the Xiāng (湘) River,
expressing his frustration in "Diào Qū" (弔屈),
the structure was thorough and the content factual,
the words were clear and the reasoning sorrowful;
it was the pioneering work.
As for Sīmǎ Xiāngrú's (司馬相如) "Diào Èr Shì" (弔二世),
it was entirely in the rhapsody style.
Huán Tán (桓譚) believed that its words were mournful
and made readers sigh.
The concluding chapter was essential and poignant,
decisive and capable of evoking sorrow.
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) "Diào Qū" (弔屈),
showed accumulated thought but lacked merit,
its intent was deeply rooted in "Fǎn Sāo" (反騷),
so the rhyme and rhythm were dull and ponderous.
Bān Biāo (班彪) and Cài Yōng (蔡邕)
were both quick at delivering their messages,
but merely shadowed the Jiǎ (賈) style,
making it difficult to run alongside him.
Hú (胡) and Ruǎn’s (阮) "Diào Yí Qí" (弔夷齊)
praised without reservation;
Wáng Càn’s (王粲) work
criticized and rebuked skillfully.
Thus, Hú (胡) and Ruǎn (阮) admired their purity,
while Wáng Zǐ (王子) lamented their narrow-mindedness,
each according to their own inclinations.
Mí Héng's (禰衡) "Diào Píng Zǐ" (弔平子)
was elaborate and graceful, yet light and airy;
Lù Jī's (陸機) "Diào Wèi Wǔ" (弔魏武)
was skillfully arranged and elaborately written.
After these,
there has been nothing worth mentioning.
Although diào (弔) has ancient roots,
refined language had not yet been created.
If refinement goes too far and the rhythm becomes loose,
it transforms into a rhapsody.
It is essential to correct the meaning to align with reason,
reveal virtue and block transgression,
clearly distinguish praise and blame,
and to be sorrowful and righteous,
then there will be no violation of ethics.
Commentary says:
The sorrow of the words
lies in those who are young and tender.
To sprout but not blossom
has been a cause of grief since ancient times.
Even with great talent,
losing direction and control
is a cause for grief for thousands of years,
and is conveyed through allegorical language.
Miscellaneous Writings, Fourteenth
The sons of wisdom and skill,
the men of broad learning and elegance,
their refined language overflows from their words,
and their words are filled with spirit.
To cultivate a garden of literary emotions
results in new and unique qualities every day.
Sòng Yù (宋玉), possessing talent,
somewhat defied convention.
He first created "Duì Wèn" (對問)
to express his aspirations,
freeing his mind in the vastness,
which was driven by his spirit.
When M 枚 Chéng (枚乘) displayed his brilliance,
he first created "Qī Fā" (七發),
rich in language and cloud-like structure,
extravagant and awe-inspiring.
"Qī Fā" (七發) originates from the seven orifices,
arising from desires and passions,
starting with indulgence and ending with correction,
so it is a warning to the sons of the wealthy.
Yáng Xióng (揚雄), with deep thought and broad writing,
had deep learning and comprehensive descriptions.
He composed fragmented sentences and jade-like words,
and first created "Lián Zhū" (連珠),
where words are linked like pearls.
Although small, they are bright and lustrous.
These three,
are branches of literature,
and creations of leisure and recreation.
Following "Dui Wen" (《對問》, "Questions and Answers"),
Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) imitated and expanded upon it,
calling it "Kè Nàn" (《客難》, "Difficulties for the Guest"),
entrusting ancient examples to console his aspirations,
being detached yet articulate.
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) "Jiě Cháo" (《解嘲》, "Dispelling Ridicule"),
mixed with jesting,
circling back to explain himself,
was also quite skillfully done.
Bān Gù's (班固) "Bīn Xì" (《賓戲》, "Guest's Jest"),
contained the splendor of elegant expression;
Cuī Yīn's (崔駰) "Dá Zhǐ" (《達旨》, "Expressing Intent"),
displayed the refinement of classical language;
Zhāng Héng's (張衡) "Yìng Jiàn" (《應間》, "Responding to Interrogation"),
was subtle yet elegant;
Cuī Shí's (崔寔) "Kè Jī" (《客譏》, "Guest's Criticism"),
was organized yet subtly simple;
Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) "Shì Huì" (《釋誨》, "Explaining Admonition"),
possessed profound substance and radiant prose;
and Jǐng Chún's (景純) "Kè Ào" (《客傲》, "Guest's Arrogance"),
revealed emotion and vibrant language.
Although they mutually imitated each other,
they were still among the best of their type.
As for Chén Sī's (陳思) "Kè Wèn" (《客問》, "Guest's Questions"),
the language was elevated, but the reasoning was sparse;
Yǔ Gǎi's (庾敳) "Kè Zī" (《客咨》, "Guest's Inquiries"),
had ambitious ideas but withered prose.
There are so many of this kind
that there is nothing to take from them.
Now, the establishment of this literary form
was to express one's aspirations with passion.
When one's person is thwarted, one relies on the triumph of virtue;
when times are difficult, one finds solace in emotional contentment.
All of these works have hearts as deep as the abyss and mountains,
and literary styles like the lín (麟) and fèng (鳳) (mythical creatures),
which are the grand essentials of establishing the form.
From "Qī Fā" (《七發》, "Seven Stimuli") onward,
authors followed in succession.
Observing Méi Shèng's (枚乘) initial creation,
it was truly outstanding and magnificent.
As for Fù Yì's (傅毅) "Qī Jī" (《七激》, "Seven Excitations"),
it possessed the skill of clear conciseness;
Cuī Yīn's (崔駰) "Qī Yī" (《七依》, "Seven Dependencies"),
attained the cleverness of extensive erudition;
Zhāng Héng's (張衡) "Qī Biàn" (《七辨》, "Seven Discriminations"),
wove together elaborate language;
Cuī Yuán's (崔瑗) "Qī Lì" (《七厲》, "Seven Admonitions"),
established upright principles;
Chén Sī's (陳思) "Qī Qǐ" (《七啟》, "Seven Awakenings"),
took beauty from grandeur;
and Zhòng Xuān's (仲宣, i.e., Wáng Càn 王粲) "Qī Shì" (《七釋》, "Seven Explanations"),
achieved clarity in matters of principle.
From Huán Lín's (桓麟) "Qī Shuō" (《七說》, "Seven Discourses") and
Zuǒ Sī's (左思) "Qī Fěng" (《七諷》, "Seven Satires") onward,
they branched out and followed like shadows,
numbering more than ten families.
Some had beautiful language but divergent meanings,
while others had pure principles but clumsy language.
Observing their general trend,
all of them lavishly discussed palaces and mansions,
and grandly spoke of hunting.
They exhausted extravagant and exotic foods,
and reached the extreme of seductive sounds and sights.
The sweetness moved the bones and marrow,
and the alluring words penetrated the soul and consciousness.
Although they began with indulgence and extravagance,
they ended with dwelling in righteousness.
However, satirizing one thing to advise on a hundred is
a momentum that cannot be reversed.
This is what Zǐ Yún (子雲, i.e., Yáng Xióng 揚雄) meant by "first displaying the sounds of Zhèng (鄭) and Wèi (衛),
and then playing refined music at the end."
Only "Qī Lì" (《七厲》, "Seven Admonitions") narrates worthies
and returns to Confucian doctrines,
and although its language is not outstanding,
its meaning is truly exceptional.
From "Lián Zhū" (《連珠》, "Linked Pearls") onward,
imitators occasionally appeared.
People like Dù Dǔ (杜篤) and Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵),
and the likes of Liú Zhēn (劉珍) and Pān Xù (潘勖),
wanted to pierce bright pearls,
but mostly strung together fish eyes.
It could be said that they were like Shòu Líng (壽陵) crawling,
no longer walking in the manner of Hándān (邯鄲);
a village woman clutching her heart,
not related to Xī Shī's (西施) frown.
Only Shì Héng (士衡, i.e., Lù Jī 陸機) employed his thoughts,
with fresh ideas and nimble writing;
and his composition and sentence structure
were broader than previous works.
Could he have been admiring Zhū Zhòng's (朱仲) four-inch earring?
Now, short compositions are easy to complete,
and leisurely thought can be abundant.
It is enough to make the meaning clear and the language pure,
the subject matter complete and the sound polished,
turning smoothly and continuously,
and then it can be called a pearl.
Examining the miscellaneous writings since the Hàn dynasty,
the names and categories are numerous.
Some are ordinances, announcements, oaths, and inquiries,
others are outlines and summaries of chapters,
others are musical pieces and ballads,
and still others are recitations of satire and songs.
To summarize their names,
they all fall under the category of miscellaneous writings;
to distinguish their meanings,
each enters the realm of discussion.
Grouping them by category creates a connected structure,
so I will not describe them in detail.
Appended Praise:
Great were the former worthies,
with firm learning and abundant talent.
With remaining literary strength,
they flew and fluttered, displaying their skill.
Their techniques and language intertwined and reflected,
glittering like the stars of Orion and the Pleiades.
The heart of admiring a frown
is thereby disturbed.
Chapter Fifteen: Jests and Riddles
Chapter Fifteen: Jests and Riddles
A poem by Ruì Liángfū (芮良夫) says:
"Having their own hearts and minds,
they caused the people to go completely mad."
Indeed, a heart as treacherous as a mountain,
and a mouth as blocked as a river,
resentful emotions are not uniform,
and humorous words are boundless.
In the past, when Huá Yuán (華元) abandoned his armor,
the city dwellers sang songs with glaring eyes;
when Zāng Hē (臧紇) lost a battle,
the people of the state created songs about dwarfs.
Both mocked physical appearances,
turning inner resentment into jesting.
Furthermore, vulgar sayings about silkworms and crabs,
and lewd songs about civet cats,
if they can be used for admonishment,
are recorded in the classics.
Therefore, it is known that humorous sayings and riddling words
are also not to be discarded.
The word "xié (諧)" means "all."
Language that is shallow and meets the customs
brings joy and laughter to all.
In the past, Qí Wēi (齊威) indulged in pleasure,
and Chúnyú Yuè (淳于說) spoke of sweet wine;
Chǔ Xiāng (楚襄) gathered for feasts,
and Sòng Yù (宋玉) composed about a love for beauty.
The intention was subtle satire,
and there was something worth seeing in it.
And Yōu Zhān's (優旃) satire on the painted city,
and Yōu Mèng's (優孟) admonishment about burying the horse,
both used cunning words and embellished explanations
to restrain foolish tyranny.
Therefore, Zǐcháng (子長, i.e., Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷) compiled history
and included a biography of "Huá Jī" (《滑稽》, "Jesters"),
because although their words were distorted,
their intentions returned to righteousness and correctness.
However, since the essence is not elegant,
its current easily becomes corrupt.
Therefore, Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) and Méi Gāo (枚皋),
ate dregs and drank thin wine,
without correcting anything,
but instead slandered and made disrespectful jests.
Therefore, what they called fù (賦)
was actually also pai (俳, jesting).
Being seen as merely entertainers,
they also had regrets.
As for Wèi Wén (魏文) composing "Xiào Shū" (《笑書》, "Book of Laughter") based on jesting tales,
and Xuē Zōng (薛綜) issuing mocking jokes during banquets,
although there was clapping, laughter, and joyful clothing,
it did nothing to benefit the times.
However, even those with beautiful writing
could not avoid being led astray;
things like Pān Yuè's (潘岳) "Chǒu Fù" (《醜婦》, "Ugly Woman"),
and types like Shù Xī's (束晳) "Mài Bǐng" (《賣餅》, "Selling Cakes"),
went even further and imitated them,
numbering in the hundreds.
The jesters of the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties
greatly encouraged each other.
Consequently, Yìng Yáng's (應瑒) nose
was compared to a robber slicing eggs;
and Zhāng Huá's (張華) form
was compared to holding a pestle for hulling grain.
This was truly like noxious weeds,
impairing virtuous words.
Could it not be the reckless laughter of those drowning,
and the wild songs of the convicts?
Yǐn (讔) means yǐn (隱),
or hidden;
using evasive language to conceal meaning,
employing cunning metaphors to indicate matters.
In the past, Huán Shè (還社) sought rescue from the Chǔ (楚) army,
using the metaphor of a dry well and calling it màiqu (麥麴);
Shū Yí (叔儀) begged for grain from the Lǔ (魯) people,
singing about jade pendants and calling out gēng guǐ (庚癸);
Wǔ Jǔ (伍舉) satirized the Jīng (荊) king with a large bird,
a Qí (齊) guest mocked Lord Xuē (薛) with a sea fish,
Zhuāng Jī (莊姬) entrusted her words to the Dragon Tail Star,
Zāng Wén (臧文) mistakenly wrote on a sheepskin coat.
The use of hidden language
is recorded in chronicles and biographies.
The great use of it leads to the rise of governance and benefits the self,
the lesser use of it assists in correcting errors and clarifying doubts.
Indeed, meaning arises from expediency and stratagem,
and matters stem from timely wit and urgency,
together with humorous language,
which can complement each other.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the "Book of Hidden Language" 《隱書》
had eighteen chapters.
Xīn Gù (歆固) compiled the text,
and recorded it at the end of his rhymeprose compositions.
In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ (楚莊) and King Wēi of Qí (齊威)
were by nature fond of hidden language.
As for Dōngfāng Mànqiàn (東方曼倩),
he was particularly skilled in descriptive language.
However, absurd and derogatory language
is of no benefit for guidance or supplementation.
Since the Wèi (魏) dynasty and later,
it has been regarded as something other than acting,
and the cultured's jesting and concealing
has transformed into riddles.
A riddle is
the revolving and alternating of words,
causing confusion and bewilderment.
Sometimes it takes the form of written characters,
or depicted images and items,
subtle tricks to toy with the mind,
shallow observations to flaunt language,
the meaning should be gentle yet upright,
the words should be hidden yet clear.
Xún Qīng's (荀卿) "Ode to the Silkworm" 《蠶賦》
already foreshadowed its form.
During the time of Wèi Wén (魏文) and Chén Sī (陳思),
it was concise and precise;
the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng (高貴鄉公)
extensively cited various items.
Though there was some ingenuity,
its use deviated from the grand and far-reaching.
When we observe the ancient use of hidden language,
its principles encompass essential affairs.
How could it be a childish jest,
slapping thighs and laughing aloud?
However, the presence of humor and hidden meaning in literary compositions
is like the presence of minor tales among the Nine Schools;
they are gathered by the writers of unofficial histories
to broaden sight and sound.
If one imitates them without end,
then one would be like shaving the head and baring the shoulders to enter the room,
the friendship of Zhān Mèng (旃孟) would be like stone!
In praise:
The mocking and concealing of the ancients
revived dangers and relieved weariness.
Though there are silk and hemp,
do not discard coarse grasses.
Understanding the meaning and fitting the time,
it greatly benefits admonishments and warnings.
Empty jesting and buffoonery
greatly ruin virtuous sounds.
Chapter Sixteen: History and Biographies
In the opening of the primitive mists,
the ages stretched out long and far.
To reside in the present and know the past,
it is through the records.
In the era of Xuānyuán (軒轅),
there was the historian Cāng Jié (蒼頡),
whose duty was to oversee writing.
Its origins are long ago.
The *Qū Lǐ* (曲禮) says:
"Historians carry brushes."
The historian,
is a messenger;
holding a brush to the left and right,
they are used to record.
In ancient times, the left historian recorded words,
the right historian wrote matters.
Words that pass through the classics are the *Shàngshū* (尚書),
matters that pass through the classics are the *Chūnqiū* (春秋).
The Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) flowed into the *Diǎn Mó* (典謨),
the Xià (夏) and Shāng (商) were recorded in proclamations and oaths.
When the Zhōu (周) mandate was renewed,
Duke Jī (姬) established the laws,
drawing from the Three Dynasties to distribute the calendar,
and stringing together the four seasons to connect events.
The feudal lords established states,
each with its own state history,
manifesting good and abhorring evil,
establishing a reputation for them.
Since King Píng (平) was weak,
his administration did not reach correctness,
rules and regulations were scattered and disordered,
and moral principles were abandoned.
In the past, Master Kǒng (孔) lamented the deficiency of the kingly way,
and grieved the decline of this culture,
dwelling in silence to sigh at the phoenix,
and weeping at the unicorn in the streets.
Therefore, he went to the grand master to correct the *Yǎ* (雅) and *Sòng* (頌),
and relied on the history of Lǔ (魯) to revise the *Chūnqiū* (春秋),
raising gains and losses to show promotion and demotion,
and examining survival and extinction to mark encouragement and warning;
praise seen in a single word
is worth more than carriages and official hats;
blame found in a single phrase
is like a punishment deeper than axes and hatchets.
However, the wise intent is deep and hidden,
the classic text is gentle and restrained,
Qiū Míng (丘明), who was contemporary to Master Kǒng,
truly grasped the subtle words;
therefore, he traced the origin and reached the end,
creating the commentary style.
Commentary,
is to transmit;
transmitting and receiving the classic intent,
to bestow it upon posterity,
truly the wings and feathers of the sagely texts,
and the crown and hat of the records.
Even in the era of alliances and counter-alliances,
the office of the historian still existed.
When Qín conquered the seven kingdoms,
the Warring States period had its *Cè*.
These likely recorded events without narrating them,
hence their simple and concise titles.
When Hàn destroyed Yíng and Xiàng,
after years of military achievements,
Lù Jiǎ researched the ancient past
and wrote *Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū*.
Then came Tài Shǐ Tán,
who only kept records,
and his son, Zǐcháng, continued his aspirations,
carefully arranging the achievements of emperors.
To compare him to Yáo using *Diǎn*,
would place him among the worthy officials;
to follow Kǒngzǐ in titling classics,
would make his writing unprofound.
Thus, he took the model of *Lǚ Lǎn*,
generally calling them *Jì*,
the name *Jìgāng*,
which is also a grand title.
Therefore, *běnjì* is used to narrate emperors and kings,
*lièzhuàn* to compile accounts of lords and nobles,
*Bā Shū* to elaborate on political systems,
*Shí Biǎo* to chronicle years and ranks.
Although different from ancient forms,
they achieve an orderly account of events.
Indeed, his work embodies the principle of recording without concealment,
the talent of broad learning and eloquent reasoning,
the tendency to love the unusual and rebel against convention,
and the flaw of scattered and imprecise organization,
as Shū Pí has discussed in detail.
When Bān Gù wrote the *Hàn Shū*,
he followed the previous work.
Observing Sīmǎ Qiān's writing,
his thoughts were more than half based on reality.
His *Shí Zhì* are comprehensive and rich,
his prefaces and eulogies magnificent and beautiful,
his elegance refined,
truly leaving behind a lasting flavor.
As for his adherence to the classics as a standard and the sagely as a model,
his merit in establishing a complete framework,
his fault in neglecting relatives to praise others,
and his offense of seeking bribes and selling his pen,
public reason has judged thoroughly.
Consider how Zuǒ Qiūmíng connected events,
interspersing them within the *Jīng*,
making the writing concise,
but leaving the clans difficult to understand.
When Sīmǎ Qiān wrote individual biographies,
people began to see detailed and easy-to-read accounts,
and subsequent narrators followed his example.
When Xiàohuì delegated authority
and Empress Lǚ took control of the government,
the historians Bān followed suit in their *Jì*,
both violating the truth of the classics.
Why?
Since Páo Xī,
there has never been a female emperor.
The Hàn dynasty's fortune was such that
it is difficult to make it a model for later generations.
"The hen does not announce the morning,"
was the first oath of King Wǔ;
"Women should not participate in state affairs,"
was the covenant set forth by Duke Huán of Qí;
Empress Xuān brought chaos to Qín,
and the Lǚ clan endangered Hàn.
It is not only that political affairs should not be entrusted lightly,
but also that titles should be carefully considered.
Zhāng Héng, as the historian,
either agreed with Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
or wanted to establish *Jì* for the two empresses who leveled the imperial line in the first year,
which is also greatly mistaken.
This is also a great error.
Although Zǐ Hóng's lineage is spurious,
he was still the successor to Emperor Xiàohuì;
Rúzǐ was indeed insignificant,
but he did succeed Emperor Píng.
These two sons can be recorded,
so why the two empresses?
As for the *Hòu Hàn Shū*'s *Jì* and *Zhuàn*,
they originated from the *Dōng Guān*.
The works of Yuán and Zhāng
were biased and uneven.
The writings of Xuē and Xiè
were superficial, flawed, and lacked credibility.
If one seeks detail and accuracy, like Sīmǎ Biāo's work,
or precision and appropriateness, like Huá Qiáo's,
then those are the best.
During the Wei Dynasty,
records and biographies emerged in abundance.
Works such as the *Yáng Qiū* and *Wèi Lüè*,
and the *Jiāng Biǎo* and *Wú Lù*,
were either vehemently controversial and difficult to verify,
or superficial and lacking in essential points.
Only Chén Shòu's *Sān Zhì*
had a refined and balanced style,
leading Xún and Zhāng to compare him to Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
which is not an undeserved compliment.
As for the books of the Jìn dynasty,
they were entrusted to the *Zhù Zuò*.
Lù Jī began the work but did not complete it,
Wáng Sháo continued it but did not finish.
Gān Bǎo, in narrating *Jì*,
sought to be thorough in correctness and order;
Sūn Shèng's *Yáng Qiū*
aimed for skillful summarization.
Based on the *Chūnqiū* and its *Jīngzhuàn*,
he cited examples to explain general principles.
From *Shǐ Jì* and *Hàn Shū* onward,
there has been no standard.
It was not until Dèng Càn's *Jìn Jì*
that regulations were first established.
Furthermore, it abandoned the Hàn and Wèi models,
and took the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties as its norms.
Even though it was a provincial work from Xiāngzhōu,
it still aspired to the model of *Diǎn Mó*.
When Ān Guó established precedents,
they followed Dèng's regulations.
Originally, the creation of written records
must encompass the hundred schools
and be passed down for thousands of years,
manifesting prosperity and decline,
providing a mirror for rise and fall,
so that the institutions of a generation
may endure with the sun and moon,
and the deeds of kings and hegemons
may last as long as heaven and earth.
Therefore, at the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
the office of the historian was highly regarded.
The records and statistics from the commanderies and kingdoms
were first gathered in the office of the Grand Historian,
so that he could have a detailed understanding of the state.
Examining the stone chambers,
opening the golden cabinets,
unrolling the silk,
inspecting the bamboo slips,
was to ensure broad and practiced research into the past.
Therefore, in establishing principles and selecting words,
one should rely on the classics to set the standard;
in encouraging or discouraging, rewarding or punishing,
one must adhere to the sages as the foundation;
only then can interpretation and evaluation be clear and orderly,
and excessive or unfair judgments be avoided.
However, with annals and biographies as the format,
compiling events chronologically,
the writing should not be a general discussion,
but rather based on facts.
As years pass, it becomes difficult to closely examine similarities and differences,
and as events accumulate, it becomes easy to overlook beginnings and endings;
this is indeed the difficulty of comprehensive compilation.
Sometimes, the same event is attributed to several individuals,
and several people share the credit.
To record it in both accounts would lead to redundancy,
while to mention only one would be incomplete;
this is the difficulty of proper allocation.
Therefore, Zhāng Héng pointed out the errors and exaggerations of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
and Fù Xuán criticized the excessive detail of the *Hòu Hàn Shū*;
these are all examples of this kind.
As for recounting the distant past,
the further back in time, the more falsehoods there are.
Gōngyáng Gāo said,
"Transmitted accounts differ."
Xún Kuàng stated,
"Record what is recent and omit what is distant."
For doubtful passages, it is better to leave them out and
value reliable history.
However, people generally love the unusual,
not caring about true principles.
In transmitting accounts, they want to magnify the events,
and in recording the distant past, they want to detail the traces,
thus abandoning what is the same and embracing what is different,
making conjectures and citing side accounts.
"What the old history does not have,
my book will transmit"—
this is the source of errors and exaggerations,
and the great blight of recounting the distant past.
As for recording events of the same era,
it is easy for falsehoods to arise,
even with the subtle words of Duke Dìng and Duke Āi,
because of worldly interests and harms.
Families with meritorious achievements,
even the mediocre are fully embellished;
scholars who have suffered setbacks,
even those of great virtue are slandered and buried.
Bestowing frost or warmth,
cold or heat, is at the tip of the pen;
this is the injustice of contemporary records,
which is lamentable.
Therefore, recounting the distant past leads to such falsehoods,
and recording the recent past leads to such distortions;
to analyze principles and remain impartial,
one must have a pure heart!
To respect the worthy and conceal [their] faults
was indeed the sagacious intention of Ní Fù 尼父;
for minor flaws cannot tarnish a jade ornament.
To punish and warn against the wicked
is truly the straightforward writing of a good historian.
When a farmer sees weeds,
he will certainly hoe them out.
Such principles
are a standard for all ages.
As for the skill of seeking simplicity in complexity,
the importance of adhering to facts and discarding the bizarre,
the clear order of beginning and end,
the careful consideration of precedents and examples,
if one understands their main points,
then all principles can be connected.
However, the responsibility of history
is to encompass an entire era,
to bear the responsibility for everything within the realm,
and to incur the greatest amount of censure.
To hold the writing brush and bear the burden
is more laborious than anything else.
Si Qian 遷固 (Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷 and Bān Gù 班固) were thorough,
yet were consistently criticized by later generations.
If one indulges emotions and deviates from correctness,
the writing will be perilous!
Commentary:
History began with Xuān Yuán 軒轅,
and its structure was perfected by Zhōu 周 and Kǒng 孔.
The world has been recorded in these books;
good and evil are all included.
Praise is bestowed, and blame is meted out;
for ten thousand ages, spirits are stirred.
The style follows Qiū Míng 丘明,
and the honesty returns to Nán Dǒng 南董.
The Philosophers, Number Seventeen
The philosophers are
books that reveal the will of those who entered the Way.
The highest is to establish virtue;
the next is to establish words.
The masses who live together
suffer from confusion and obscurity;
the gentleman who lives in the world
is concerned that his reputation and virtue are not manifest.
Only outstanding talents
shine brightly and leave behind writings,
spreading their names
and hanging them like the sun and moon.
In the past, Fēng Hòu 風后, Lì Mù 力牧, and Yī Yǐn 伊尹
all belonged to this category.
Their written accounts
are ancient sayings
recorded during the Warring States period.
When Yù Xióng 鬻熊 understood the Way,
and Wén Wáng 文王 consulted him,
the remaining writings and anecdotes
were recorded as *Yùzǐ* 《鬻子》.
Among the philosophers,
nothing predates this.
When Bó Yáng 伯陽 understood ritual,
and Zhòng Ní 仲尼 inquired of him,
he then arranged morality and virtue
to be the foremost of the hundred schools.
Thus, Yù was merely a literary friend,
while Lǐ 李 was actually Kǒng's 孔 teacher.
Sages and worthies coexisted,
but the classics and the philosophers diverged into different streams.
During the time of the Seven Warring States,
talented individuals emerged in swarms.
Mèng Kē 孟軻 embraced Confucianism with humility,
Zhuāng Zhōu 莊周 expounded the Way and soared freely,
Mò Dí 墨翟 adhered to a frugal and steadfast doctrine,
Yǐn Wén 尹文 assessed the correspondence between names and realities,
the rustic old man governed the state through geographical advantages,
Zōu Zǐ 騶子 cultivated governance through astronomy,
Shēn Shāng 申商 used knives and saws to establish order,
Guǐ Gǔ 鬼谷 used rhetoric to plan meritorious deeds,
Shī Jiǎo 尸佼 comprehensively mastered various techniques,
and the court historians crookedly pieced together street gossip.
Those who followed and branched out
were too numerous to count.
They all flew with eloquence and raced with techniques,
indulging in generous salaries and abundant honors.
When the violent Qín 秦 dynasty used raging fire,
its power blazed like Kūnlún 崑崙 mountain,
but the poison of the flames
did not reach the philosophers.
When Hàn 漢 Chéng 漢成 (Hàn Chéngdì 漢成帝) extensively pondered and
Zǐ Zhèng 子政 collated and proofread,
the *Qī Lüè* 《七略》 then flourished,
and the nine streams gathered like scales,
the bamboo slips that were compiled
numbered more than one hundred and eighty schools.
Until the Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉 dynasties,
authors emerged intermittently,
wild words were preserved,
and trivial sayings were recorded.
Classifying and searching for them
could fill boxes and load wagons.
Although voluminous words accumulated,
the main body is easy to summarize:
describing the Way and discussing governance
are branches of the *Five Classics* 《五經》.
Those that are pure enter the square,
while those that are flawed deviate from the compass.
*Lǐjì‧Yuèlìng* 《禮記‧月令》 takes
from the records of *Lǚshì* 《呂氏》;
*Sān Nián Wèn* 《三年問》 on mourning
copies from the book of *Xúnzǐ* 《荀子》;
these are examples of the pure.
As for Tāng's 湯 question to Jí 棘,
saying that the eyelash of a mosquito has the sound of thunder;
Huì Shī's 惠施 response to the King of Liáng 梁,
saying that on a snail's horn there is a battle with corpses lying prone;
*Lièzǐ* 《列子》 has talk of moving mountains and crossing seas;
*Huáinán* 《淮南》 has sayings of overturning the sky and breaking the earth;
these are examples of the flawed.
Therefore, the world despises the philosophers
for their chaotic and empty exaggerations.
Examining the classic of *Guī Cáng* 《歸藏》,
it greatly clarifies the eccentric and strange,
even claiming that Yì 羿 shot down ten suns
and Héng'é 姮娥 fled to the moon.
The *Yīn Yì* 《殷易》 is like this;
how much more so the philosophers!
As for *Shāng* 《商》 and *Hán* 《韓》,
the "Six Lice" and "Five Vermin,"
abandoning filial piety and discarding benevolence,
the disaster of dismemberment for selling medicine
was not a false occurrence.
Gōngsūn's 公孫 "White Horse" and "Lone Calf,"
with clever words but clumsy logic,
Wèi Mú 魏牟 compared them to owls;
it was not a groundless disparagement.
In the past, Dōngpíng 東平 sought the philosophers' *Shǐjì* 《史記》,
but the Hàn 漢 dynasty did not grant it.
This was because *Shǐjì* 《史記》 contained many military strategies,
while the philosophers mixed in deceitful techniques.
However, learned scholars
should grasp the main points,
examine the flowers and eat the fruit,
discard the heretical and adopt the correct,
and thoroughly discern the discrepancies;
this is also a grand spectacle for students of learning.
Investigating what Mèng (孟) and Xún (荀) described,
their principles are excellent and their language refined;
the chapters of Guǎn (管) and Yàn (晏)
concern matters of fact and their words are polished;
the book of Liè Yǔkòu (列御寇),
has grandeur in spirit and extraordinary brilliance in its writing;
the doctrines of Zōu Zǐ (鄒子),
have extravagant ideas and powerful language;
Mò Dí (墨翟) and Suí Cháo (隨巢),
have clear intentions and simple words;
Shī Jiǎo (尸佼) and Wèi Liáo (尉繚),
have comprehensive strategies but their writing is dull;
*Hé Guān* (鶡冠) is continuous and profound,
frequently expressing deep insights;
*Guǐ Gǔ* (鬼谷) is vast and obscure,
repeatedly circling its meaning;
with acute discernment and eloquent expression,
Wén Zǐ (文子) excels in his abilities;
with concise and refined language,
Yǐn Wén (尹文) grasped its essence;
Shèn Dào (慎到) analyzes with ingenious precision,
Hán Fēi (韓非) is known for the richness of his extensive analogies,
*Lǚ Shì* (呂氏) is far-sighted and comprehensive in its structure,
*Huáinán* (淮南) widely gathers and its writing is beautiful;
this then is to obtain the brilliant essence of a hundred schools,
and the general outline of their diction and spirit.
As for Lù Jiǎ's (陸賈) *Xīn Yǔ* (新語),
Jiǎ Yì's (賈誼) *Xīn Shū* (新書),
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) *Fǎ Yán* (法言),
Liú Xiàng's (劉向) *Shuō Yuàn* (說苑),
Wáng Fú's (王符) *Qián Fū* (潛夫),
Cuī Shí's (崔寔) *Zhèng Lùn* (正論),
Zhòngcháng's (仲長) *Chāng Yán* (昌言),
Dù Yí's (杜夷) *Yōu Qiú* (幽求),
all expound on the classics,
or elucidate political strategies,
although they bear the name of essays,
they belong to the philosophers.
Why is this?
To broadly understand myriad affairs is to be a philosopher (子),
to appropriately discern a single principle is to be an essay (論);
these all extensively mix various theories,
therefore they enter the stream of philosophical works.
Before the Six States (六國),
it was not far from the sages,
therefore they were able to discourse loftily, surpassing their era,
and opening their own windows.
After the Two Han dynasties (兩漢),
the style and momentum gradually weakened,
although they understood the clear path,
they mostly relied on borrowing.
This is the gradual change from near to far.
Alas!
The person is at odds with the times,
but the will shares the way;
setting one's heart above ten thousand ages,
and sending one's thoughts to a thousand years hence,
gold and stone will decay,
will their voices be silenced?
A eulogy:
A great man living in the world,
cherishes his treasure and stands out in excellence.
Discriminatingly carving the myriad things,
his wisdom encompasses the universe.
Establishing virtue, why hide it?
Holding the Dao, it must be imparted.
The different schools have various explanations,
as if there are boundaries and enclosures.
Discourse: Chapter 18
The constant teachings of the Sages and Worthies are called Jīng (經),
and expounding on Jīng and elucidating principles is called Lùn (論).
A Lùn
is a lún (倫),
meaning a principle or an order;
if the ethical principles are flawless, then the sagely intent will not perish.
In ancient times, when Zhòngní spoke in subtle words,
his disciples recorded them later;
thus, its Jīng title was suppressed,
and it was called the Lúnyǔ (論語);
this was probably the beginning of naming collections of Lùn.
From before the Lúnyǔ,
the character lùn (論) was not found in Jīng titles;
as for the Liù Tāo (六韜) and Èr Lùn (二論),
were they later titles added by subsequent generations?
A detailed examination of the Lùn form
reveals many types:
those that present policies align with Yì (議) and Shuō (說);
those that interpret Jīng combine with Zhuàn (傳) and Zhù (注);
those that analyze history proceed in parallel with Zàn (贊) and Píng (評);
and those that evaluate literature are recorded alongside Xù (序) and Yǐn (引).
Thus, the Yì (議) speaks appropriately;
the Shuō (說) narrates words;
the Zhuàn (傳) transmits the master's teachings;
the Zhù (注) focuses on explanation;
the Zàn (贊) clarifies meaning;
the Píng (評) assesses reason;
the Xù (序) orders events;
and the Yǐn (引) extends discourse.
Though these eight names are distinct,
they all adhere to the same principle as Lùn.
A Lùn
encompasses all words,
and refines a single principle.
This is why Zhuāng Zhōu's (莊周) Qí Wù (齊物)
took Lùn as its name;
Bù Wéi's (不韋) Chūnqiū (春秋)
clearly listed six Lùn;
then, the discussions on arts at Shíqú (石渠)
and the lectures at Báihǔ (白虎),
expounding on the Sages and comprehending the Jīng,
represent the proper form of Lùn writers.
As for Bān Biāo's (班彪) Wáng Mìng (王命)
and Yán Yóu's (嚴尤) Sān Jiàng (三將),
they elaborate on emotions,
skillfully entering into the historical form.
When Wèi (魏) first established its hegemony,
its methods combined Míngjiā (名家) and Fǎjiā (法家) schools;
Fù Gǔ (傅嘏) and Wáng Càn (王粲)
analyzed and practiced nominal principles.
By the Zhèngshǐ (正始) era,
the focus was on preserving texts;
Hè Yàn (何晏) and his followers
began to extensively promote Xuánlùn (玄論).
Thereupon, Dān (聃) and Zhōu (周) were in ascendancy,
contending with Nífù (尼父) for prominence.
A detailed look at Lán (蘭) and Shí's (石) talents and dispositions,
Zhòngxuān's (仲宣) Qù Fá (去伐),
Shúyè's (叔夜) Biàn Shēng (辨聲),
Tàichū's (太初) Běn Xuán (本玄),
Fǔsì's (輔嗣) two Lì (例),
and Píngshú's (平叔) two Lùn,
all demonstrate independent thought and unique insights,
with keen and precise arguments,
truly the luminaries among humankind.
As for Lǐ Kāng's (李康) Yùn Mìng (運命),
it is similar to Lùn Héng (論衡) but surpasses it;
Lù Jī's (陸機) Biàn Wáng (辨亡),
emulates Guò Qín (過秦) but falls short;
yet, they are still beautiful in their own right.
Next, Sòng Dài (宋岱) and Guō Xiàng (郭象)
sharpened their thoughts in the realm of subtle spirits;
Yífǔ (夷甫) and Péi Wěi (裴頠)
debated intensely in the domain of being and non-being;
all of them were preeminent in their time,
leaving a lasting reputation for later generations.
However, those who adhered to existence were entirely bound by concrete forms and functions,
while those who valued non-being exclusively clung to emptiness and tranquility.
They merely sharpened partial understandings,
none reaching the true principle.
To profoundly stir the source of the spirit,
isn't that the ultimate state of Bānruò (般若)?
Later, the collective discussions south of the Jiāng (江),
were solely focused on Xuán (玄);
although there was daily innovation,
many merely extracted from earlier threads.
As for Zhāng Héng's (張衡) Jī Shì (譏世),
its style resembles satirical discourse;
Kǒng Róng's (孔融) Xiàolián (孝廉)
merely engaged in jesting talk;
Cáo Zhí's (曹植) Biàn Dào (辨道)
had a form similar to transcribed notes;
if talent cannot sustain a Lùn,
how can it be considered adequate?
Originally, the form of Lùn
is to distinguish right from wrong,
to exhaust what is numerable,
to pursue what is formless,
to trace the firm and seek the comprehensible,
to delve deep and grasp the ultimate;
it is the trap and snare for a hundred thoughts,
and the balance and scale for myriad affairs.
Therefore, its meaning must be comprehensive and fluent,
and its words should avoid fragmentation;
it must ensure that the mind and principle are integrated,
so seamlessly that no gaps are visible;
the words and mind must be closely aligned,
so that opponents cannot find an advantage;
this is its essential point.
Thus, a Lùn is like splitting firewood,
it is crucial to be able to break through the principle.
A sharp axe
can cut across the grain;
eloquent words
can reverse meaning to achieve understanding;
though the writing may seem clever,
upon closer examination, its falsity is known.
Only a Jūnzǐ (君子) can understand the will of all under Heaven,
how can one use crooked arguments?
As for notes and commentaries as words,
they dissect the Lùn form;
though the miscellaneous texts vary,
their overall purpose is the same.
For example, Qín Yánjūn's (秦延君) commentary on Yáo Diǎn (堯典)
was over a hundred thousand characters;
Zhū Pǔ's (朱普) explanation of Shàng Shū (尚書)
was three hundred thousand words;
for this reason, knowledgeable people dislike such verbosity
and are ashamed to study mere chapters and sentences.
However, Máo Gōng's (毛公) annotations on Shī (詩),
Ānguó's (安國) commentary on Shū (書),
Zhèng Jūn's (鄭君) interpretations of Lǐ (禮),
and Wáng Bì's (王弼) explanations of Yì (易),
are concise and clear,
and can serve as models.
Persuasion (shuō)
is delight (yuè);
Duì represents the mouth and tongue,
thus speech relies on pleasing and delighting.
Excessive pleasing inevitably leads to falseness,
hence Shùn was alarmed by slanderous persuasion.
Among the good practitioners of persuasion:
Yī Yǐn, by discussing flavors, brought prosperity to Yīn;
Tài Gōng, by discoursing on fishing, made Zhōu flourish;
and Zhú Wǔ's mission relieved Zhèng;
Duānmù's departure saved Lǔ.
These are also its merits.
When the Warring States
competed for supremacy, debaters emerged like clouds;
they participated in Zònghéng
strategies, contending with their strengths and weaknesses;
Zhuǎnwán displayed its clever rhetoric,
Fēiqián concealed its subtle art.
The persuasion of one person
was valued more than the treasures of the Jiǔ Dǐng;
a three-inch tongue
was stronger than an army of a million;
six seals were grandly worn,
five great cities were granted as fiefs, prosperous and hidden.
By the time Hàn pacified Qín and Chǔ,
debaters had restrained their influence.
Master Lì had already perished in Qí's cauldron,
and Master Kuǎi nearly entered Hàn's cauldron.
Although Lù Jiǎ
was highly renowned, Zhāng Shì
was adept at adapting to circumstances, Dù Qīn
was eloquent and argumentative, and Lóu Hù
was skillful with his tongue.
and breathed upon the seats of dukes and ministers;
all relied on the favorable wind to gain momentum,
none could go against the current.
Persuasion values accommodation,
with flexibility and firmness following each other.
It does not solely rely on gentle speech,
but also on official documents.
Fàn Suī's advice on affairs,
Lǐ Sī's stopping the expulsion of foreign guests,
both carefully considered the crucial points,
and their every word hit the mark.
Although they touched the emperor's inverted scale,
their achievements were complete and their plans successful.
This is excellent persuasion in memorials.
As for Zōu Yáng's persuasion of Wú and Liáng,
his analogies were clever and his principles profound,
therefore, although he was in danger, he incurred no blame.
Jìng Tōng's persuasion of Bào and Dèng,
though the matter was not urgent, his writing was elaborate;
that is why he exerted himself for a long time but rarely met with success.
The core essentials of all persuasion
must ensure that the timing is favorable and the principles are upright.
When advancing, it must conform to the task at hand;
when retreating, it must not hinder one's honor.
Unless outwitting an enemy,
then it is solely about loyalty and trustworthiness.
Offering one's heart and liver (sincerity) to the lord,
and employing eloquent and agile writing to aid one's discourse;
this is the foundation of persuasion.
Yet Master Lù directly called persuasion "brilliant yet deceitful,"
why is this?
Eulogy says:
Principles take form in words,
explaining principles forms an argument.
Words penetrate to man and heaven,
reaching far from an inch (of the heart).
Yīn and Yáng
are not dual, spirits and gods do not flee.
Persuasion, your Fēiqián,
discourages or encourages in an instant.
Edicts, Chapter Nineteen
When the emperor governs the realm,
his words are divine.
Silent behind the embroidered screen,
yet his voice echoes throughout the four quarters,
all through his edicts and pronouncements!
In ancient times, during the eras of Xuānyuán and Táng Yú,
these were collectively called "mìng."
The meaning of mìng
is the foundation of regulating one's nature.
During the Three Dynasties,
it encompassed both "gào" and "shì."
Shì were used to instruct the military,
gào to announce policies,
and mìng were likened to coming from Heaven,
thus they were used to grant offices and bestow heirs.
The "Gòu" hexagram in the *Yìjīng* states:
"The sovereign issues commands and proclamations to the four quarters."
Gào and mìng move the people,
like the wind blowing across the world.
Down to the Seven Warring States,
all were called mìng.
Mìng
means "to send" or "to command."
When Qín unified the realm,
mìng was changed to "zhì."
In the early Hàn dynasty, when rituals and regulations were established,
mìng had four categories:
First, cèshū (investiture texts);
second, zhìshū (imperial decrees);
third, zhàoshū (imperial edicts);
and fourth, jièchì (admonitions and injunctions).
Chì warned and instructed prefectures and commanderies;
zhào proclaimed to all officials;
zhì issued pardons;
and cè enfeoffed kings and marquises.
Cè
means "to choose" or "to simplify."
Zhì
means "to regulate" or "to decide."
Zhào
means "to announce" or "to tell."
Chì
means "to correct" or "to regulate."
The *Shījīng* says:
"Fear this cèshū."
The *Yìjīng* states:
"The noble person thereby sets up rules and measures."
The *Lǐjì* says:
"Proclamations of the bright spirits."
The *Shūjīng* says:
"To uphold the mandate of Heaven."
All these names were established based on the classics.
Calling distant commands "zhào" and close ones "mìng"
was following the Qín system.
Records refer to "sīlún" (imperial pronouncements),
which were used to respond to and interact with the various lords.
Yú (Shùn) valued "nàyán" (accepting advice),
and Zhōu esteemed "hóushé" (the imperial spokesman).
Therefore, in both the Western and Eastern Hàn, imperial edicts and proclamations
were the responsibility of the Shàngshū (Grand Minister Secretary).
The great words of the ruler
were immediately recorded in historical annals.
Their issuance was like a rope drawing water,
and their non-recall was like sweat, unable to be reabsorbed.
This is why Huáinán had brilliant talents,
and Emperor Wǔ sent Sīmǎ Xiāngrú to draft documents;
Lǒngyòu had many literati,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ paid special attention to their writings;
this was not merely to seek beauty at the time,
but also to show reverence and caution for future generations.
Looking at the period before Emperors Wén and Jǐng,
the style of imperial edicts was often shallow and mixed.
Emperor Wǔ honored Confucianism,
and his choice of words became grand and profound.
His cè for enfeoffing the Three Kings
had a style similar to ancient canons;
his admonitions were deep and elegant,
setting a standard for later generations.
When he issued a zhì and gào to Yán Zhù,
he even said he was tired of "Chéngmíng Lú" (the imperial study);
this was an act of favor to talent.
Emperor Xiàoxuān's xǐshū (sealed letter),
which rebuked Chén Suì for his extensive knowledge,
also showed the warmth of old acquaintances.
By the time Emperor Guāngwǔ suppressed the chaos,
he paid attention to such literary matters,
but in his haste, his joys and angers
sometimes led to partiality and excess.
When he issued a zhào to Dèng Yǔ,
he praised Sītú (Grand Minister over the Masses) as Yáo;
when he issued a chì to Hóu Bà,
he said, "Once the yellow axe descends."
Such instances
truly deviated from the constitutional principles.
When Emperors Míng and Zhāng honored learning,
elegant zhào were occasionally issued.
When Emperors Hé and Ān's governance slackened,
and there were few talents in the imperial court,
whenever zhào and chì were needed,
they would borrow hands from outside requests.
At the end of the Jiàn'ān era,
literary styles flourished anew.
Pān Xù's *Jiǔxī* (Nine Bestowals)
was elegant and outstanding.
Wèi Jì's *Chángào* (Edict of Abdication)
was brilliant and splendid in its style,
nothing could surpass it.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, gào and cè
were the responsibility of the Zhōngshū (Central Secretariat).
Liú Fàng and Zhāng Huá
alternately managed this responsibility,
issuing decrees and commands,
their words filling the ears.
When Emperor Wèi Wén issued zhào,
his words and meanings were often magnificent,
but as for "wielding power and conferring blessings,"
was that one of his myriad flaws?
During the restoration of the Jìn dynasty,
only Emperor Míng revered talent.
Because Wēn Jiǎo's writings were pure,
he was consequently brought into the Zhōngshū.
From then on,
the imperial style and character became refined.
The words of the ruler are profoundly secret,
a grand spectacle from above,
so that all officials take them as their model,
and all states put their trust in them.
Therefore, when granting office and selecting the worthy,
their meaning shines with the brilliance of a double sun;
when composing elegant documents for enfeoffment cè,
their spirit contains the moistness of wind and rain;
when issuing chì and constant gào,
the brush spews forth the splendor of stars and rivers;
when managing the army and suppressing invasions,
their voice has the majesty of rolling thunder;
when pardoning calamities and faults,
their words have the nourishment of spring dew;
when clarifying punishments and rectifying laws,
their words have the severity of autumn frost;
this is the general outline of zhào and cè.
Chì and jiè writings
are the most urgent of zhào.
King Mù of Zhōu commanded Jiāofù to receive chì and xìan (ordinances);
this is an example of it.
Wèi Wǔ said that when writing chì and jiè, one should address specific matters,
and not be vague;
this shows he understood the essence of governance.
When Emperor Jìn Wǔ issued chì and jiè,
he fully informed all officials:
he enjoined dūdū (military governors) on military essentials,
admonished zhōu mù (provincial governors) on their oversight,
warned jùn shǒu (commandery administrators) to care for the vulnerable,
and ordered yámén (officials in charge of military guards) to defend the capital.
These contained instructional principles.
Jiè
means "caution" or "to be careful."
Yǔ said, "Be cautious in using auspiciousness."
The sovereign and father are most exalted,
and in the three generations, they reached the same apex.
Hàn Gāozǔ's *Chì Tàizǐ* (Injunction to the Crown Prince)
and Dōngfāng Shuò's *Jiè Zǐ* (Admonition to My Son)
were also composed as dying instructions.
And from Mǎ Yuán onwards,
many left behind "family admonitions."
Bān Jī's *Nǚjiè* (Admonitions for Women)
can truly be called a maternal teacher.
Jiào
means "to imitate" or "to emulate," meaning that when words are issued, the people emulate them.
Qì spread the Five Teachings,
which is why kings and marquises refer to "jiào."
In ancient times, when Zhèng Hóng served as Nányáng administrator,
his articles of instruction were recounted by later generations,
showing the clarity of his administrative affairs.
When Kǒng Róng served as Běihǎi administrator,
his literary teachings were beautiful but rarely implemented,
showing the misalignment of his governance.
As for Zhūgě Kǒngmíng's thoroughness and conciseness,
and Yǔ Zhìgōng's clarity and decisiveness,
both achieved proper principles and appropriate wording,
which constitutes good jiào.
Below jiào,
there is also mìng.
The *Shījīng* says:
"There is a mìng from Heaven."
This indicates that mìng is important.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
"The Shīshì (Grand Tutor) issued zhào to the king."
This indicates that zhào is less important.
The fact that zhào is now considered more important than mìng
is a change from ancient times to the present.
A eulogy says:
When the August Kings issue their commands,
they are solemn and reverent, like ancestral pronouncements.
When I have words to convey,
the myriad people welcome them.
Their illustrious sounds rise grandly,
their mighty influence reaches afar.
Meaning soars, words fly,
broadcasting their great proclamation.
On Xíyí (檄移), Chapter Twenty
Thunder begins with dazzling lightning;
raising an army precedes awe-inspiring pronouncements.
Therefore, observing lightning, one fears the might of thunder;
hearing a pronouncement, one fears the awe of military power.
The military preceding the pronouncement
has a long history.
In ancient times, Yǒu Yú (有虞) first warned within the state;
the Xiàhòu (夏后) first swore an oath in the army;
the Yīn (殷) swore oaths outside the army gate;
the Zhōu (周) swore oaths when about to engage in battle.
Thus, we know that in the age of the Dì (帝), warnings were issued to the army;
the Sān Wáng (三王) swore oaths to the army,
to instruct their own troops,
but not yet reaching the enemy.
When Zhōu Mù (周穆) campaigned westward,
Jì Gōng Móu Fù (祭公謀父) spoke of "ancient commands of awe-inspiring yielding,
and words of literary proclamations,"
which are the origin of the xí (檄).
When the Chūnqiū (春秋) period saw campaigns and conquests,
issuing forth from the zhūhóu (諸侯),
fearing the enemy would not submit,
it was necessary for troops to have a reason when they marched out,
to display this awe-inspiring power,
and expose the enemy's disorder and confusion.
This is what Liú Xiàn Gōng (劉獻公) meant by "informing them with written words,
and controlling them with military force."
Qí Huán (齊桓) campaigned against Chǔ (楚),
questioning the lack of fragrant reeds;
Jìn Lì (晉厲) attacked Qín (秦),
reproaching them for burning Jī (箕) and Gào (郜);
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) and Lǚ Xiàng (呂相)
delivered messages ahead of the army.
Examining their meaning in detail,
they are the xíwén (檄文) of today.
During the Zhànguó (戰國) period,
they began to be called xí (檄).
Xí (檄) means
jiǎo (皦), meaning clear.
It is announced openly to the outside,
clearly and plainly.
Zhāng Yí (張儀) sent a xí (檄) to Chǔ (楚),
written on a foot-two scroll,
a clear document,
sometimes called lùbù (露布).
Lùbù (露布) means
an open, unsealed board,
broadcast for all to see and hear.
As for military action to quell disorder,
none dared to act on their own authority.
When the Tiānzǐ (天子) personally took up arms,
it was called Gōng (龔) carrying out Heaven's punishment;
when the zhūhóu (諸侯) led armies,
it was said they were reverently carrying out the King's execution.
Therefore, to divide the command and appoint a general,
to take up the charge and punish the wicked,
is not only to achieve results through steadfastness,
but also to make one's words formidable for martial prowess.
Making their voice like a headwind's assault,
their spirit like a comet's sweep,
rousing martial fury,
totaling the crimes of the offenders,
exposing the ripeness of their wickedness,
revealing the full measure of their iniquity,
shaking the hearts of traitors,
and strengthening the resolve of the trustworthy and cautious,
so that a hundred-foot battering ram
is broken by a tiny letter,
and a city of ten thousand battlements
topples with a single xí (檄).
Observe Wēi Xiāo's (隗囂) xí (檄) against the fallen Xīn (新) dynasty,
exposing its three rebellions.
The writing was unadorned,
but the language was incisive and the facts clear.
The literati of Lǒngyòu (隴右) grasped the essence of the xí (檄).
Chén Lín's (陳琳) "Xí Yùzhōu" (檄豫州)
is robust and unyielding.
Although it implicates traitorous eunuchs and their adopted children,
the details are too dense,
like digging up graves and taking gold,
falsifying excessive charges beyond reality;
nevertheless, the defiant words expose the transgressions,
clearly and firmly.
Daring to point a spear at Cáo Gōng (曹公),
he was fortunate to escape the slaughter by Yuán Dǎng's (袁黨) faction.
Zhōng Huì's (鍾會) xí (檄) to Shǔ (蜀)
provided very clear evidence;
Huán Wēn's (桓溫) xí (檄) to the Hú (胡)
was especially incisive in observing their flaws.
Both are powerful writings.
The general structure of a xí (檄)
is either to describe the splendor and brightness of one's own side,
or to narrate the harshness and tyranny of the other;
it points to the celestial timing,
examines human affairs,
calculates strength and weakness,
compares power and influence,
displays milfoil and tortoise shell as prior proofs,
and presents mirrors as reflections of what has already happened.
Although primarily based on national trust,
it actually incorporates military stratagem.
It employs cunning and deception to convey its message,
and brilliant eloquence to express its arguments.
All these many points
must be adhered to.
Therefore, when establishing righteousness and proclaiming words,
the emphasis is on strength and vigor.
Feathers are inserted to indicate speed,
so the words must not be slow;
the board is exposed to announce to the public,
so the meaning must not be hidden.
It must be that facts are clear and logic is discernible,
spirit is strong and words are decisive.
This is the essence.
If it relies on subtle twists and intricate cleverness,
it will gain no merit.
Furthermore, when prefectures and states recruit officials,
it is also called a xí (檄);
this signifies a clear declaration.
Yí (移) means
change.
To change customs and alter traditions,
so that commands are issued and the people follow.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's (司馬相如) "Nán Shǔ Lǎo" (難蜀老)
is clear in language and broad in analogy,
possessing the essence of a xí (檄) used for change.
As for Liú Xīn's (劉歆) "Yí Tàicháng" (移太常),
its words are firm and its meaning clear,
making it the foremost of literary yí (移).
Lù Jī's (陸機) "Yí Bǎiguān" (移百官)
is concise in words and evident in facts,
making it the most important of martial yí (移).
Therefore, the uses of xí (檄) and yí (移)
encompass both civil and martial affairs.
In times of war,
rebel factions use xí (檄),
while loyal masses rely on yí (移).
They are used to cleanse the people's hearts
and firmly establish covenants.
Their intended uses are slightly different, but their core meaning is largely the same,
intermingled with xí (檄),
hence not discussed separately.
A eulogy says:
Three drives loosen the net,
nine campaigns begin with discourse.
Mirrors reflect fortune and misfortune,
milfoil and tortoise shells decide success and failure.
They crush whales and dragons,
strike down hornets and scorpions.
They transform treasures and change customs,
like grass bending to the wind's sweep.
On Fēngshàn (封禪), Chapter Twenty-One
Indeed, to assume the correct position of the North Star,
facing south towards the light,
thereby turning the celestial pivot
and nurturing the myriad people,
how could it ever not be through traversing the Way and weaving virtue
to engrave imperial achievements!
The Lǜ Tú (綠圖) says:
"Vast and profound,
numerous and orderly,
all things are transformed."
This speaks of the reach of ultimate virtue.
The Dān Shū (丹書) says:
"If righteousness overcomes desire, there is compliance;
if desire overcomes righteousness, there is misfortune."
This is the utmost in caution and prudence.
Thus, through caution and prudence, one exalts one's virtue;
through ultimate virtue, one consolidates one's transformative power.
Seventy-two rulers
thus performed the Fēngshàn (封禪) sacrifices.
In ancient times, Huángdì (黃帝) was divine and spiritual,
able to receive great auspicious omens.
He inscribed his achievements on Jiáo Yuè (喬岳)
and cast tripods on Jīng Shān (荊山).
Dà Shùn (大舜) inspected the sacred mountains,
which is clearly described in the 《Yú Diǎn》 (《虞典》).
Chéng Kāng (成康) performed the Fēngshàn (封禪) sacrifices,
as heard in the 《Yuè Wěi》 (《樂緯》).
When Qí Huán (齊桓) became hegemon,
he tried to emulate the deeds of kings.
However, Yí Wú (夷吾) cleverly argued
against it, citing portents.
Thus, it is known that jade tablets and golden inscriptions
belong exclusively to emperors.
However, the western jiān (鶼) and eastern dié (鰈),
the southern máo (茅) and northern shǔ (黍) –
empty talk does not constitute evidence,
only meritorious deeds do.
This is why Sī Qiān (司遷)'s 《Bā Shū》 (《八書》),
which clearly describes the Fēngshàn (封禪) sacrifices,
is indeed a special rite of sacrificial offerings,
a secret prayer for inscription,
and a grand spectacle of worshipping Heaven.
Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇)'s inscription on Dài (岱)
was composed by Lǐ Sī (李斯).
Its legalist rhetoric
lacks a grand and refined style.
Yet, though terse, it is powerful,
and also a unique masterpiece of its time.
Surveying the flourishing periods of the two Hàn (漢) dynasties,
Xiàowǔ (孝武) performed the Fēngshàn (封禪) at Sùrán (肅然),
and Guāngwǔ (光武) performed it at Liángfù (梁父).
To sing of their virtues and inscribe their merits
was indeed the task of great writers.
Sī Rú (司如)'s 《Fēngshàn》 (《封禪》)
stands out as the foremost.
It sets forth the origins,
narrates the imperial kings,
illuminates the dark omens,
reflects the grand achievements,
brings the ancient past into the present,
and elevates brilliant virtues above all previous sages.
It sings of auspicious omens
and praises the great hills.
This masterpiece, unique in its writing,
is truly a work of innovation.
When Guāngwǔ (光武) erected his stele,
the text was by Zhāng Chún (張純).
It began by continuing the ancient canons,
and ended like a prayer.
It cited 《Gōuchèn》 (《鉤讖》),
narrated divisions,
calculated military achievements,
and described civil virtues.
The events were factual, the principles well-argued;
it was less flowery but more substantial.
Both these works
are actual records from Dàizōng (岱宗).
As for Yáng Xióng (揚雄)'s 《Jù Qín》 (《劇秦》)
and Bān Gù (班固)'s 《Diǎn Yǐn》 (《典引》),
though not engraved on stone,
their style was dictated by the chronicle of Fēngshàn (封禪).
《Jù Qín》 (《劇秦》), as a composition,
shadows Cháng Qīng (長卿).
With its strange words and reclusive rhetoric,
it encompasses gods and monsters.
Yet its structure is intricate and precise,
and its language smooth and coherent.
It claims to be the pinnacle of thought,
with no effort spared.
What 《Diǎn Yǐn》 (《典引》) narrates
has a refined and elegant quality.
Reviewing previous works,
it is able to grasp the essential.
Its way of presenting principles and composing text
shows an abundance of refined skill.
Therefore, it is said that "Sī Rú's (司如) 《Fēngshàn》 (《封禪》) is elaborate but not classic,
while Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) 《Jù Qín》 (《劇秦》) is classic but not factual."
Is this not because later observation makes things clearer,
and following the trend makes things easier to achieve?
As for Hándān (邯鄲)'s "Shòumìng" (受命),
it merely echoes previous voices.
Weak in style and lacking power,
it merely compiles rhymes into an ode.
Although its literary structure is somewhat orderly,
it fails to soar.
Chén Sī (陳思)'s 《Wèi Dé》 (《魏德》)
adopts a dialogue format between a guest and a host.
The questions and answers are slow and circuitous,
and already a thousand words long.
It is deep in effort but sparse in achievement,
lacking brilliance and vigor.
This type of writing
is generally the official document of an era.
At the start of its composition,
one should clearly grasp the main structure,
establish the framework in the realm of classical canons,
and choose words from the path of grandeur and richness,
so that the ideas are ancient yet not obscure in profundity,
and the language is modern yet does not fall into shallowness.
If the meaning emits radiance
and the language forms a sharp edge,
then it will be great.
Although the themes may be exhausted
and ultimately repetitive,
those who daily renew their brilliance
will surely surpass their predecessors.
Eulogy:
Fēng (封) and Lè (勒) record imperial achievements,
responding to Heaven's blessings.
Afar, one hears the high mountains,
their heroic voices resounding.
Stones are erected in the nine heavens,
gold inscribed in the eight abysses.
Grand rhythms entwine with splendor,
like dragons and hornless dragons.
Chapter 22: Biǎo (章表)
Now, the establishment of official positions and the division of duties
links high and low positions.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) lowers his jade beads to listen,

and clearly assess based on merit.

not relying on written documents.

he again wrote in praise.

and the matter was thus revealed.

and the literary principles became even more prosperous.

statements of gratitude and refusal can be seen.

the ancient forms were not changed.

red and white are called zhāng.

skillful adaptation to circumstances,

petitions submitted to the imperial presence

Evaluating according to name and assessing based on reality,

essential but not terse,
clear but not shallow.

Extensively reporting at the vermilion palace,

Reports and Petitions, Twenty-third
In antiquity, the officials of Táng and Yú
presented their statements verbally;
the advisors of Qín and Hàn
submitted written memorials called zòu (奏).
They laid out government policies,
offered ceremonial protocols,
reported urgent changes,
and impeached transgressions and errors,
all collectively called zòu.
Zòu
means "to advance" (進).
It articulates the feelings of those below
and advances them to those above.
Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) first established the zòu,
but the Legalists lacked literary refinement.

the language was plain and the meaning direct;

is to reach/convey.

the "Zhōulǐ" (zhōu lǐ) has "three Cì" (cì);
matters are conveyed to each other,
like a needle passing through a knot.
Jiě 者 (zhě),
is to explain.
To clarify confusion and obstructions,
to adduce facts in response.
Dié 者 (zhě),
is a leaf.
Short slips woven into a Dié (dié)
are like leaves on a branch. [92)Wēn Shū (wēn shū) cutting reeds
is an example of this.
When governmental proposals are undecided,
short Dié (dié) are used for consultation.
A particularly concise Dié (dié)
is called a Qiān (qiān).
Qiān 者 (zhě),
is something fine and concise.
Zhuàng 者 (zhě),
is appearance/form.
To embody the original form,
to capture the facts.
Ancient worthies' posthumous titles
all have Xíngzhuàng (xíng zhuàng),
which are the most significant Zhuàng (zhuàng).
Liè 者 (zhě),
is to arrange/display.
To arrange and display affairs,
making them clearly visible.
Cí 者 (zhě),
are words from the tip of the tongue,
to communicate oneself to others. [116)Zǐ Chǎn (zǐ chǎn) had Cí (cí),
on which the feudal lords relied,
which could not be dispensed with.
Yàn 者 (zhě),
is straightforward speech.
Eulogies for the deceased also do not rely on florid language,
hence condolences are also called Yàn (yàn).
Street talk is simple speech,
with substance but no embellishment. [125)Zōu Mùgōng (zōu mù gōng) said:
"A bag leaking into storage."
These are all of this type.
"Tàishì" (tài shì) says:
"The ancients had a saying:
'A hen does not herald the dawn.'"
"Dàyǎ" (dà yǎ) says:
"People also have a saying:
'Only worry makes one old.'"
These are all ancient proverbs,
which can be cited from the "Shī" (shī) and "Shū" (shū).
As for Chén Lín's (chén lín) admonition,
which referred to "covering one's eyes to catch a sparrow,"
and Pān Yuè's (pān yuè) lament,
which referred to "a precious pearl of a spouse,"
these both cited popular sayings to form literary expressions.
Among literary expressions, none are more rustic and vulgar
than proverbs,
yet the sagely worthies' poems and books
adopted them into their discourse.
How much more so, then, those that exceed this [in refinement],
how can they be neglected!
Observing these four categories,
they are all encompassed by official writings:
some matters are inherently interconnected,
yet their literary meanings differ;
some rely entirely on simplicity,
some mix with ornate language.
Establishing the form according to the matter,
the key is to be precise and essential.
If the meaning lacks one character, the sense is incomplete;
if a phrase is one word too long, the expression is hindered.
These are the practical duties of officials,
and what florid prose often overlooks.
However, those whose talent excels in grand writing
often neglect official documents.
This is like Jiǔfāng Yīn (jiǔ fāng yīn) recognizing a swift horse,
but not knowing its color or gender.
Words are the outward manifestation of oneself,
and trustworthiness is also a national omen.
Scholars of the Hanlin Academy (hàn lín)
should ponder the truth of this.
Eulogy says:
Literary embellishment flows forth,
entrusted to the pen and tablet.
It gallops forth like metal images,
and also operates with wooden simplicity.
Through ten thousand ages, fame is recommended,
and from a thousand li, talents are drawn forth.
Innumerable affairs are complex,
but through writing, they are comprehended.
Shénsī (shén sī) Twenty-Sixth.
Ancient people said:
“Though the form is on the rivers and seas,
the heart dwells beneath Wèiquè.”
This refers to inspired thought.
As for literary thought,
its spirit is profound.
Thus, in quiet contemplation,
thought connects with a thousand years;
in an unconscious movement of expression,
vision encompasses ten thousand lí;
amidst recitation and chanting,
it breathes forth the sound of pearls and jade;
before the eyebrows and eyelashes,
it unfurls and retracts the colors of wind and clouds.
Is this not the ultimate reach of reasoned thought!
Therefore, reasoned thought is subtle,
and the spirit roams with things.
The spirit resides in the breast,
and will and qi govern its locks;
things enter through the ears and eyes,
and rhetoric manages their crucial mechanisms.
When the crucial mechanisms are open,
no form of things remains hidden;
when the locks are about to be obstructed,
the spirit will have a hidden heart.
Therefore, in shaping literary thought,
it is essential to be empty and tranquil,
to cleanse the five zàng,
to bathe and purify the spirit,
to accumulate learning to store treasures,
to draw upon principles to enrich talent,
to diligently study to exhaust understanding,
and gradually to lead forth words.
Then, the master of profound understanding
will seek out prosody and settle the lines;
the craftsman of singular insight
will glimpse intentions and images and wield the axe.
This is indeed the foremost art of controlling writing,
the great principle of planning a composition.
When inspired thought is in motion,
ten thousand paths emerge competitively;
rules and measures are as if in a void,
carving and etching the formless.
Climbing a mountain, emotions fill the mountain;
gazing at the sea, intentions overflow the sea.
The extent of my talent
will compete alongside the wind and clouds.
Just as one grasps the brush,
the qi is twice that before the words;
yet by the time the chapter is complete,
only half the heart’s intent remains.
Why is this?
Ideas soar into the void and are easily extraordinary,
while words that align with reality are difficult to make skillful.
Therefore, intention is given by thought,
and words are given by intention;
when close, there are no boundaries,
when distant, it is a thousand lí away.
Sometimes the principle lies within a square cùn,
yet one seeks it beyond the region;
sometimes the meaning is within a zhǐchǐ,
yet thought is separated by mountains and rivers.
Therefore, in holding to the heart and cultivating the art,
one should not trouble oneself with bitter thoughts;
in encompassing brilliance and controlling the key,
there is no need to exhaust one's feelings.
People’s innate talents
differ in their speed;
the forms of literature
vary in their efficacy according to size.
Xiāngrú held his brush until the tip decayed,
Yáng Xióng picked up his brush and startled his dreams,
Huán Tán was severely afflicted by arduous thought,
Wáng Chōng exhausted his qi in deep deliberation.
Zhāng Héng researched the Jīng Fù for ten years,
Zuǒ Sī refined the Sān Dū Fù for twelve years.
Though these were great works,
they were also slow in their thought process.
Huáinán completed the Sāo in a single morning,
Méi Gāo composed fù in response to imperial decrees,
Zǐjiàn seized a writing tablet as if reciting from memory,
Zhòngxuān raised his brush as if he had composed it long ago,
Ruǎn Yǔ wrote documents while seated on a saddle,
Ní Héng drafted memorials during a meal.
Though these were short pieces,
they were also fast in their thought process.
As for those with soaring talent,
their minds grasp the essential techniques,
their quickness precedes deliberation,
and they make decisions immediately in response to the moment.
Those who contemplate deeply,
their emotions are rich with diverging paths,
their discernment follows doubt,
and deliberation finally settles.
Quickness leads to success even in haste,
while deliberation and doubt lead to achievement over time.
Though the ease and difficulty differ,
both rely on extensive practice.
If learning is shallow and one is idly slow,
or talent is sparse and one is merely fast,
to achieve greatness with such conditions
has never been heard of.
Therefore, when composing a piece and arranging thoughts,
there are inevitably two pitfalls:
one whose principles are stagnant suffers from poverty of thought,
one whose words are chaotic is harmed by disarray.
Thus, extensive knowledge is the sustenance for the poor in thought,
and unification is the medicine for disarray.
To be extensive yet capable of unifying,
this also aids the mind’s power.
If emotions and situations are intricate and varied,
and forms change and shift,
clumsy words may sometimes conceive clever meanings,
and ordinary matters may sometimes generate new ideas.
Like seeing hemp on the loom,
though it is said not yet to have been expended,
only when the shuttle and loom have accomplished their work
does it brightly become precious.
As for subtle meanings beyond thought,
and profound nuances outside the text,
what words cannot reach,
the brush certainly knows where to stop.
Only after reaching utmost refinement can its subtlety be elucidated;
only after reaching utmost transformation can its laws be understood.
Yī Zhì could not explain the tripod,
and Lún Biǎn could not speak of the axe.
How profound this is!
Eulogy says:
The spirit’s function connects with images,
conceived by the transformations of emotion.
Things are sought by their appearance,
the mind responds according to principle.
Carving and etching prosody,
germinating bì and xīng.
Concluding thought and controlling the key,
drawing the curtain to secure victory.
Chapter 27: Shén Sī
Indeed, feelings are moved, and speech takes form;
principles are expressed, and patterns become visible.
This is because they proceed from the hidden to the manifest,
and from the inner to correspond with the outer.
However, talent has its ordinary and its outstanding,
vitality has its strong and its gentle,
learning has its shallow and its profound,
and habits have their refined and their rustic.
These are all forged by one's nature and disposition,
and solidified by one's cultivation and influence.
This is why the realm of the brush is like shifting clouds,
and the garden of literature is full of surging waves.
Therefore, if the rhetoric and principles are ordinary or outstanding,
none can alter that talent;
if the temperament is strong or gentle,
how could anyone change that vitality;
if the matters and meanings are shallow or profound,
none has heard of a deviation from that learning;
if the styles and forms are refined or rustic,
few can reverse that habit.
Each follows their formed disposition,
their differences are like faces.
If we summarize their general tendencies,
then they can be exhaustively categorized into eight styles:
The first is Diǎnyǎ (典雅, Elegant and Refined),
the second is Yuǎnáo (遠奧, Remote and Profound),
the third is Jīngyuē (精約, Precise and Concise),
the fourth is Xiǎnfù (顯附, Clear and Engaging),
the fifth is Fánrù (繁縟, Ornate and Elaborate),
the sixth is Zhuànglì (壯麗, Grand and Beautiful),
the seventh is Xīnqí (新奇, Novel and Unique),
the eighth is Qīngmí (輕靡, Light and Frivolous).
Diǎnyǎ (典雅) means
molding one's style after the classics and edicts,
and keeping pace with the Confucian school.
Yuǎnáo (遠奧) means
drawing fragrance from classical texts,
and managing recondite principles.
Jīngyuē (精約) means
scrutinizing words and economizing sentences,
analyzing with utmost precision.
Xiǎnfù (顯附) means
straightforward language and clear meaning,
touching principles and satisfying the heart.
Fánrù (繁縟) means
extensive metaphors and rich ornamentation,
radiating branches and offshoots.
Zhuànglì (壯麗) means
lofty discussions and grand structures,
brilliant with extraordinary splendor.
Xīnqí (新奇) means
rejecting the old and competing with the new,
daringly strange and whimsical.
Qīngmí (輕靡) means
superficial rhetoric and weak construction,
vague and catering to popular taste.
Thus, elegance is the opposite of uniqueness,
profundity differs from clarity,
elaboration clashes with conciseness,
grandeur goes against lightness.
The roots and leaves of literature,
are all contained within these.
As for the frequent changes in the eight styles,
skill is achieved through learning,
while talent and vigor reside within,
originating from one's blood and vital energy.
Vital energy gives substance to ambition,
and ambition determines speech.
The expression of brilliance,
is all born of one's nature and disposition.
This is why Jiǎ Shēng (賈生) was brilliant and quick-witted,
hence his writing was pure and his style clear;
Cháng Qīng (長卿) was arrogant and unrestrained,
