hence his principles were extravagant and his words overflowing;
Zǐ Yún (子雲) was quiet and reclusive,
hence his ambition was hidden and his flavor deep;
Zǐ Zhèng (子政) was simple and straightforward,
hence his charm was evident and his topics broad;
Mèng Jiān (孟堅) was elegant and graceful,
hence his structure was meticulous and his thought refined;
Píng Zǐ (平子) was extensive and well-versed,
hence his deliberations were comprehensive and his ornamentation intricate;
Zhòng Xuān (仲宣) was restless and competitive,
hence his talent was sharp and his abilities decisive;
Gōng Gàn (公幹) was narrow in spirit,
hence his words were bold and his emotions startling;
Sì Zōng (嗣宗) was unconventional and uninhibited,
hence his resonance was unrestrained and his tone distant;
Shú Yè (叔夜) was brilliant and chivalrous,
hence his inspiration was lofty and his expression fervent;
Ān Rén (安仁) was light and nimble,
hence his wit was sharp and his rhythm flowing;
Shì Héng (士衡) was dignified and serious,
hence his feelings were complex and his words subtle.
By extending this principle to other cases,
the outer and inner will invariably correspond.
Is this not the constant endowment of nature,
and the general outline of talent and vitality?
Indeed, talent is a natural endowment,
and learning requires caution in its initial practice.
Carving catalpa wood and dyeing silk,
the effort lies in the initial transformation.
Once the vessel is formed and the colors set,
it is difficult to alter or change.
Therefore, when educating a child,
one must first instill refined norms.
Following the root to seek the leaves,
thought will naturally develop.
Though the eight styles are distinct,
they ultimately converge and unite.
If one grasps their central point,
then all aspects will come together and complement each other.
Thus, it is proper to emulate styles to establish habits,
and cultivate talent according to disposition.
This is the guiding principle of literature,
and the way it is applied.
A eulogy says:
Talent and nature occupy different realms,
literary styles are complex and diverse.
Words are the skin and roots,
but purpose is truly the bone marrow.
Elegance and splendor are like ceremonial robes,
excessive artifice is like common reds and purples.
Habit, too, solidifies truth,
and skill proceeds gradually.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Fēnggǔ (風骨, Wind and Bone)
The Odes (《詩》) encompass six principles,
with Fēng (風, Wind/Airs) leading them.
This is indeed the origin of transformative influence,
and the very essence of aspiration and vital energy.
Therefore, when expressing feelings with melancholy,
one must begin with Fēng (風);
when pondering and crafting language,
nothing precedes Gǔ (骨, Bone).
Thus, language's reliance on Gǔ (骨)
is like a body's reliance on its skeleton;
the inclusion of Fēng (風) in emotion
is like a form's containing vital energy.
If speech is upright and direct,
then the Gǔ (骨) of the writing is formed;
if the spirit and vital energy are bold and clear,
then the Fēng (風) of the writing is pure.
If the rich ornamentation is sufficient,
but the Fēnggǔ (風骨) does not soar,
then its brilliance loses freshness,
and its renown lacks power.
Therefore, when deliberating and composing a chapter,
one must strive for fullness and maintain vital energy.
Once strength and vigor are truly present,
radiant splendor will then be new.
Its function in writing
is like a soaring bird using its wings.
Therefore, those skilled in Gǔ (骨)
will have precise word choices;
those profound in Fēng (風)
will express emotions clearly.
Words are forged firm and difficult to alter,
the resonance is condensed yet not stagnant –
this is the power of Fēnggǔ (風骨).
If the meaning is meager and the language bloated,
chaotic and lacking coherence,
then it is a sign of having no Gǔ (骨).
If thought is not comprehensive,
and composition lacks vital energy,
then it is proof of having no Fēng (風).
In the past, Pān Xù (潘勖) received the mandate for Wèi (魏),
and his thoughts emulated the classics.
All other talents sheathed their brushes;
this was because his Gǔsuǐ (骨髓) was stern.
Xiāng Rú (相如) composed rhapsodies about immortals,
his vital energy was said to reach the clouds.
He rose to become a literary master;
this was because his Fēnglì (風力) was robust.
One who can discern these essentials
can properly evaluate writing.
If this method is disregarded,
do not bother with elaborate ornamentation.
Therefore, Wèi Wén (魏文) said, "Literature values *qì* above all,
*qì*'s clarity or turbidity has a form,
it cannot be forced or obtained through effort."
Thus, in his evaluation of Kǒng Róng (孔融),
he said, "His *tǐ qì* is lofty and wondrous";
in his evaluation of Xú Gàn (徐幹),
he said, "At times he possesses the *qì* of Qí (齊)";
in his evaluation of Liú Zhēn (劉楨),
he said, "He possesses an untrammeled *qì*."
Gōng Gàn (公幹) also said:
"Kǒng (孔) is outstanding and remarkable,
truly containing an extraordinary *qì*;
the essence of his writing
is virtually unsurpassable."
All of these emphasize the importance of *qì*.
Pheasants and painted birds possess vibrant colors yet can only flutter a hundred paces;
they are fleshy but lack strength.
Hawks and falcons lack brilliant hues, yet their wings soar to the heavens;
their bones are strong and their *qì* is fierce.
Literary talent and ability
are similar to this.
If wind and bone lack color,
then fierce birds will gather in the writing world;
if color lacks wind and bone,
then pheasants will hide in literary gardens.
Only when adorned with brilliance and soaring high
is literature the *míng fèng* (鳴鳳, calling phoenix).
As for those who melt and mold the models of the classics,
gather and assemble the techniques of the philosophical and historical texts,
deeply understand emotional changes,
and fully illuminate literary styles,
only then can they sprout new ideas
and carve out wondrous expressions.
Illuminating style makes new ideas orderly,
understanding change makes wondrous expressions not tedious.
If bone and color are not yet complete,
and wind and expression are not yet refined,
yet one attempts to surpass the old models
and gallop after new compositions,
although one might obtain clever ideas,
failures will also be numerous.
How can one simply piece together unusual characters
and create light pieces through mistakes?
The *Zhōu Shū* (周書) says:
"In writing, value essence and conciseness,
do not simply favor being different."
This is to prevent literary excess.
However, the art of literature has many paths,
each suited to individual preferences;
the enlightened do not impart,
the students do not emulate.
Thus, they practice extravagance and follow excess,
drifting and forgetting to return.
If one can firmly establish the correct form,
making literature strong and healthy,
then the wind will be clear and the bone upright,
and the structure of the piece will be brilliant and luminous.
If one can thoroughly investigate these considerations,
what distance is there to go?
Eulogy says:
Emotion and *qì* go together,
expression and form align.
Literature is strong and healthy,
then jade tokens are offered in betrothal.
Vibrant is that wind-force,
firm are those bone-fishbones.
Talent's sharpness stands tall,
the symbols and colors are clearly radiant.
Chapter 29: Versatility
The structures of setting up writing have constancy,
but the ways of changing writing have no fixed rule.
How can one make this clear?
Generally, poetry, *fù* (賦), letters, and records
have principles that are mutually dependent;
this is the constant aspect of structure.
Literary expression, *qì*, and strength,
through versatility endure;
this is the aspect of having no fixed rule.
Principles have constancy,
so structure must rely on past realities;
versatility has no fixed rule,
so method must draw upon new sounds.
Therefore, one can roam along endless roads
and drink from inexhaustible sources.
However, a short rope will thirst for water,
and tired feet will stop on the road.
It is not that the resources of writing have been exhausted,
but rather that the skill of versatility is lacking.
Therefore, the way to discuss literature
is like plants and trees:
roots and trunks are beautiful in the soil and share a common nature,
but scents and flavors bask in the sun and have different qualities.
Therefore, the songs of the nine generations
align in intention and literary principles.
The Yellow Emperor's song "*Duàn Zhú*" (斷竹)
is the epitome of simplicity;
the songs of Táng (唐) in former times
were broader than those of the Yellow Emperor's era;
the songs of Yú (虞), such as "*Qīng Yún*" (卿雲),
were more refined than those of the Táng period;
the songs of the Xià (夏), such as "Carved Walls,"
were more ornate than those of the Yú dynasty;
the odes of the Shāng (商) and Zhōu (周)
were more elegant than those of the Xià years.
As for ordering intentions and describing the times,
their principle is the same.
Even the *Sāo* (騷) style of Chǔ (楚)
followed the models of the Zhōu people;
the *fù* and eulogies of the Hàn (漢)
were shadows and copies of the Chǔ period;
the composition methods of the Wèi (魏)
admired and emulated the Hàn style;
the literary compositions of the Jìn (晉)
looked up to the refined style of the Wèi.
If we analyze them in detail:
then the Yellow Emperor and Táng were pure and simple;
Yú and Xià were simple yet discerning;
Shāng and Zhōu were elegant and refined;
Chǔ and Hàn were extravagant and flamboyant;
Wèi and Jìn were shallow and ornate;
the early Sòng (宋) was distorted and new.
From simplicity to distortion,
the closer one gets, the more insipid it becomes.
Why is this?
Because people compete for the present and neglect the past,
the spirit of the age declines.
Today, talented scholars
diligently study literature,
mostly neglecting Hàn works
and modeling themselves on Sòng collections.
Although they read both ancient and modern works,
they are close to the near and distant from the far.
Indigo is born from the *lán* plant,
and crimson is born from the *qiàn* plant.
Although they surpass the original color,
they cannot revert to it.
Huán Jūnshān (桓君山) said:
"I have seen the beautiful writings of newcomers,
beautiful but lacking brilliance;
and when I see the words of Liú Yáng (劉揚),
I always gain something."
This is proof of it.
Therefore, refining indigo and washing crimson
must return to *lán* and *qiàn*;
correcting distortions and reversing shallowness
returns to the *Jīng* (經, classics) and *gào* (誥, proclamations).
This is to deliberate between simplicity and refinement,
and to measure between elegance and vulgarity;
one can then discuss versatility.
Exaggerating sound and appearance
reached its peak in the early Hàn;
from then on,
they circulated and influenced each other.
Although they soared out of the tracks,
they ultimately entered the cage.
Méi Chéng's (枚乘) "*Qī Fā*" (七發) says:
"Looking out over the eastern sea,
the rainbow pierces through the blue sky."
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's (司馬相如) "*Shàng Lín*" (上林) says:
"Looking at it, there is no end;
observing it, there is no limit;
the sun rises from the eastern marsh,
the moon is born from the western bank."
Mǎ Róng's (馬融) "*Guǎng Chéng*" (廣成) says:
"Heaven and earth pierce through each other like a rainbow,
and indeed have no end or limit;
the great sun rises from the east,
the moon is born from the western bank."
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) "*Xiào Liè*" (校獵) says:
"Entering and exiting the sun and moon,
heaven and earth blend together."
Zhāng Héng's (張衡) "*Xī Jīng*" (西京) says:
"The sun and moon rise and set here,
resembling the *fú sāng* (扶桑) tree in the misty vastness."
These all broadly use extreme descriptions,
and the five authors are like one.
All such examples
follow each other,
mixing and changing,
which is the method of versatility.
Therefore, planning and governing literary works
should prioritize the overall structure.
Begin with extensive reading for careful examination,
grasping the main principles and encompassing details.
Then, open up the avenues,
establish key points,
hold the long reins for distant journeys,
proceeding leisurely with measured steps.
Rely on emotions to achieve thorough understanding,
draw on spirit to adapt to changes,
collecting ideas like a rainbow displaying its vibrant colors,
shining with brilliance like a mythical bird spreading its wings.
This is the literature of outstanding talent.
If one is narrow-minded in limited interpretations,
or stubbornly insists on a single viewpoint,
this is merely pacing around in a courtyard;
how can it be a carefree stride across vast distances!
Commentary:
Literary rules revolve continuously,
with each day bringing new endeavors.
Change allows for endurance,
thorough understanding prevents deficiency.
Seize opportunities with determination,
take advantage of the moment without hesitation.
Look to the present to create something unique,
refer to the past to establish norms.
Establishing Momentum, Section Thirty
Emotions and sentiments differ in their expression,
literary styles vary in their techniques,
but all are based on emotions to establish structure,
and from that structure to create momentum.
Momentum [shì] is
creating a system by taking advantage of favorable conditions.
It is like an arrow shot straight from a machine,
or a winding stream turning in a ravine,
a natural inclination.
A circle follows the form of a compass,
and its momentum is naturally to rotate;
a square follows the shape of a T-square,
and its momentum is naturally to remain stable.
The structure and momentum of literature
are simply like this.
Therefore, those who take the classics as a model
naturally enter the realm of elegance and refinement;
those who imitate the *sāo* style in their compositions
inevitably gravitate towards the splendor of exuberance;
those who synthesize ideas superficially
tend to lack depth;
those who cut off phrases concisely
often deviate from elaboration;
it is like turbulent water without ripples,
or a bare tree without shade,
a natural disposition.
Therefore, in painting, colors are used to depict images,
and in writing, emotions are expressed to their fullest.
When colors are blended, different forms like dogs and horses emerge;
when emotions intersect, elegant and common styles diverge.
Each model or pattern
has its own master craftsman.
Even without strict boundaries,
it is difficult to transgress.
However, those who are deeply versed in literature
comprehend all types of momentum.
Although the unexpected and the orthodox are opposite,
they must be understood and reconciled;
although strength and gentleness are different,
they must be applied according to the occasion.
If one loves elegance but dislikes flamboyance,
the principle of comprehensive understanding is compromised,
like a person from the Xià 夏 dynasty arguing over a bow and arrow,
unable to shoot alone with just one.
If elegant and vulgar styles are combined in one piece,
the overall momentum of unity is disrupted,
like a person from Chǔ 楚 selling spears while praising shields,
unable to sell both effectively.
Therefore, encompassing various styles
requires careful discrimination.
Musical notes and colors
should be matched according to the situation.
Memorials and petitions
should adhere to elegance and correctness;
rhyme-prose and songs
should be adorned with purity and beauty;
official documents and letters
should be models of clarity and decisiveness;
historical treatises and commentaries
should be examples of accuracy and conciseness;
admonitions and epitaphs
should embody profound and comprehensive structures;
linked verse and heptasyllabic poems
should be dedicated to ingenuity and splendor.
This is how momentum is created by following the structure,
and how merit is established by adapting to changes.
Even when convergence and divergence intermingle,
and regulations and embellishments mix together,
it is like a brocade of five colors,
where each color maintains its original essence as the base.
Huán Tán 桓譚 said, "Literary scholars each have their own preferences;
some favor superficial elegance without knowing true substance,
while others admire abundance without seeing essential brevity."
Chén Sī 陳思 also said:
"Writers in the world
either favor verbose and extensive collection,
making their meaning profound and deep;
or they like to isolate words and analyze sentences,
examining every detail with utmost precision;
their practices are different,
and their objectives vary."
This refers to the distinction in momentum.
Liú Zhēn 劉楨 said:
"The substance of literature,
its emptiness and fullness, strength and weakness,
making its words exhaustive yet leaving momentum in reserve;
to unite the world as one,
is unattainable."
Gōng Gàn's 公幹 remarks
also incorporate spirit to a considerable extent.
However, in literature's employment of momentum,
momentum has strength and gentleness.
It is not necessary to have grand and impassioned words
to be considered momentum.
Also, Lù Yún 陸雲 himself claimed, "In the past, when discussing literature,
I prioritized diction over emotion,
valuing momentum without seeking pleasure and smoothness.
Now that Zhāng Gōng 張公 discusses literature,
I want to follow his words."
Indeed, emotion precedes diction,
and momentum truly requires smoothness;
it can be said that he was initially lost but later able to follow the good.
Since recent times, writers
have generally favored novelty and ingenuity.
Examining their substance,
it is a transformation of erroneous momentum,
disgusted with old styles,
so they seek novelty through forced interpretations.
Observing their distorted intentions,
it seems difficult but in reality it is nothing more than a trick,
reversal and opposition.
Therefore, reversing proper writing leads to deficiency,
and reversing diction leads to novelty.
The method of pursuing novelty
necessarily involves inverting sentences,
suppressing the lower characters with the upper characters,
and pushing the inner diction outwards,
making reversals and alternations frequent,
to achieve a new appearance.
Indeed, the main roads are smooth and level,
but many take shortcuts
because they seek closeness and convenience;
proper writing is clear and straightforward,
but they often employ reversed language
because they cater to popular tastes.
However, those who subtly understand achieve ingenuity with new ideas,
while those who merely seek difference create monstrosities by losing the essence.
Those skilled through long practice
maintain correctness while employing novelty;
those newly initiated and eager to learn
pursue novelty and lose correctness;
if the momentum flows without reversal,
the literary style will become corrupt.
Holding onto these emotions and techniques,
how can one not reflect!
Commentary:
Forms are born, and momentum develops,
beginning and end succeeding each other.
Eddies curve like a compass,
arrows shoot straight like a string.
Take advantage of favorable conditions to display restraint,
and emotions and colors will naturally solidify.
Learning to walk with restrained reins
will only reach Shòulíng 壽陵 with exhaustion.
Emotion and Color, Section Thirty-One
The writings of saints and sages
are collectively called *wénzhāng*,
and if not ornamental, what are they?
Water is by nature vacuous, yet ripples form;
wood is by nature solid, yet flowers and calyxes bloom.
Ornamentation is attached to substance.
If tigers and leopards had no patterns,
their hides would be no different from those of dogs and sheep.
Rhinoceroses and buffaloes have hides,
but their color relies on vermilion and lacquer.
Substance depends on ornamentation.
As for comprehensively recounting one's nature and spirit,
and elaborating on the forms of things,
carving one's heart into bird tracks,
and weaving words onto fishnets,
the resulting brilliance
is indeed called rich splendor.
Therefore, in the way of establishing writing,
its principles are threefold:
First is *xíngwén* (form-ornamentation),
which is the five colors;
second is *shēngwén* (sound-ornamentation),
which is the five notes;
third is *qíngwén* (emotion-ornamentation),
which is the five sentiments.
The five colors blend to form embroidered patterns;
the five notes combine to form the *Sháo* and *Xià* music;
the five sentiments are expressed as *cízhang* (rhetorical compositions).
This is the natural order of divine principles.
The *Xiàojīng* sets forth its canons, stating
that mourning words should not be ornate.
Thus, we know that the constant words of a *jūnzǐ*
are never merely substantial.
Lǎozǐ disliked pretense,
hence he said, "Fine words are not trustworthy."
Yet his five thousand profound and exquisite words
do not mean he discarded beauty.
Zhuāng Zhōu said,
"Debate sculpts all things."
This refers to embellishment.
Hán Fēi said,
"How enchanting is eloquent persuasion."
This refers to beauty.
Beauty through enchanting persuasion,
embellishment through sculpting debate—
the transformations of literary expression
reach their zenith here.
If one studies and savors *Xiào* and *Lǎo*,
one will know that ornamentation and substance are attached to nature and emotion.
If one carefully observes *Zhuāng* and *Hán*,
one will see that floridness and substance exceed the bounds of extravagance.
If one chooses the source from the flows of the Jīng and Wèi rivers,
and guides the reins on the path of right and wrong,
one can also control literary ornamentation.
Lead white and dark pigments are used to adorn the face,
but allure arises from a graceful demeanor.
Literary ornamentation is used to adorn words,
but eloquent beauty originates from emotion and nature.
Therefore, emotion
is the warp of writing;
diction
is the weft of principle.
Only after the warp is straight can the weft be formed;
only after the principle is settled can the diction be smooth.
This is the fundamental source of establishing writing.
In ancient times, poets in their ten-chapter works
created writing for emotion;
rhetoricians in their *fù* and *sòng*
created emotion for writing.
How can this be explained?
When *fēng* and *yǎ* arose,
thoughts and feelings harbored indignation,
and sentiments were expressed in verse,
to satirize their superiors.
This is creating writing for emotion.
Followers of the various philosophers,
whose hearts were not troubled by sorrow,
indulged in extravagant embellishments,
selling their fame and angling for worldly recognition.
This is creating emotion for writing.
Therefore, those who write for emotion are concise and truthful;
those who write for ornamentation are excessive and superfluous.
Later authors
favored superfluity and neglected truth,
abandoning *fēng* and *yǎ* far behind,
and imitating *cífù* close at hand.
Thus, compositions embodying emotion became daily more scarce,
while works pursuing ornamentation grew increasingly abundant.
Hence, some harbored deep ambitions for officialdom,
yet vaguely sang of swamps and highlands.
Some were entangled in administrative duties,
yet emptily recounted things beyond the human realm.
With true essence absent,
they were completely reversed.
Peach and plum trees do not speak, yet paths form beneath them,
because they bear fruit.
A man may plant orchids, but they will not be fragrant,
because he lacks the proper feeling.
Even humble plants
rely on emotion and depend on substance.
How much more so for *wénzhāng*,
which takes the expression of intent as its foundation?
If words contradict intent,
how can writing be worth appealing to?
Therefore, when joining words and combining ornamentation,
the intention is to clarify principle.
If ornamentation is excessive and words are tricky,
then the mind's principle becomes even more obscured.
Thus, we know that emerald lines and cassia bait
are, on the contrary, the way to lose fish.
"Words conceal splendor"
probably refers to this.
Therefore, wearing a brocade gown covered with a plain robe
is to dislike excessive ornamentation.
The *Bì* hexagram depicting an ox stripping itself of color
values returning to the origin.
One who can set up a model to position principle,
and map out the ground to place the mind—
only after the mind is settled should sounds be formed;
only after principle is upright should ornamentation be spread.
This ensures that ornamentation does not obscure substance,
and broad knowledge does not drown the mind.
Let the proper colors shine among vermilion and indigo,
and secondary colors be screened out from crimson and purple.
Only then can one be said to have carved and polished the composition,
and be a refined *jūnzǐ*.
A eulogy says:
Words endure through embellishment;
this indeed is a true verification.
When the mind's method takes shape,
its brilliance becomes abundant.
Wú brocade is prone to fading,
the *shùnyīng* flower is merely superficially charming.
Excessive ornamentation with little emotion,
if tasted, will certainly sicken.
Chapter 32: *Róngcái* (Melting and Cutting)
With emotion and principle properly placed,
literary ornamentation proceeds within them.
Firmness and flexibility establish the foundation,
adaptability and change keep pace with the times.
Establishing the foundation has its proper form,
but intent may err on the side of excessive length.
Keeping pace with the times has no fixed method,
and diction may become redundant and cluttered.
The critical points controlled
by *róngcái* are
to straighten emotion and principle,
and to prune and refine literary ornamentation.
To regulate the fundamental structure is called *róng* (melting);
to cut away superfluous words is called *cái* (cutting).
With *cái*, weeds do not grow;
with *róng*, the main points are clear and smooth.
This is like the plumb line discerning divisions,
and the axe cutting and carving.
Webbed toes and supernumerary fingers
are excesses of nature;
superfluous growths and hanging tumors
are indeed excesses of form.
One idea expressed twice
is the webbed toes of meaning;
repetitive phrases and clauses
are the tumors and growths of writing.
Whenever thoughts first emerge,
diction and ornamentation are often mixed and confused.
If the mind does not act as a balance,
the weight will inevitably be uneven.
Therefore, when first drafting a grand composition,
one should first set three standards:
When embarking at the beginning,
establish emotion to position the structure;
when correcting in the middle,
weigh events to draw analogies;
when concluding at the end,
select words to summarize the main points.
Then, spread out the blossoms and fruits,
and select or reject according to the formal principles.
Beyond the plumb line,
good material has already been hewn.
Thus, the beginning and end can be perfectly integrated,
and the threads of thought can be consistently ordered.
If the method is not pre-established,
but one yields to the dictates of words,
different excesses will accumulate,
and redundancy and superfluity will be inevitable.
Therefore, once the three standards are established,
the next step is to examine the words and phrases.
If a phrase can be removed,
it clearly shows its looseness;
if a word cannot be reduced,
then its compactness is evident.
Concise discourse is the essence of brevity;
free-flowing thought and elaborate phrasing is the essence of prolixity;
to let the mind roam and embellish phrases
is the ultimate form of elaboration;
the so-called elaboration and brevity
are simply suited to individual preferences.
If you draw it out and expand upon it,
then two phrases can be spread into a chapter;
if you condense it and string it together,
then a chapter can be reduced to two phrases.
Those with abundant thoughts excel at expansion,
those with precise talent excel at deletion.
Those who excel at deletion remove words but retain the meaning,
those who excel at expansion use different words to make the meaning clear.
If words are deleted and the meaning is lost,
then it is a deficiency of brevity, not precision;
if phrases are expanded and the language becomes redundant,
then it is verbose and lacks boldness.
In the past, Xiè Ài and Wáng Jì,
literary men of Xīhé,
Zhāng Jùn said of them, "Ài's writing is so elaborate that it cannot be reduced,
Jì's writing is so concise that it cannot be added to."
These two men
can be said to have mastered the art of refinement and understood elaboration and brevity.
As for Shì Héng (Lù Jī), his talent was superior,
but his writing was particularly verbose;
Shì Lóng (Lù Yún)'s thoughts were inferior,
but he had a refined taste for clarity and conciseness.
When Yún commented on Jī's work,
he often regretted its verbosity,
yet praised its fresh and seamless flow,
not considering it a flaw,
probably out of respect for a friend.
When beautiful brocade is used to make clothing,
the length is measured appropriately;
even though one admires its colors,
one does not double the collar and sleeves.
Skill alone makes it difficult to elaborate,
how much more so if one is unskilled?
Yet the *Wén Fù* ("Rhapsody on Literature") suggests that brambles and shrubs should not be pruned
and that mediocre sounds are sufficient for melodies.
It's not that its understanding is lacking,
but rather that it suffers from a reluctance to cut back on verbosity.
The hundred joints form the body,
relying on each other for nourishment and defense;
the myriad elements come together to form literature,
inseparable from diction and emotion.
If emotions are complete without being verbose,
and diction flows without being excessive,
how can it be achieved without refinement and careful construction!
How else can this be achieved!
Encomium:
Chapters and sections are like doors and windows,
facing each other from left to right.
Words are like flowing rivers,
overflowing into excess.
Balance gains and losses,
judging thickness and thinness.
Prune the verbose and cut away the impurities,
relieving the burden.
Chapter Thirty-Three: Sound and Tone
The origin of musical tones
lies in the human voice.
The voice contains the *gōng* and *shāng* tones,
originating from one's physical constitution;
the ancient kings used this
to create music and songs.
Therefore, instruments imitate the human voice,
the voice does not learn from instruments.
Thus, language
is the crucial mechanism of brilliance in writing,
inhaling and exhaling the musical scale,
using only the lips and mouth.
In ancient singing instruction,
they first measured it according to the rules,
making one call out the *gōng* tone quickly,
and call out the *zhēng* tone slowly.
The *zhēng* and *yǔ* tones resonate high,
the *gōng* and *shāng* tones sound low;
the differences in raising the throat and adjusting the tongue,
the differences in gathering the lips and striking the teeth,
the cheek and flesh are compared,
and can be clearly distinguished.
If one plays a zither out of tune,
one will surely know to adjust the strings;
if one composes a piece with discordant passages,
one will not know where to adjust.
The sound is in the string,
and one can achieve harmony,
but the sound originates in my heart,
yet I lose the sense of harmony,
why is this?
It is because external listening is easier to master,
while internal listening is difficult to discern.
Therefore, external listening is easy
because the strings are adjusted by the hand;
internal listening is difficult
because the sound is confused with the heart;
it can be sought with numbers,
but it is difficult to pursue with words.
All sounds have rising and falling tones,
resonances have movement and stillness.
Repeating sounds separated by a character will inevitably be flawed,
overlapping rhymes in mixed phrases will certainly be discordant;
if the tone is low, the resonance starts and stops,
if the tone is high, the sound rises and does not return.
It is like a pulley going back and forth,
or scales placed next to each other;
to force their convergence
will cause going forward to be difficult and coming back to be delayed.
This illness
is the stammering of a literary writer.
The fault of stammering in writing
arises from a fondness for the unusual;
pursuing the new and seeking the different,
the throat and lips become tangled.
If you want to untie the knot,
you must be firm and decisive.
If there is an obstacle on the left, seek the right;
if there is a delay at the end, examine the beginning;
then the sound turns on the lips,
ringing like shaking jade;
the words delight the ear,
clustered like strung pearls.
Therefore, the beauty or ugliness of sound and tone
is vested in recitation;
flavor flows in the following phrases,
strength ends in harmonious rhyme.
Different tones following each other are called harmony,
the same sounds responding to each other are called rhyme.
Once the rhyme is established,
the remaining sounds are easily sent forth;
the harmonious form has rising and falling tones,
so the lingering sounds are difficult to match.
Adding brushstrokes is easy to master,
but selecting harmony is extremely difficult;
connecting texts is difficult to refine,
but creating rhyme is extremely easy.
Although subtle meanings change in complex ways,
it cannot be fully expressed in words,
but grasping the main principles
does not go beyond this discussion.
A grand harmony of *gōng* and *shāng*
is like playing the *yuè* flute;
turning around and taking the average is
quite similar to tuning a *sè* zither.
The *sè* relies on moving the bridges,
so sometimes there are discrepancies;
the *yuè* contains fixed pipes,
so nothing goes without unity.
Chén Sī (Cáo Zhí) and Pān Yuè
are like the tone of playing the *yuè* flute;
Lù Jī and Zuǒ Sī
are like the harmony of the *sè* bridges.
Generalizing and extrapolating,
you can see similar patterns.
Also, poets combine rhymes,
usually with clarity and precision;
the *Chǔ Cí* ("Songs of Chǔ") uses the language of Chǔ,
so inaccurate rhymes are especially common.
When Zhāng Huá discussed rhyme,
he said that Shì Héng (Lù Jī) used too much Chǔ dialect;
the *Wén Fù* ("Rhapsody on Literature") also says that choosing enough is not easy.
It can be said that he inherited the lingering sounds of Líng Jūn (Qū Yuán)
and lost the correct sound of the *huángzhōng* bell.
All movements of rhyme
are like turning a circle;
the creation of inaccurate sounds
is worse than a square peg in a round hole;
avoiding the square peg in the round hole
is not a great error.
Refining talent and penetrating insight,
analyzing words and drilling into sounds,
a broad knowledge and wide scope
follows the sounds encountered,
like a long wind passing through the pipes,
or Dōngguō playing the *yú* flute.
The jade pendants of the ancients
had *gōng* on the left and *zhēng* on the right,
to regulate their steps,
so the sound did not lose its order.
Using sound to regulate literature,
how can it be forgotten!
The Eulogy says:
To pursue emotions is to distance oneself;
to compare sounds is to approach.
Blowing the pitch-pipe from the heart and mind,
tuning the bell with the lips.
The sound obtains the flavor of salt and plums,
the resonance is as smooth as elm and hibiscus.
Abandoning the fragmented and disjointed,
the *gōng* and *shāng* scales are difficult to conceal.
Chapter and Sentence, Thirty-Fourth
Now, establishing emotions has its proper place,
positioning words has its proper rank;
the dwelling place of emotion is called a chapter,
the rank of words is called a sentence.
Therefore, a chapter
is clarity;
a sentence
is a boundary.
To define words is
to connect characters to delineate territory,
to clarify emotions is
to encompass meanings to embody wholeness.
Domains are different,
yet avenues are interconnected.
When a person composes words,
sentences are born from characters,
chapters are formed from accumulating sentences,
and a piece is completed by accumulating chapters.
The brilliance of a piece
lies in the flawlessness of its chapters;
the clarity and elegance of a chapter
lie in the unblemished nature of its sentences;
the clarity and excellence of a sentence
lie in the non-arbitrariness of its words.
Grasp the root and the branches will follow,
understand one and all will be complete.
When crafting compositions with a skillful pen,
pieces have varying lengths;
separating chapters and joining sentences,
the rhythm has its slow and fast paces.
Adapting to changes and fitting the occasion,
no fixed standard is to be seen.
A sentence controls several characters,
waiting to be connected for use;
a chapter encompasses a single idea,
requiring the exhaustive expression of meaning to achieve completeness.
Its controlling and guiding of emotions and reason,
its welcoming and meeting of junctures,
are like the dance's circular movements,
which have positions to mark the transitions;
the song's gentle and flowing voice,
which has measured ascents and descents.
Examining the poets' metaphors,
although one extracts meaning from a single chapter,
the chapter and sentence within the piece
are like drawing silk from a cocoon,
tracing the origin and requiring the end,
the body must be arranged in order.
The opening words
foreshadow the intention of the middle of the piece;
the concluding words
accompany and complement the meaning of the previous sentence;
therefore, the external writing is intricately interwoven,
the internal meaning flows like a pulse,
the calyxes and corollas connect to each other,
the beginning and end form a single body.
If the words lose their companions,
they are like travelers without friends;
if the matters deviate from their order,
they are like drifters without a home.
Therefore, searching for sentences avoids inversions,
crafting chapters values sequence;
this indeed is the aim of emotional appeal,
the common destination of writing skill.
As for chapters and sentences having no fixed length,
words have a regulated number,
four characters are dense but not rushed,
six characters are structured but not lax,
or changing them to three or five,
are the expedient adjustments depending on the situation.
As for the grand forms of the *Shī* (Odes) and *Sòng* (Hymns),
four-character lines are the standard,
only "Qí Fǔ zhào yīn" 祈父肇禋
uses two-character sentences.
Examining two-character lines originating in the era of Huáng Dì 黃帝,
the ballad of *Zhú Tán* 竹彈 is an example;
three-character lines arose during the time of Yú 虞,
the poem about the "original head" (元首) is an example;
four-character lines became widespread in the Xià 夏 dynasty,
the song of the Luò Ruì 洛汭 is an example;
five-character lines appeared in the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
the chapter *Xíng Lù* 行露 is an example.
Six-character and seven-character lines
were interspersed in the *Shī* (Odes) and *Sāo* (Elegies),
and the form of the poem
was completed in the two Hàn 漢 dynasties,
the range of emotions and numbers completed its cycle,
and was used according to the era.
As for changing rhymes to follow the melody,
this is how one regulates the temperament of the writing,
Jiǎ Yì 賈誼 and Méi Chéng 枚乘
changed rhymes after every two rhyming words;
Liú Xīn 劉歆 and Huán Tán 桓譚
did not change after a hundred sentences;
each had his own aim.
In the past, Wèi Wǔ 魏武 discussed *fù* (rhapsodies),
disliking the accumulation of rhymes,
and favoring their exchange and substitution.
Lù Yún 陸雲 also said, "For four-character phrases, changing the rhyme
every four lines is best."
Looking at their methods of rhyme,
their aims were the same as Méi Chéng's 枚乘 and Jiǎ Yì's 賈誼.
However, changing rhymes after every two rhyming words
makes the sound and rhyme slightly rushed;
not changing after a hundred sentences
makes the lips and mouth weary;
when brilliant talent is stimulated and uplifted,
although touching upon thoughts is beneficial and auspicious,
how does it compare to taking the middle path of harmony,
to ensure preservation without fault?
Moreover, poets include the character *xī* 兮 within the sentence's limit,
the *Chǔ Cí* 楚辭 uses it,
with the character outside the sentence's limit.
Looking at the character *xī* 兮 continuing the sentence,
it is a particle that aids the meaning, a lingering sound.
Shùn 舜 sang the Southern Wind,
using it for a long time,
but Wèi Wǔ 魏武 did not like it,
wasn't it because it didn't benefit the meaning of the writing?
As for *fū* 夫, *wéi* 惟, *gài* 蓋, and *gù* 故,
they are the initial sounds of the beginning;
*zhī* 之, *ér* 而, *yú* 於, and *yǐ* 以
are the old forms of filling in sentences;
*hū* 乎, *zāi* 哉, *yǐ* 矣, and *yě* 也
are also the standard practice of ending sentences.
Judging by the matter, they seem idle,
but in practice, they are truly essential.
Skilled ones maneuver them,
mending the form of the writing,
making it so that beyond several sentences,
one can obtain the help of a single character.
It is difficult to err with external characters,
how much more so with chapters and sentences!
The Eulogy says:
Extracting chapters has its rules,
accumulating sentences is not constant.
Reason relies on being matched with a master,
words avoid losing their companions.
Revolving emotions and drafting tones,
gracefully rising and falling.
Separating the same and combining the different,
in order to exhaust one's abilities.
Elegant Words, Thirty-Fifth
The Creator gives form,
limbs must be in pairs;
divine principle is used,
affairs are not isolated.
Now, the mind generates literary compositions,
planning and deciding on myriad thoughts,
high and low mutually depending
naturally forming pairs.
In the times of Táng Yáo (唐堯) and Yú Shùn (虞舜),
words had not yet reached literary refinement,
yet Gāo Yáo (皋陶) praised, saying:
"When in doubt about a crime, err on the side of leniency;
when in doubt about a merit, err on the side of reward."
Yì (益) presented counsel, saying:
"Complacency invites loss,
humility receives benefit."
Were these elaborate phrases?
They were merely spontaneous pairs.
The *Wén Xì* (文繫) of the *Yì* (易),
is the sage's wondrous thinking.
Explaining the four virtues of *Qián* (乾),
then eight phrases are linked together;
the dragon and tiger resonate,
then each character is paired;
*Qián* (乾) and *Kūn* (坤) are easy and simple,
then they subtly complement each other;
sun and moon come and go,
then across lines they are suspended and united;
although sentences and words may differ,
the paired meaning is one and the same.
As for poets pairing stanzas,
and high officials connecting phrases,
odd and even appropriately change;
not needing elaborate management.
Since Yáng Xióng (揚雄), Sīmǎ Xiàngrú (司馬相如), Zhāng Héng (張衡), and Cài Yōng (蔡邕),
greatly valued ornate language,
like Sòng (宋) paintings and Wú (吳) metalwork,
meticulously shaping forms and engraving methods,
beautiful sentences and profound embellishments flowed together,
paired meanings and unrestrained rhymes burst forth in unison.
Reaching the Wei (魏) and Jin (晉) dynasties' assembly of talents,
dissecting sentences became more meticulous,
linking words to combine interests,
analyzing down to the finest hair.
But those who grasp the opportunity enter with skill,
while those who merely feign achieve nothing.
Therefore, the forms of ornate language,
generally have four types of pairing:
verbal pairing is easy,
factual pairing is difficult,
antithetical pairing is superior,
parallel pairing is inferior.
Verbal pairing
is when two empty phrases are compared;
factual pairing
is when examples from people's experiences are cited together;
antithetical pairing
is when principles differ but interests align;
parallel pairing
is when affairs differ but meanings are the same.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's (司馬相如) *Shàng Lín* (上林) says:
"Cultivating appearance in the garden of rites,
soaring in the grove of books."
This is the type of verbal pairing;
Sòng Yù's (宋玉) *Shén Nǚ Fù* (神女賦) says:
"Máo Qiáng (毛嬙) covering her sleeve
is not enough to be a standard,
Xī Shī (西施) hiding her face
when compared, has no color."
This is the type of factual pairing;
Wáng Càn's (王粲) *Dēng Lóu* (登樓) says:
"Zhōng Yí (鍾儀) in captivity performed the Chǔ (楚) music,
Zhuāng Xì (莊舄) in prominence chanted the Yuè (越) song."
This is the type of antithetical pairing;
Zhāng Zǎi's (張載) *Qī Āi* (七哀) says:
"Emperor Gāo (高祖) of Hàn (漢) thought of Fényú (枌榆),
Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) longed for Báishuǐ (白水)."
This is the type of parallel pairing.
In all paired phrases within one's heart and mind,
verbal pairing is therefore easy;
in verifying people's knowledge,
factual pairing is therefore difficult;
in hidden and manifest sharing the same ideals,
antithetical pairing is therefore superior;
in both valuing common intentions,
parallel pairing is therefore inferior.
Furthermore, verbal pairing and factual pairing,
each have their correct and reverse forms,
by pointing out the categories and seeking them,
myriad paths will naturally be revealed.
Zhāng Huá's (張華) poem states, "Wandering geese fly wing to wing,
returning wild geese know to touch feathers."
Liú Kūn's (劉琨) poem says, "Xuān Ní (宣尼) grieved over the capture of the *lín*,
the western hunt caused Kǒng Qiū (孔丘) to weep."
If such repetition occurs,
then it is the superfluous branch of a paired sentence.
Therefore, verbal pairing, though beautiful,
values being refined and skillful;
factual pairing should prioritize
being appropriate and fitting.
If two matters are matched,
but the quality is uneven,
it is like a *jì* (驥) on the left as an outside horse,
with an inferior horse as the right horse.
If a matter is isolated,
and has nothing to pair with,
it is like Kuí's (夔) one foot,
hobbling along.
If the spirit lacks unique categories,
and the writing lacks distinct embellishments,
then dull and ordinary ornate language
will cause the eyes and ears to slumber.
One must make the principles complete and the affairs meticulous,
linking them like jade bracelets in their chapters,
alternating the use of odd and even,
ornamented with miscellaneous pendants,
then it will be esteemed.
Think in this manner,
and the principle will be seen.
Eulogy says:
Bodies invariably have pairs,
words invariably have matching.
Lifting on the left and pulling on the right,
exquisite flavors are concurrently conveyed.
Brightly gleaming linked blossoms,
mirror-still containing appearances.
Jade-like moistness flows in two streams,
like those *héng* (珩) and *pèi* (佩) pendants.
Analogy and Evocation, Thirty-sixth
The *Shī* (詩) texts are expansive and profound,
encompassing the six meanings,
Máogōng (毛公) in his commentary,
especially emphasizes the form of evocation,
is it not because *fēng* (風) communicates and *fù* (賦) is similar,
analogy is explicit and evocation is implicit?
Therefore, analogy
is attachment;
evocation
is arising.
Attaching to principles is to closely categorize in order to point to affairs,
arousing emotions is to subtly imitate and contemplate.
Arousing emotions is why the form of evocation is established,
attaching to principles is why the ratio of analogy is born.
Analogy then accumulates resentment in order to express words,
evocation then uses circular metaphors in order to convey satire.
Indeed, the meanings according to the times are not uniform,
therefore the ambitions of poets are twofold.
Observing the reliance on allegory of evocation,
subtle and forming chapters,
what is named is small,
what is categorized is large.
*Guān jū* (關雎) has distinction,
therefore the empress embodies virtue;
the turtledove is chaste and singular,
therefore the lady models righteousness.
Righteousness takes its chastity,
without following from ordinary birds;
virtue values its distinction,
not disliking birds of prey;
clear but not fused,
therefore it is only seen after explanation and annotation.
Furthermore, what is called analogy?
It is roughly describing objects to attach meaning,
raising words to closely correspond with affairs.
Therefore, gold and tin are used to metaphorically describe bright virtue,
*guī* (珪) and *zhāng* (璋) are used to compare outstanding people,
the caterpillar is used to categorize teaching,
the cicada is used to describe shouting,
washing clothes is used to imitate worries,
rolling up the mat is used to exemplify steadfast determination;
all such close images
are the meanings of analogy.
As for linen clothing like snow,
and two outside horses like dancing,
such categories
are all types of analogy.
King Xiāng (襄) of Chǔ (楚) believed in slander,
and Sān Lǘ (三閭) was loyal and upright,
following the *Shī* (詩) in creating the *Sāo* (騷),
satire combined analogy and evocation.
Although the Yán (炎) Hàn (漢) was prosperous,
its writers were flattering and sycophantic,
the path of satire was lost,
therefore the meaning of evocation disappeared.
Thereupon encomiums and odes were the first to resound,
therefore the form of analogy built up like clouds,
confused and jumbled,
trusting in old chapters.
Now, the meaning of analogy
lies in its inconstant selection of similar objects.
Sometimes it alludes to sounds,
sometimes it imitates appearances,
sometimes it corresponds to emotions,
sometimes it compares to events.
Sòng Yù’s 宋玉 "Gāo Táng" 《高唐》 says:
"The slender branches mournfully sing,
their sound resembling the *yúlài* 竽籟."
This is an example of analogy involving sound.
Méi Chéng’s 枚乘 "Tù Yuán" 《菟園》 says:
"Blazing and scattering,
like white clouds amidst dust."
This is an example of analogy involving appearance.
Jiǎ Yī’s 賈誼 "Fú Niǎo" 《鵩鳥》 says:
"Calamity and fortune,
how are they different from tangled hemp?"
This is using an object to analogize a principle.
Wáng Bāo’s 王褒 "Dòng Xiāo" 《洞簫》 says:
"Gentle and tender,
like a loving father's love for his son."
This is using sound to analogize emotion.
Mǎ Róng’s 馬融 "Cháng Dí" 《長笛》 says:
"Complex and elaborate,
like the discourses of Fàn 范 and Cài 蔡."
This is using sound to analogize debate.
Zhāng Héng’s 張衡 "Nán Dū" 《南都》 says:
"Rising to the *zhèng* 鄭 dance,
the seal dragging its cord."
This is using appearance to analogize an object.
Such examples as these,
are what *cí* and *fù* prioritize.
Daily, they employ analogy,
monthly, they forget inspiration.
Grasping the small and discarding the large,
is why literature declined after the Zhōu 周 people.
As for the likes of Yáng 揚 and Bān 班,
and Cáo 曹 and Liú 劉 that followed,
in depicting mountains and rivers,
and shadowing clouds and objects,
they all wove together analogical meanings
to spread their brilliance.
To startle the hearing and turn the gaze,
they relied on this to achieve success.
Furthermore, Pān Yuè’s 潘岳 "Yíng Fù" 《螢賦》 says:
"Molten gold lies in the sand."
Jì Yīng’s 季鷹 "Zá Shī" 《雜詩》 says:
"The green branches are like bundles of jade."
These are all instances of such meaning.
Therefore, although the types of analogy are numerous,
closeness and aptness are valued.
If one were to carve a crane resembling a duck,
it would be utterly worthless.
Commentary:
Poets use analogy and inspiration,
perceiving the world in its entirety.
Though objects are as distant as Hú 胡 and Yuè 越,
when combined, they are as close as the liver and gall.
Imitating appearances and grasping emotions,
decisions in rhetoric must be bold.
Amassing diverse songs and ballads,
like a river in full spate.
Exaggeration: Chapter Thirty-Seven
That which is above form is called the Dào 道;
that which is below form is called a vessel.
The divine Dao is difficult to depict;
exquisite words cannot pursue its limit.
Forms and vessels are easy to describe;
grandiose language can convey their essence.
Talent is not a matter of being short or long,
but rather, the principles themselves are easy or difficult.
Therefore, from the Heavens and Earth downwards,
making preliminary entry to sound and appearance,
whatever literature touches upon,
exaggeration invariably exists.
Even in the refined language of the *Shī* 詩 and *Shū* 書,
where the style instructs the world,
matters must necessarily be broadened,
and the writing, too, will be excessive.
Thus, in speaking of height, Sōng Gāo 嵩高 reaches the sky;
in discussing narrowness, the Hé 河 cannot accommodate a skiff;
in speaking of numerousness, children and grandchildren number a thousand million;
in speaking of scarcity, the people have no one left.
The overflowing waters of Xiāng Líng 襄陵 are cited,
and the theory of clubs floating in the blood of the overturned army is established.
Although the words are excessive,
their meaning is harmless.
Moreover, can the ugliness of the owl's cry
be transformed into beauty by the Pàn Lín 泮林?
Can the bitterness of *tú* 荼 herb
be made into candy by the Zhōu Yuán 周原 fields?
Because the intent involves deep praise and admiration,
the meaning is achieved through affected exaggeration.
This is recorded by the great sages
to establish a model.
As Mèng Kē 孟軻 said, "In discussing the *Shī* 詩, one should not let the words obscure the phrases,
nor let the phrases obscure the intent."
From Sòng Yù 宋玉 and Jǐng Chāi 景差 onwards,
exaggeration began to flourish.
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú 司馬相如, relying on the wind,
became even more extravagant and excessive.
Thus, in the halls of the Shàng Lín 上林 park,
shooting stars and winding rainbows enter the windows;
in the grand hunting expeditions,
Fēi Lián 飛廉 and Jiāo Míng 焦明 are both captured.
When Yáng Xióng 揚雄 wrote "Gān Quán" 《甘泉》,
he sampled its remaining waves.
In speaking of strangeness and wonder, he borrows treasures from the jade trees;
in speaking of utmost height, he falls into talk of ghosts and spirits.
As for the conjoined fish of the "Dōng Dū" 《東都》 and
the Hé Ruò 海若 of the "Xī Jīng" 《西京》,
if one examines the principles, there is no principle to be examined;
if one exhausts the embellishments, the embellishments are still inexhaustible.
Furthermore, in Zǐyún’s 子雲 "Xiào Liè" 《校獵》,
he whips Mì Fēi 宓妃 to feed Qū Yuán 屈原;
in Zhāng Héng’s 張衡 "Yǔ Liè" 《羽獵》,
he confines Xuán Míng 玄冥 in the northern wilderness.
That lovely Luò Shén 洛神,
is certainly not a *chīmèi* 魑魅;
and this water monster,
is also not a *wǎngliǎng* 魍魎;
yet they are vainly used with excessive forms--
is this not negligent?
This is an attempt to exaggerate his power,
but the events and meanings clash.
As for the air and appearance of mountains and seas,
the structure and disposition of palaces and halls,
the towering and soaring,
the glittering and luminous states,
the glowing radiance that seems about to ignite,
the imposing sounds and appearances that seem about to move—
all of these rely on exaggeration to achieve their form,
and follow embellishment to obtain their wonder.
Thereupon, later talents,
raise their spirit and amplify their voices,
soaring and eager to take flight,
bounding and ashamed to walk with small steps.
The language enters a fiery brilliance,
so that the vernal algae cannot measure its beauty;
the words lie in withered desolation,
so that the cold valleys cannot adequately form its decay.
In discussing joy, words and laughter come together;
in discussing sorrow, voices and weeping combine.
Truly, they can release the hidden and unleash the stagnant,
uncover the blind and startle the deaf.
However, when embellishment exhausts its essentials,
the heart's voice and sharp words arise;
when exaggeration exceeds its principles,
name and reality both diverge.
If one can draw from the expansive intent of the *Shī* 詩 and *Shū* 書,
and trim the excessive grandiosity of Yáng 揚 and Mǎ 馬,
so that exaggeration has restraint,
and embellishment is not deceptive,
then it can be called admirable.
Commentary:
Exaggeration lies in its application;
literature is surely not restrained by norms.
Words must be like the flight of the *péng* 鵬 bird,
the spirit must not resemble the gradual progress of a goose.
Dredging the sea for pearls,
and overturning Kūnlún 崑崙 to take jade.
Expansive without overflowing,
extravagant without blemish.
Use of Historical Examples: Chapter Thirty-Eight
The use of historical examples
involves drawing on events outside the text,
using historical events to categorize meanings,
and citing the past to verify the present.
In the past, King Wén 文 of Zhōu 周, in explicating the *Yì* 易,
analyzed and judged the positions of the lines.
In "Jìjì" 既濟, line nine three,
he remotely cited Gāo Zōng’s 高宗 campaign;
in "Míng Yí" 明夷, line six five,
he closely recorded Jī Zǐ’s 箕子 steadfastness.
This is selectively citing human events
to verify the meaning.
As for the "Yìn Zhēng" 《胤征》 of Xī Hé 羲和,
presenting the teachings of proper conduct,
and the "Pán Gēng" 《盤庚》 addressing the people,
narrating the words of Chí Rèn 遲任,
these are wholly citing established phrases
to clarify the principle.
Thus, clarifying principles involves citing established phrases,
and verifying meanings involves citing human events.
These are the grand schemes of sages and worthies,
and the universal standards of classics and scriptures.
The image of "Dà Xù" 《大畜》:
"The *jūnzǐ* 君子 thereby learns much of past words and deeds."
Also encompasses this within literature.
Looking at the works of Qū Yuán 屈原 and Sòng Yù 宋玉,
they are called imitators of the *Shī* 詩 (Poetry),
and although they cite ancient events,
they rarely take old phrases.
Only Jiǎ Yì's 賈誼 "Fú (Rhapsody) on the Owl" (鵩賦)
began to use the saying about the Héguān 鶡冠 (pheasant-feather cap);
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú's 司馬相如 "*Shànglín* (Superior Grove) Rhapsody" (上林)
excerpted and quoted from Lǐ Sī's 李斯 writing;
this is a one in ten thousand instance.
When it comes to Yáng Xióng's 揚雄 "*Liù Guān Zhēn* (Admonitions to the Six Ministries)," (六官箴)
he draws considerably from the *Shī* 詩 (Poetry) and the *Shū* 書 (Documents);
Liú Xīn's 劉歆 "*Suìchū Fù* (Rhapsody on the Beginning of My Retirement)" (遂初賦)
narrates events from histories and biographies;
gradually there was comprehensive selection.
As for Cuī Yóu 崔駰, Bān Gù 班固, Zhāng Héng 張衡, and Cài Yōng 蔡邕,
they gathered and selected from the classics and histories,
richness and substance were broadly displayed,
and they established merit through books,
all being models for later generations.
Ginger and cinnamon depend on the soil,
and their pungency is inherent in their nature;
writing depends on learning,
and talent lies in natural endowment.
Talent arises from within,
and learning is achieved from without.
There are those who are replete with learning but lack talent,
and there are those who are rich in talent but poor in learning.
Those poor in learning
are troubled in matters of event and meaning;
those lacking in talent
toil in matters of diction and emotion;
this is the distinct division between inner and outer.
Therefore, when directing one's mind to create literature,
the heart collaborates with the brush,
talent is the leader,
and learning is the assistant.
When the leader and assistant are in harmony,
literary brilliance will surely dominate;
when talent and learning are narrow and limited,
though beautiful, there will be little achievement.
Even with Ziyún's 子雲 (Yáng Xióng 揚雄) talent,
he admitted to not having studied,
but after viewing books in the Stone Chamber,
he achieved great brilliance.
Inner and outer support each other;
this is the same in ancient and modern times.
Therefore, Wèi Wǔ 魏武 (Cáo Cāo 曹操) called Zhāng Zǐ's 張子 (Zhāng Miǎo 張邈) writings clumsy,
but his learning was superficial
and his knowledge was not broad.
He specialized in picking up and compiling trivial pieces by Cuī 崔 and Dù 杜,
and what he produced cannot be easily challenged,
but if challenged, one would not know where his material came from.
This is the defect of limited knowledge.
The classics are profound and deep,
and the recorded books are vast and abundant.
They are truly the central domain of the words of the masses,
and the sacred borderland of talent and thought.
From Yáng 揚 (Yáng Xióng 揚雄) and Bān 班 (Bān Gù 班固) downward,
none did not draw resources from them.
If one diligently plows and weeds,
or freely hunts and fishes,
and one can cut with skill,
then one will surely divide the fertile fat.
Therefore, to provide amply for talent and ability,
one must strive to see broadly.
A fox's armpit cannot be warmed by a single pelt,
and one must eat several thousand chicken feet to be full.
Therefore, comprehensive learning lies in breadth,
selecting material values brevity,
rehearsing requires precision,
selecting principles requires verification,
all beauties converge,
and inner and outer shine forth.
Liú Shào's 劉劭 "*Zhào Dū Fù* (Rhapsody on the Capital of Zhào)" (趙都賦) says:
"The guests of the Gōngzǐ 公子 (Lord)
scold the stalwart Chǔ 楚 emissaries, ordering them to take an oath with blood;
the library slaves
berate the powerful Qín 秦 envoys, making them beat the earthen jar."
Using references like this
can be called reasoned and essential in meaning.
When the allusion has grasped its essence,
even if it is small, it will achieve great things,
like an inch-long linchpin controlling a wheel,
or a foot-long pivot operating a gate.
If subtle words and beautiful events
are placed in a random and neglected fashion,
it is like attaching gold and jade to the ankles and shins,
or applying fine powder and rouge to the chest and breast.
In general, when using old material, if it fits the occasion,
it will seem as though it came from one's own mouth;
if the citation is erroneous,
it will be a flaw even after a thousand years.
Chén Sī 曹植 was the hero among the talents of his group,
and in his "*Bào Kǒng Zhāng Shū* (Reply to Kǒng Zhāng's Letter)," (報孔璋書) he says:
"The music of Gétiānshì 葛天氏,
is sung by a thousand people,
and harmonized by ten thousand,
causing the listeners to despise the *Sháo* 韶 and the *Xià* 夏."
This is truly an erroneous citation.
According to accounts, the song of Gétiān 葛天
was only sung and harmonized by three people.
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú's 司馬相如 "*Shànglín* (Superior Grove) Rhapsody" (上林) says:
"Perform the dance of Táo Táng 陶唐,
listen to the song of Gétiān 葛天,
sung by a thousand people,
and harmonized by ten thousand."
Singing and harmonizing by thousands of people
was an exaggeration made by Sīmǎ Xiāngrú 司馬相如;
however, his extravagant use of Gétiān 葛天,
transforming three into ten thousand,
shows that believing in fantastical rhapsodies and reckless books
leads to such errors.
Lù Jī's 陸機 poem "Garden Sunflower" (園葵) says:
"Sheltering the feet is the same intelligence,
nourishing life involves different ends."
That sunflowers can protect the feet
is criticized by Bào 鮑 and Zhuāng 莊;
that kudzu vines shelter the roots
is a phrase from Lè Yù 樂豫;
if he compared kudzu to sunflowers,
then his citation is erroneous;
if he said that "sheltering" is superior to "protecting,"
then he changed the event and lost its truth.
This is also the problem of lacking precision.
Even with Zǐjiàn's 子建 (Cáo Zhí 曹植) clarity and knowledge
and Shìhéng's 士衡 (Lù Jī 陸機) depth and care,
they could not avoid errors.
What should Cáo Hóng's 曹洪 mistakes about Gāotáng 高唐
be mocked for?
Mountains of timber are measured by skilled artisans,
and the classics and books are selected by men of letters.
The beauty of the wood is determined by the axe and chisel,
and the beauty of the allusion is crafted by the knife and brush.
Scholars who research and contemplate
should not feel ashamed before the artisan Shí 匠石.
Eulogy says:
The classics and books are deep and rich,
and their principles are far-reaching and vast.
They are as bright as rivers and seas,
and as luxuriant as the Kūnlún 崑崙 and Dèng 鄧 mountains.
Let us gather together the catalpa and the zi trees,
and exchange pieces of fine jade.
Use others like you use yourself,
and from ancient times, there will be no confusion.
Refining Words, chapter thirty-nine.
When patterns were displayed, knotted cords were superseded;
when bird tracks became clear, written contracts were made.
These are the physical forms of language,
and the dwelling of literary composition.
When Cāng Jié (倉頡) created them,
ghosts wailed and grain rained down;
when Huáng Dì (黃帝) used them,
officials governed and the people were observant.
The teachings of the ancient kings,
in writing, always maintained a uniform script.
The envoys on light carriages
recorded the words of various customs,
in order to unify the script
and encompass diverse sounds.
In the Rites of Zhōu (周禮), the Master of Preservation (Bǎoshǐ 保氏)
was in charge of teaching the six scripts.
When Qín (秦) abolished the old regulations,
officials became the teachers.
Then Lǐ Sī (李斯) simplified the Dàzhuàn (大篆) and the Qín zhuàn (秦篆) arose;
Chéng Miǎo (程邈) created the lìshū (隸書) and the gǔwén (古文) fell into disuse.
In the early Hàn (漢) dynasty, laws were drafted,
clearly establishing their methods.
Grand scribes and school children
were taught and tested on the six scripts.
Moreover, when officials and common people submitted memorials,
any error in a character was immediately impeached.
Thus, because the character mǎ (馬) lacked a stroke,
Shí Jiàn (石建) feared death.
Though it is said he was by nature cautious,
this also shows the seriousness of characters at the time.
Reaching the reign of Xiào Wǔ (孝武),
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú (司馬相如) composed his pieces.
Then, under the two emperors Xuān (宣) and Chéng (成),
scholars of elementary learning (xiǎoxué 小學) were summoned.
Zhāng Chǎng (張敞) transmitted his knowledge through correcting readings,
and Yáng Xióng (揚雄) compiled his dictionary with unusual characters.
They both thoroughly studied the Yǎ (雅) and Sòng (頌),
and comprehensively reviewed sounds and meanings.
Those who composed prose
were all thoroughly enlightened.
Furthermore, many fu (賦) describing capitals and parks
used phonetic and semantic loans.
This is why the elementary learning of the Former Hàn (前漢)
often contained many unusual characters.
It was not only that they deliberately created oddities,
but rather that they collectively understood difficult characters.
As for the Later Hàn (後漢),
elementary learning gradually declined.
Complex characters and obscure meanings
were mostly criticized.
When it came to the ornamentations of the Wèi (魏) dynasty,
characters had regular norms.
Looking back at Hàn (漢) works,
they became obscure and difficult.
Therefore, Chén Sī (陳思) said:
"The works of Yáng (揚) and Mǎ (馬)
have profound meanings and deep purport.
Readers cannot analyze their words without a teacher's transmission,
nor can they grasp their principles without extensive learning."
It was not merely a difference in talent,
but also the obscurity of the characters.
Since the Jìn (晉) dynasty, the use of characters
has generally followed simplicity.
As everyone at the time practiced ease,
who would choose difficulty?
Now, if a single character is unusual,
the whole sentence will be startled;
if three people don't recognize it,
it will become a "character demon."
What later generations commonly understand,
though difficult, becomes easy;
what the times collectively abandon,
though easy, becomes difficult.
The choice between these
must not be overlooked.
The Éryǎ (爾雅)
was compiled by Confucius's (Kǒngzǐ 孔子) disciples,
and is the foundation of the Shī (詩) and Shū (書).
The Cāng Jié Piān (蒼頡篇)
was compiled by Lǐ Sī (李斯),
and is a remnant of the bird script and dàzhuàn (大篆).
The Yǎ (雅) provides the origin of glosses and explanations,
the Jié (頡) contains a treasury of unusual characters.
These different bodies complement each other,
like left and right shoulders and thighs.
Understanding the old to know the new,
one can also compose texts.
As for the meanings and explanations, ancient and modern,
their flourishing and decline having different uses;
and character forms, simple and complex,
their beauty and ugliness varying:
the mind entrusts its sound to words,
and words in turn entrust their form to characters.
In recitation, skill lies in musical harmony;
in composition, ability returns to character forms.
Therefore, when arranging characters to form a text,
one must carefully select:
first, avoid unusual characters;
second, reduce repeated radicals;
third, weigh repetitions;
fourth, balance simple and complex characters.
Unusual characters (guǐyì 詭異) are
those with strange and peculiar forms.
Cáo Chú's (曹攄) poem says: "How could I not desire this journey,
but my narrow heart dislikes the clamor."
These two characters are unusual,
a great blemish on a beautiful piece.
How much more so if it goes beyond this;
how could it be worth reading!
Repeated radicals (liánbiān 聯邊) are
characters that share a common component.
Describing mountains and rivers,
this has been used by all throughout history.
But applied to ordinary prose,
it becomes a flaw like clashing implements.
If it cannot be avoided,
it can be tolerated up to three instances.
Beyond three instances,
is it a dictionary?
Repetitions (chóngchū 重出) are
instances where the same character is used offensively.
In the Shī (詩) and Sāo (騷), they occur appropriately,
but recent generations avoid sameness.
If both characters are essential,
then it is better to have the repetition.
Therefore, a good writer
is rich in myriad pieces,
but poor in a single character.
It is not that characters are few,
but avoiding repetition is difficult.
Simple and complex characters (dānfù 單複) are
those with thin or dense forms.
If thin characters accumulate in sentences,
they appear sparse and the lines weak;
if dense characters fill a text,
it appears dark and the piece obscure.
A skillful balancer of characters
mixes simple and complex characters,
making them clear and luminous like pearls.
All these four points:
though a text may not necessarily have them,
the stylistic principles are indispensable.
If one encounters them but fails to realize,
then one lacks deep understanding.
As for the obscurities in the classics,
and the numerous bamboo and silk texts,
where slips are worm-eaten and silk torn,
repeated copying changes characters,
sometimes due to phonetic errors,
sometimes due to graphic alterations.
Zǐ Sī's (子思) disciple,
read "wū mù (於穆)" as "bù sì (不似)"—
this is an error due to phonetic similarity.
The Jìn (晉) historical record says "three pigs cross the river (sān shǐ dù hé 三豕渡河)"—
this is a mistake due to graphic alteration (where shǐ 豕 was mistaken for jǐ 己, leading to "three pigs" instead of "three days" or "three seasons").
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn (尚書大傳) has "bié fēng huái yǔ (別風淮雨)";
the Dìwáng Shìjì (帝王世紀) says "liè fēng yín yǔ (列風淫雨)".
"Bié (別)," "liè (列)," "huái (淮)," "yín (淫)"—
the characters seem to have subtly shifted.
"Yín (淫)" and "liè (列)" are appropriate in meaning but not unusual;
"huái (淮)" and "bié (別)" are logically inconsistent yet newly unique.
Fù Yì (傅毅) in his elegy
already used "huái yǔ (淮雨)";
Yuáncháng (元長) in his preface
also used "bié fēng (別風)".
It is clear that the love for the unusual
is the same throughout ancient and modern times.
Regarding lacunae in historical texts,
the sages were cautious.
If one abandons the unusual based on meaning,
then one can rectify characters.
Eulogy says:
Zhuàn (篆) and Lì (隸) fused,
Cāng Jié (蒼頡) and Éryǎ (爾雅) classified and explained.
Ancient and modern paths diverge,
beauty and ugliness are separately defined.
Characters are not of a different current,
but texts are blocked and difficult to circulate.
Sounds and strokes clearly precise,
ink and color soaring with vigor.
Obscurity and Elegance, Chapter 40
The movements of the mind's artistry are far-reaching,
the transformations of literary emotion are profound.
The source is abstruse, and the branches sprout;
the roots are luxuriant, and the spikes are lofty.
Thus, among the excellent flowers of literature,
there are those that are conspicuous and those that are hidden.
That which is hidden
is the profound meaning beyond the text;
that which is conspicuous
is that which stands out uniquely within the piece.
The hidden is skillful through complex meaning,
the conspicuous is clever through its outstanding excellence.
These are the splendid achievements of old writings,
the auspicious confluence of talent and emotion.
The hidden as a form
has meaning born outside the text,
with secret resonances communicating from the side,
latent brilliance subtly emitted.
It is like the transformations of hexagram images into complementary bodies,
or rivers and streams containing pearls and jade.
Therefore, complementary bodies transform hexagrams
and thereby complete the four phenomena;
pearls and jade lie submerged in water,
yet their ripples manifest squares and circles.
"The cool wind stirs the autumn grasses,
the border horses long for home"—
the air is cold and the matter sorrowful,
this is the lament of one on a journey.
Of all victorious pieces in a collection of writings,
not one in ten are truly outstanding;
of the beautiful lines in essays,
perhaps one in fifty.
They are encountered when thoughts converge naturally,
not by painstaking deliberation.
Some there are who take obscurity for profundity;
though abstruse, it is not hidden.
Others carve and chisel to achieve cleverness;
though beautiful, it is not conspicuous.
Hence, natural harmony is subtle and wonderful,
like the blossoming of flowers and trees in their prime;
embellishment for beauty
is like dyeing silk fabrics in vermilion and green.
Vermilion and green dyed on silk
are deep and richly vibrant;
the prime blossoms shining on trees
are light and resplendent.
Conspicuous lines illuminate the literary garden
for this very reason.
A eulogy says:
Profound writing, hidden and dense,
its lingering flavor subtly encloses.
Words born from complementary bodies,
somewhat like transformed hexagrams.
When speech is conspicuous,
a myriad thoughts converge as one.
Stirring the heart and startling the ear,
its excellent echoes like a *shēng* and *páo*.
Critiquing Faults (Zhǐxiá) Chapter Forty-One
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) once said:
"That which flies without wings is sound;
that which is firm without roots is emotion."
If this is so, then sound needs no wings,
its flight is very easy;
emotion needs no roots,
its firmness is not difficult.
To apply this to writing,
how can one not be cautious!
Literary talents throughout history,
from different eras compete:
some are swift and clear with exceptional talent,
others are meticulous with refined thought.
Yet, when thoughts move, it is difficult to be perfectly complete,
few are without flaws or defects.
The writings of Chén Sī (陳思) [Cáo Zhí (曹植)]
are among the finest of all talents,
yet his "Elegy for Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì)" says:
"The venerable spirit eternally hibernates."
His "Eulogy for Emperor Míng (Míng Dì)" says:
"The holy body floats lightly."
Floating lightly resembles a butterfly,
eternally hibernating somewhat suggests insects.
To apply these to the highest dignities,
how can it be appropriate!
Zuǒ Sī's (左思) "Seven Admonitions"
preaches filial piety but does not follow it;
to go against the Way like this,
the rest is not worth observing.
Pān Yuè (潘岳) as a talent
was skilled in lamentation;
yet when grieving for his maternal cousin,
he says he was moved by his "mouth's moisture";
when grieving for his deceased young son,
he says his "heart was like doubt."
The language of ritual is for the highest dignities,
but he applied it to the humble;
though the words are sorrowful enough,
the meaning is hereby debased.
A gentleman, when comparing people,
must compare them within their proper category.
Yet Cuī Yuàn's (崔瑗) "Elegy for Duke Lǐ (Lǐ Gōng)"
compares his conduct to Huáng (黃) and Yú (虞);
Xiàng Xiù's (向秀) "Rhapsody on Master Jī (Jī Shēng)"
compares his crime to Lǐ Sī (李斯).
Between these errors,
it is better to be presumptuous than abusive;
however, the poetry of 'high and thick'
is utterly dissimilar.
Clever words are easily marked,
clumsy phrases are hard to conceal.
These blemishes in speech
are truly deeper than on white jade.
Numerous examples are hard to enumerate,
therefore only four points are briefly listed.
As for the Way of composing text,
it lies solely in words and meaning.
Words are made correct by their definitions,
meaning is elucidated by reason.
However, the writings of the late Jìn (晉) period
only vaguely grasp this principle,
beginning with expressions like "appreciate the wonder" and "reach the extreme,"
and ending with phrases like "touch and knock," "respond and arrive."
They often single out a word
and point to it as emotion.
Now, *shǎng* (賞) means to bestow or grant,
how does it relate to understanding the heart?
*Fǔ* (撫) means to hold or grasp,
what connection does it have with emotion or reason?
It was unheard of in the *Yá* (雅) and *Sòng* (頌),
and unused in Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏).
If one strains to grasp the meaning, it seems plausible,
but when tested in context, it makes no sense.
This is truly a perversion caused by erroneous feelings
and the decline of writing leading to corruption.
Yet, the talents of the Sòng (宋) dynasty
have not changed it;
old habits have become custom,
not in a single day.
Modern literati
are mostly given to suspicion and jealousy;
they even compare words to seek out faults,
and reverse sounds to find blemishes.
Although they disdain the ancients,
they are selective about the present.
Moreover, if one's composition is identical to another's,
it should rightly be deleted or revised.
If one arranges another's beautiful phrases
and takes credit for them as one's own work,
then precious jade and a great bow,
in the end, are not truly his.
To copy entirely is to steal from a chest,
to borrow partially is to pick from a pouch.
However, those from distant times are too lightly regarded,
while those of the same era are considered worse.
As for writing commentaries,
it is for the purpose of clarifying facts and principles.
However, some err in their research
or make arbitrary judgments based on their own ideas.
The "Rhapsody on the Western Capital (Xījīng Fù)" mentions the likes of Zhōng Huáng (中黃) and Yù Huò (育獲),
but Xuē Zōng (薛綜) erroneously commented
that they were eunuch officials.
This shows he had not heard of those who captured carving tigers.
Also, in the "Well Field Tax (Jǐng Fù)" of the *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮),
there was traditionally "a *pǐ* (疋) of horses";
but Yīng Shào (應劭) explained *pǐ* (疋)
as either counting heads or hooves.
How could this be essential for distinguishing things!
Originally, the correct nomenclature of the ancients
was "two *liǎng* (兩) of chariots" and "a *pǐ* (疋) of horses."
*Pǐ* (疋) and *liǎng* (兩) are terms
used for paired couplings.
For chariots, two accompany the driver;
for horses, two are yoked as a team.
Since carriages and teams are not singular,
their names must be plural.
Once the name is correctly plural,
even a single one is a *pǐ* (疋).
A *pǐ* (疋) husband and *pǐ* (疋) wife
also signify a paired meaning.
These are small points regarding chariots and horses,
yet overlooked for generations;
and *cí* (辭) and *fù* (賦) are recent matters,
yet errors diverge by a thousand *lǐ*.
How much more, then, when scrutinizing the classics,
can one avoid error!
Indeed, to discuss words by counting heads and hooves,
and select the brave by driving out eunuch officials,
is too great an error in reasoning.
Therefore, these are cited as warnings.
Paintings initially shine but later fade,
while literature grows brighter with age.
If one can revise and refine in a single day,
one can be without shame for a thousand years.
A eulogy says:
Yì-shì's (羿氏) archery went awry,
Dōngyě's (東野) charioteering failed.
Though one may have outstanding talent,
errors lead to many apologies.
A single blemish in a statement
will not change for a thousand years.
If a chapter is faultless,
it is still second to the best.
Nourishing Qi (養氣), forty-second
In ancient times, Wáng Chōng (王充) wrote a book,
composing a chapter on "Nourishing Qi" (養氣).
He based it on his own experience;
how could it have been idly fabricated?
Ears, eyes, nose, and mouth
are servants of life;
mind, thought, speech, and words
are functions of the spirit.
If one follows one's will and yields to harmony,
then principles will be integrated and feelings will flow smoothly;
if one over-drills and over-polishes,
then the spirit will be fatigued and qi (氣) will decline.
This is the natural law of temperament.
The Three Sovereigns (三皇) were plain in speech,
their minds cut off from the splendor of the Dao (道);
during the Imperial Ages (帝世), writing began,
and words were valued for their presentation and memorials;
during the Three Dynasties (三代) and the Spring and Autumn (春秋) period,
though successive eras grew more ornate,
they all expressed what was fitting to the heart,
not forcing talent beyond its capacity.
