During the Warring States (戰代), there was cunning and deceit,
attacking with ingenious arguments and embellished theories;
from the Hàn (漢) dynasty until now,
words have striven for daily novelty,
competing for brilliance and peddling colorful phrases,
and thought has been exhausted.
Therefore, when plain words are compared to elaborate rhetoric,
simplicity and adornment are separated by a thousand years;
when following one's will is contrasted with exhausting one's emotions,
labor and ease differ by ten thousand li.
This is why the ancients had ample leisure,
and later generations had no time.
Generally, the young have shallow discernment and vigorous will,
while the elderly have firm knowledge and declining qi (氣).
Those with vigorous will have keen thoughts and overcome fatigue;
those with declining qi (氣) have meticulous thoughts and injure the spirit.
This is truly the common endowment of ordinary people,
a major distinction of the passage of years.
If one's capacity is limited,
but one's intellectual application is boundless,
or if one gradually mimics a duck's short legs and a crane's long legs,
draining words and engraving thoughts,
then the vital essence will dissipate internally,
like the waves of Wěilǘ (尾閭);
the spirit and will will be externally harmed,
like the trees of Niúshān (牛山);
the onset of severe anxiety
can also be inferred.
As for Zhòngrèn (仲任) setting out his inkstone to compile and narrate,
and Shūtōng (叔通) carrying his brush to specialize,
they were warmed by the sequence of years,
and also tormented by the hours and days.
This is why Cáo Gōng (曹公) feared that writing would harm his life,
and Lù Yún (陸雲) sighed that exerting thought exhausted the spirit;
these were not empty words.
Learning lies in diligence,
hence there is the self-exertion of piercing one's thigh with an awl;
if one is devoted to literature,
then there is the expression of suppressed emotions.
Therefore, it is best to follow one's feelings with ease,
and gently adapt to the occasion.
If one consumes one's vital essence and courage,
and constrains one's harmonious qi (氣),
holding a writing tablet to hasten one's life,
and sprinkling ink to harm one's nature,
how could this be the original intention of sages,
or the direct principle of composing literature?
Moreover, thought has its sharpness and dullness,
and time has its openness and obstruction.
If one is "immersed," the mind is overwhelmed,
and sometimes even acts abnormally.
When the spirit is in a state of confusion,
repetition only worsens the defilement.
Therefore, in the expression of literary arts,
it is essential to regulate expression,
to keep the mind clear and harmonious,
and to make the qi (氣) flow smoothly.
When fatigued, immediately stop,
do not allow it to become blocked.
When ideas come, unfold your feelings and take up the brush;
when principles are elusive, put down the brush and wrap them in your bosom.
Relax to alleviate fatigue,
talk and laugh to cure weariness.
Always reserve leisure at the peak of talent,
and store up surplus for literary vigor,
so that the blade is as new when it strikes,
and the textures are unobstructed.
Though this is not the myriad techniques of embryonic breathing,
it is also a method for protecting one's qi (氣).
A eulogy says:
How varied are the myriad phenomena!
How laborious are a thousand thoughts!
The profound spirit should be treasured,
and the vital qi (氣) nourished.
Water, when still, reflects;
fire, when calm, illuminates.
Do not disturb literary thoughts,
nor oppress this vital essence.
Cohesion (附會), forty-third
What is cohesion?
It means to integrate the literary principles,
unify the beginning and end,
determine what to include and omit,
and connect the boundaries,
to complete an entire piece,
making it diverse but not divergent.
It is like building a house which requires a foundation,
or tailoring clothes which require sewing.
For a talented youth studying literature,
it is essential to establish the proper structure.
One must regard emotion and will as the spirit,
matter and meaning as the bones and marrow,
diction and adornment as the skin and flesh,
and melody and rhythm as the voice and qi (氣).
Only then can one discern the subtle and profound,
display and reveal the precious and splendid,
offer what is acceptable and replace what is not,
to regulate its appropriateness.
This is the regular process of composing thoughts.
In general, lengthy articles
often have many branches and offshoots.
To organize the offshoots, follow the source;
to manage the branches, follow the trunk.
Therefore, when joining words and combining meanings,
it is crucial to unify the main points,
to guide ten thousand paths to the same destination,
and to align a hundred thoughts towards a single purpose,
so that even if the many principles are complex,
there is no disorder from inverted placement,
and even if the numerous words are abundant,
there is no confusion like tangled threads.
It should grow outward in the light,
and conceal its traces in the shade,
with a comprehensive and meticulous beginning and end,
and an internal and external unity.
This is the art of cohesion.
A painter who carefully draws hairs easily loses the likeness,
an archer who aims at a fine thread misses the wall.
Being overly focused on minute skill
necessarily neglects the overall structure.
Therefore, it is better to bend an inch to straighten a foot,
and to sacrifice a foot to make a zhang (尋) straight.
Abandon the cleverness of partial excellence,
and learn the achievement of complete beauty.
This is the general strategy for composing a piece.
Literary changes are endless,
and opinions are diverse and mixed.
If concise, the meaning becomes isolated;
if extensive, the words become disjoined.
Following old ways often leads to faults;
being overly demanding becomes detrimental to the work.
Moreover, talents differ,
and thought processes vary.
Some construct the head to connect the tail,
while others attach foot by foot and inch by inch.
However, those who can construct it entirely are few,
while those who piece it together are many.
If the main thread loses its coherence,
the flavor of the words will inevitably be chaotic;
if the vein of meaning does not flow,
then the literary piece will be withered and incomplete.
One who can foresee the inner workings
will then achieve coherence naturally,
like glue adhering to wood,
or beans joining their yellow cotyledons.
Thus, four stallions may have different strengths,
but the six reins are like a zither;
the method of managing literature
is similar to this.
To keep or to discard is up to the mind,
length and brevity are in one's hand.
Just unify its steps,
and simply hold the reins.
Thus, a skillful joiner of ideas can make diverse intentions align like liver and gallbladder,
while a clumsy one makes harmonious sounds diverge like Hú and Yuè.
To alter an existing chapter is harder than to compose a new piece;
to change a word is more difficult than to replace a whole phrase.
This is a verified truth.
In the past, Zhāng Tāng doubted his memorial and withdrew it twice,
and Yú Sōng drafted his petitions and was repeatedly censured.
Both cases stemmed from a lack of clarity in their reasoning
and a disharmony in their expression and intent.
However, when Ér Kuān redrafted,
and Zhōng Huì changed a word,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sighed in wonder,
and Emperor Jǐng of Jìn praised them.
This was because their reasoning was sound and their facts clear,
their minds nimble and their words apt.
From this perspective,
one can see that the skill and clumsiness in joining ideas
are poles apart!
As for abrupt endings and broken chapters,
they are like a boatman fumbling with his oar;
to successfully complete a work and achieve its goal
depends on writing it through to the end.
If the opening lines are splendid and flourishing,
but the subsequent phrases are withered and desolate,
then the initial force will be stifled,
and the lingering spirit will not flow freely.
This is what the *Zhōu Yì* calls "the buttocks without skin,
its movement is hindered."
Only when the beginning and end support each other
can the structure of coherence
be said to be unsurpassed.
Eulogy:
The structure of the piece is intricate,
the array of emotions and numbers dense.
From beginning to end,
sparse branches spread out into leaves.
The flavors of the Way adhere to each other,
the suspended threads spontaneously connect.
Like the harmony of music,
the heart's voice perfectly accords.
Chapter 44: General Principles
Contemporary common parlance
distinguishes between *wén* and *bǐ*,
considering compositions without rhyme as *bǐ* and those with rhyme as *wén*.
However, *wén* serves to convey words,
and its principles encompass poetry and prose;
the distinction into two names
is merely a recent phenomenon.
Yán Yánnián believed that "the essence of *bǐ*
is the refined expression of words;
the classics are words but not *bǐ*,
while historical records are *bǐ* but not words."
Allow me to seize his spear
and attack his own shield.
Why?
Is not the *Wényán* of the *Yì*
both words and *wén*?
If *bǐ* truly is verbal expression,
then it cannot be said that the classics are not *bǐ*.
He intended to establish a theory,
but his theory remains unfounded.
I believe that what is spoken is *yán* (words),
what is put to paper is *hàn* (writing),
the constant Way is *jīng* (canon),
and what expounds the canon is *zhuàn* (commentary/tradition).
The forms of *jīng* and *zhuàn*
emerge as words and enter as writing;
*bǐ* serves *yán*,
and can be strong or weak.
The *Liùjīng* (Six Classics) are considered immutable for their classical profundity,
not because of any superiority or inferiority between *yán* and *bǐ*.
Formerly, Lù Shì's *Wénfù*
was acclaimed as exhaustive;
yet it broadly discusses minutiae
but does not fully grasp the essential substance.
Hence, one knows that the "nine transformations" are not easily traversed,
and that selecting words of understanding is difficult to master.
When composing, with meticulous thought,
each vies for novelty and beauty,
many wish to refine their diction,
but few are willing to delve into the art.
Sometimes, a brilliant jade
is mixed with stones;
other times, an ordinary stone
resembles jade.
The refined are concise,
the deficient are also rare;
the erudite are comprehensive and rich,
the overgrown are also verbose;
the eloquent are clear and distinct,
the shallow are also exposed;
the profound are intricately subtle,
the strange are also circuitous.
Sometimes the meaning is splendid but the sound is withered,
sometimes the reasoning is clumsy but the writing is polished.
One realizes that tuning a bell is not easy,
and stretching the strings of a zither is indeed difficult.
A musician announcing harmony
does not necessarily reach the depths of every note;
waving a fan in use
does not necessarily encompass the full rhythm from start to finish.
Wèi Wén's comparison of literary pieces to music
certainly has its basis.
If one does not cut through tangled roots,
one cannot test sharp tools;
if one does not dissect the profundities of writing,
one cannot distinguish versatile talents.
The ability of talent to be versatile
must rely on clear understanding of principles.
Unless one has a comprehensive view of all regions
and can broadly categorize rules,
how can one control the springs of emotion
and achieve victory in the literary garden?
Therefore, wielding principles to control a piece
is like a skillful chess player exhausting all possibilities;
abandoning principles and relying on intuition
is like gambling with dice.
Thus, writing that is like gambling
borrows momentary cleverness;
though the vanguard may succeed,
the reinforcements are difficult to sustain.
When it is too brief, there is nothing to connect;
when it is too verbose, one does not know what to delete.
Thus, both brevity and verbosity are perplexing,
how then can one control beauty and ugliness?
However, writing that is like skillful chess
has constant principles.
Arranging sections and ordering elements,
it awaits the opportune moment for emotion,
adapting to timing and seizing opportunities,
never deviating from correctness in action.
When the calculations reach their peak,
and the opportunity falls into cunning,
then meaning and flavor surge forth,
and diction and spirit arrive in profusion.
To behold it is like brocade,
to hear it is like silk and pipes,
to taste it is like rich sweetness,
to wear it is like fragrance.
The achievement of perfect chapters
is most splendid at this point.
Although a swift horse is excellent,
a long tether restrains it;
even a tiny impediment
can prevent a journey of a thousand *lǐ*.
How much more so for literary forms with their many principles,
all mutually intertwined!
If one element goes astray,
the whole structure collapses.
Therefore, to list them in one chapter,
comprehensively surveying all changes in sentiment,
is like thirty spokes
jointly forming one hub.
Though this may not be a complete view,
it is still the insight of a humble person.
Eulogy:
The literary arena and the realm of writing
have their arts and their entrances.
One must prioritize the overall structure,
and one's judgment must probe the source.
By grasping one, one controls ten thousand;
by seizing the essential, one governs the complex.
Thoughts have no fixed pattern,
but principles endure forever.
Chapter 45: Temporal Sequence
When times and fortunes change,
and substance and refinement alternate,
the sentiments and principles of ancient and modern times
can perhaps be spoken of!
In the past, during the time of Táo Táng,
virtue flourished and transformation was pervasive.
Old men in the fields uttered talks of "What power!"
and children in the suburbs hummed songs of "Not knowing."
Yǒu Yú then succeeded,
government was prosperous and the people were at leisure.
The "Xūnfēng" (薰風) poem was sung to the Empress Dowager,
and the "Lànyún" (爛雲) song was sung by the myriad officials.
When their beauty reached its peak,
why was it that their hearts were joyful and their voices serene!
Then Dà Yǔ spread the land,
and the "Jiǔxù" (九序) praised his achievements;
Chéng Tāng was reverent and sagely,
and "Yīyú" (猗歟) was composed as an ode.
When the virtue of Jī Wén flourished,
the "Zhōunán" (周南) was diligent but without resentment;
when the transformation of Tài Wáng was pure,
the "Bīnfēng" (邠風) was joyful but not licentious;
when Yōu and Lì were dim-witted, the "Bǎn" (板) and "Dàng" (蕩) were angry,
and when Píng Wáng was weak, the "Shǔlí" (黍離) was mournful.
Thus we know that the principles of songs and rhymes
change with the times;
the wind moves above,
and the waves surge below.
After the Chūnqiū period,
heroes clashed,
the Liùjīng (六經) lay dormant like coiling dragons in the mud,
and the Bǎijiā (百家) surged forth like a whirlwind.
At that time,
Hán and Wèi exerted political power,
Yān and Zhào relied on authority;
the Wǔdù (五蠹) and Liùshī (六蝨) were strict under the Qín decrees.
Only the two states of Qí and Chǔ
had a fair amount of literature.
Qí opened the mansions of Zhuāngqú,
Chǔ expanded the palaces of Lántái.
Mèng Kē was a welcomed guest,
Xún Qīng was a chief magistrate.
Therefore, Jìxià fanned its pure winds,
and Lánlíng exuded its rich customs.
Zōu Zǐ flew to fame by discussing heaven,
Zōu Shì gained renown by carving dragons,
Qū Píng linked his embellishments to the sun and moon,
and Sòng Yù intertwined his brilliance with wind and clouds.
Observing their ornate expressions,
they enveloped the Yǎ and Sòng.
Thus we know that extraordinary and brilliant ideas
arise from the strange customs of horizontal and vertical alliances.
Then came the Hàn dynasty,
whose fortune followed the burning of books.
Gāozǔ esteemed military prowess,
ridiculed scholars and simplified learning.
Though rituals and laws were initially established,
the Shī and Shū were not yet prioritized.
Nevertheless, the songs of "Dàfēng" (大風) and "Hónghú" (鴻鵠)
were also inspired and brilliant creations.
This extended to Xiàohuì,
and up to Wén and Jǐng.
Classical studies gradually flourished,
but men of letters were not employed;
Jiǎ Yí was suppressed and Zōu Méi were overlooked,
which can be understood.
When Xiàowǔ revered Confucianism,
he embellished his grand enterprise.
Rituals and music competed in splendor,
and literary embellishments vied with each other:
poems for court banquets were displayed in Bóliáng,
and odes for comforting the people were composed at Jīndī.
Méi Shèng was summoned with a sedan chair,
and Zhǔfù Yàn was given a prime minister's feast.
Gōngsūn Hóng's policy proposals were selected,
and Ār Kuān's doubtful memorials were praised.
Mǎi Chén carried firewood and wore fine silks,
Xiāngrú washed dishes and wore embroidered robes.
Thus, the likes of Shǐ Qiān and Shòu Wáng,
and the group of Yán Zhōng and Méi Gāo,
their impromptu responses were boundless,
and their compositions were inexhaustible.
Their lingering styles and remaining brilliance
had no equal.
Beyond Zhāo and Xuān,
who indeed continued Wǔ's achievements,
they galloped through Shíqú,
and indulged in literary gatherings.
They gathered exceptional talents for carving and inscription,
and expressed profound metaphors in elegant prose.
Hence, people like Wáng Bāo
obtained salaries as imperial appointees.
From Yuán to Chéng,
they lowered themselves to study books,
praised the refined discussions like jade fragments,
and cleared the path to Jīnmǎ Gate.
Zǐyún sharpened his thoughts on a thousand works,
and Zǐzhèng collated and proofread the Liùyì (六藝).

From the Hàn imperial house,
up to Chéng and Āi,
although a hundred years passed,
and the men of letters underwent nine transformations,
their main inclination
was to follow the Chǔcí (楚辭);
the lingering influence of Líng Jūn
was present therein.
From the decline of Āi and Píng,
Gāngwǔ brought about the restoration.
He deeply cherished prophecies and omens,
and somewhat neglected literary embellishments.

and Bān Biāo submitted a memorial to amend decrees.
Though not actively sought,
they were not cast aside.
When Míng and Zhāng shone brightly in succession,
they highly esteemed Confucian studies.
They practiced rites in Bìtáng,
and lectured on literature in Hǔguān.
Mèng Jiān served as an imperial historian with a brush behind his ear,
and Jiǎ Kuí supplied notes for auspicious odes.
The Prince of Dōngpíng excelled in his refined writings,
and the Prince of Pèi promoted his comprehensive treatises.
The emperors were models for the feudal lords,
and their brilliance shone upon each other.
From Hé and Ān onwards,
up to Shùn and Huán,
there were Bān, Fù, the three Cuī,
Wáng, Mǎ, Zhāng, and Cài—
numerous great scholars.
Talents were never lacking for the times,
but the selection of literary works
existed without being discussed.
However, after the restoration,
the various talents gradually changed their former paths.
What they attached their essence and substance to
was based on the refinement of classical phrases.
This was likely due to the successive regimes emphasizing gatherings,
and thus gradually influenced by the Confucian style.
Down to Língdì,
the emperor had a penchant for literary composition.
He created the books of Xī Huáng,
and initiated the rhapsodies of Hóngdū.
However, the likes of Yuè Sōng
gathered shallow and vulgar people,
so Yáng Cì was called Huāndōu,
and Cài Yōng compared them to actors.
Their remaining styles and lingering writings
were probably negligible.
When Xiàndì was displaced and exiled,
literature was scattered like tumbleweeds.
At the end of Jiàn'ān,
the realm was finally brought together.
Wèi Wǔ, with the dignity of a princely king,
had a refined love for poetry and essays;
Wén Dì, with the importance of a crown prince,
was exquisitely skilled in rhapsodies and prose;
Chén Sī, with the gallantry of a noble son,
wrote with sparkling brilliance.
Their styles and manner were all outstandingly elegant,
hence talented individuals emerged like clouds.
Zhòngxuān pledged his allegiance in Hànnán,
Kǒngzhāng surrendered to Héběi,
Wěicháng served as an official in Qīngtǔ,
Gōnggàn sacrificed his life at the seashore.
Délián synthesized his brilliant thoughts,
and Yuányú displayed his elegant joy.
The likes of Wénwèi and Xiūbó,
and the companions of Zǐshū and Dézǔ,
were elegant and proud before cups and plates,
and composed on mats and beds.
They dashed off writings to compose songs in intoxication,
and mixed ink to accompany their talk and laughter.
Observing their writings of the time,
they were gracefully impassioned;
this was because the world had accumulated chaos and separation,
the customs had declined and resentments were rife.
Their aspirations were deep and their writing expansive,
hence they were broad in outline and full of spirit.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he composed poems and set them to music.
He summoned men of letters
and established the Chóngwén Monastery.
Hé and Liú, talented individuals,
illuminated each other in succession.
Young emperors followed one after another,
only Gāoguì was exceptionally refined,
his glances contained brilliance,
and his every word became a treatise.
At that time, the lingering style of Zhèngshǐ
was light and elegant in form,
and Jī, Ruǎn, Yīng, and Miáo
all excelled in the literary path.
When Jìn Xuānshǐ began his foundation,
Jǐngwén completed the structure.
Both concealed their traces in scholarly refinement,
but deeply engaged in arcane arts.
When Wǔdì initiated renewal,
he received the mandate in an era of peace,
but the chapters of the Jìnxù were bound
and not reviewed by the imperial mind.
Down to Huáimǐn,
they merely wore the imperial regalia.
Yet, though the Jìn lacked literary embellishment,
its talent was truly abundant:
Màoxiān's pen shook and scattered pearls,
Tàichōng's ink moved and spread brocade,
Yuè Zhàn shone with the brilliance of a paired jade,
Jī Yún distinguished themselves with the splendor of two paragons,
while the likes of Yīng and Fù, and the Three Zhāngs,
Sūn Zhì and Chénggōng's ilk,
all composed with clear brilliance,
their rhymes flowing with exquisite beauty.
Former historians believed that as the dynasty entered its decline,
people could not fully realize their talents.
How true this saying is,
it truly makes one sigh!
When Yuánhuáng restored the dynasty,
he promoted literature and established schools.
Liú and Diāo, though officials of ritual, were honored and favored,
while Jǐngchún, being refined in literature, was excellently promoted.
When Míngdì grasped wisdom,
he greatly enjoyed literary gatherings.
Ascending as heir apparent and then to the throne,
he diligently lectured on the arts,
honing his emotions in edicts and strategies,
and displaying his splendor in prose and poetry.
Yǔ became closer due to his writing talent,
Wēn's literary thoughts deepened even more.
His exaltation of refined elegance
made him like Hànwǔ in that era.
When Chéng Kāng had short lives,
Mù Ái brief reigns,
Jiǎnwén rose vigorously,
profoundly clear and lofty.
Subtle words and refined principles
filled the abstruse discussions,
while his serene thoughts and rich splendor
were occasionally scattered in the literary garden.
When Xiàowǔ did not continue it,
Ān Gōng's reign ended;
among their literary historians were the likes of Yuán and Yīn,
and Sūn Gàn's group.
Although their talents varied in depth,
their excellence was quite sufficient.
Since the Central Court valued profundity,
the region south of the Yangtze River became prominent.
The lingering influence of their discussions
flowed and formed a literary style.
Thus, though the age was one of extreme hardship, the sentiments of the verses were peaceful and composed;
poetry invariably followed the principles of the Zhùxià,
and rhapsodies were glosses on the meaning of Qīyuán.
Hence, we know that literary change is influenced by the temper of the age,
and its rise and fall are linked to the sequence of times.
By tracing the origin to observe the end,
even a hundred generations can be known.
Since Sòngwǔ loved literature,
and Wéndì was refined and elegant,
possessing literary virtue,
Xiàowǔ had many talents,
his splendid brilliance forming like clouds.
From Míngdì onward,
literary principles declined.
Yet, among the scholarly elite,
they rose like radiant clouds and strong winds;
Wáng and Yuán joined clans with dragon-like splendor,
Yán and Xiè had successive generations of phoenix-like brilliance.
The likes of Hé, Fàn, Zhāng, and Shěn
were too numerous to count.
As they are generally known in the world,
I shall briefly mention the most prominent.
When Huáng Qí controlled the precious realm,
the dynasty gathered in glorious brightness:
Tàizǔ received the mandate through his sagely martial prowess,
Gāozǔ inherited the enterprise with his keen literary skill,
Wéndì possessed literary brilliance as second in line,
and Zhōngzōng initiated the dynasty with supreme wisdom.
All were endowed with heavenly culture and brightness,
continuing the distant, auspicious reign.
Now, the sacred dynasty is flourishing,
literary thoughts are abundant,
deities descend from seas and mountains,
talents emerge brilliantly.
They ride flying dragons across the heavenly paths,
and drive magnificent steeds for ten thousand *lǐ*.
The classics, rituals, and ordinances
surpass Zhōu and Hàn.
The literature of Táng Yú,
how immensely prosperous it is!
Grand style and exquisite brilliance,
my humble pen dares to present;
to express praise for the era,
I entrust to the wise.
An encomium says:
Radiant through ten dynasties,
literary splendor changed nine times.
What moved within the pivot
circulated without weariness.
Simplicity and embellishment followed the times,
exaltation and decline depended on choice.
Though ancient times are far,
they are vaguely like facing them.
The Qualities of Things (Wùsè) Forty-Sixth
As spring and autumn alternate,
and yin and yang fluctuate,
with the movement of the qualities of things,
the heart also stirs.
When yang *qì* sprouts, the dark steed takes its steps;
when yin laws congeal, the vermilion bird becomes shy.
Even tiny insects are sometimes moved,
how much more so the creatures of the four seasons.
If fine jade manifests its perceptive heart,
and brilliant blossoms show forth their clear *qì*,
and the qualities of things call to each other,
who can remain undisturbed?
Therefore, when the new year brings spring,
feelings of joy and delight blossom;
in the surging early summer,
a brooding heart congeals;
when the sky is high and *qì* clear,
somber aspirations extend far;
when hail and snow are boundless,
thoughts of reverence and solemnity deepen.
Each year has its things,
and each thing its appearance;
emotions shift with things,
and words issue forth from emotions.
Even a single leaf can prompt a feeling,
and the sound of insects is enough to draw the heart.
How much more so when clear breeze and bright moon share the night,
and white sun and spring forest share the morning!
Therefore, poets, moved by things,
make endless associations;
they linger among myriad phenomena,
and ponder within the realm of sight and sound;
depicting *qì* and portraying form,
they conform to things and turn with them;
attaching splendor and appending sound,
they also wander with the heart.
Thus, *zhuózhuó* describes the freshness of peach blossoms,
*yīyī* fully conveys the appearance of willows,
*gǎogǎo* is the look of the rising sun,
*biāobiāo* mimics the state of rain and snow,
*jiējīe* imitates the sound of the oriole,
*yāoyāo* learns the rhythm of grass insects.
*Jiǎorì huìxīng*,
one word captures the essence;
*cēncī wòruò*,
two characters link form.
All use little to encompass much,
leaving nothing of emotion or appearance.
Even after a thousand years of contemplation,
how could one easily alter them?
When *Lí Sāo* rose in succession,
it extended by association,
as the forms of things were hard to exhaust,
thus it piled up and spread out descriptions,
whereby categories of *cuó'é* clustered,
and groups of *wēiruí* accumulated.
Down to the likes of Chángqīng,
with their strange stances and rare sounds,
modeling mountains and rivers,
words invariably linked like fish.
This is what is meant by poets making their beauty conform to rules and their words concise,
while rhapsodists indulge in beauty and their sentences are verbose.
As for *Yǎ* singing of crabapple flowers,
some yellow, some white;
*Sāo* describing autumn orchids,
green leaves and purple stems;
in general, when displaying the five colors,
it is precious that they appear at the right moment.
If green and yellow appear too often,
then it is verbose and not precious.
From recent times onward,
literary works have valued physical resemblance,
peering into emotions from scenery
and probing forms from flora and fauna.
The inspiration of their chants
lay solely in profound remoteness.
Their skill in describing objects was exquisite,
and their merit lay in meticulous adherence.
Thus, their ingenious words and precise descriptions
were like an imprint on clay,
without further carving or cutting,
yet subtly depicting every detail.
Therefore, one could gaze at the words and see the form,
or read the characters and know the time.
However, objects have constant forms,
but thoughts have no fixed limits.
Some may reach the pinnacle spontaneously,
while others, with elaborate thought, become more diffuse.
Moreover, what the Shī and Sāo
marked out were all essential points.
Hence, later sharp-witted writers
were timid about competing.
They all borrowed ingenuity from established methods,
and encountered marvels by following the trend.
Those skilled in adapting to essentials
will make even the old new again.
Thus, the four seasons revolve in profusion,
yet what enters as inspiration values leisure.
Though descriptions of objects are numerous,
the analysis of language still favors conciseness.
This causes the flavor to float lightly,
and the emotion to glow and renew.
From ancient times, writers,
succeeding each other through different eras,
all transformed by combining elements,
and achieved merit through reform and innovation.
Those who exhaust the depiction of objects yet leave emotion in abundance
understand comprehensive mastery.
As for mountains, forests, marshes, and fields,
they are truly the profound repository of literary thought.
To describe them briefly is to miss much;
to describe them in detail is cumbersome.
However, that Qū Píng was able to profoundly observe the emotions of the Shī and Sāo,
was it not also with the help of rivers and mountains?
A panegyric says:
Mountains piled, waters winding,
trees mingled, clouds gathered.
The eyes travel to and fro,
the heart also breathes in and out.
Spring days are long and lingering,
autumn winds sighing.
Emotion given forth is like a gift,
inspiration arising like a reply.
Talent and Conciseness, Chapter 47
The literature of the Nine Dynasties
is rich and splendid;
its eloquent and brilliant rhetoric
can be discussed briefly yet in detail.
As for the writings of Yú and Xià,
there are Gāo Táo’s Six Virtues,
Kuí’s arrangement of the eight musical tones,
Yì’s eulogies,
and the Five Sons’ songs.
Their language and meaning are gentle and elegant,
a model for ten thousand generations.
In the eras of Shāng and Zhōu,
Zhòng Huǐ recorded his admonitions,
Yī Yǐn promulgated his instructions,
and Jí Fǔ and his ilk
all narrated the Shī and Sòng.
Their meaning was indeed canonical,
and their style also served as a model.
By the time of the Dàfū of the Chūnqiū period,
they refined their rhetoric and engaged in witty discourse,
splendid like a garden of exquisite jades,
radiant like a store of patterned brocades.
Wěi’ Ào selected the excellent statutes of the State of Chǔ,
Suí Huì lectured on the rituals and laws of the State of Jìn,
Zhào Shuāi prevailed in a banquet with his writing,
Guó Qiáo defended Zhèng with his refined rhetoric,
Zǐ Tàishū was handsome and cultivated,
Gōngsūn Huī was skilled in rhetoric.
All were prominent figures in literary fame.
In the Warring States period, military might was emphasized,
yet literati never ceased to appear.
The various masters drew resources from their Daoist arts,
Qū and Sòng displayed their brilliance with the Chǔ Cí,
Yuè Yì’s reply letter was eloquent and just,
Fàn Suī’s memorial was meticulous and profound,
Sū Qín’s successive persuasions were grand and effective,
Lǐ Sī’s own memorials were elegant and moving.
If they had lived in a literary age,
they would have been peers of Yáng and Bān.
Xún Kuàng, a master of learning, created descriptive Rhapsody (fù) of names of objects.
His style and substance matched,
which was truly the sentiment of a great scholar.
In the Hàn dynasty, Lù Jiǎ
was the first to display extraordinary brilliance.
He composed the Rhapsody on Early Spring (fù Mèngchūn) and selected canonical pronouncements;
how rich his eloquence was!
Jiǎ Yì, with his brilliant talent,
surpassed even the flying rabbit.
His proposals were agreeable and his Rhapsody was clear;
how could he have achieved this without true merit!
Méi Chéng’s Seven Stimuli (Qī Fā),
Zōu Yáng’s memorials,
were rich with the oil of the brush,
and their spirit was evident in their words.
Zhòng Shū was solely a Confucian scholar,
Zǐ Cháng solely a historian,
yet their beautiful and intricate writings were formed,
which was also the lament of poets.
Xiāngrú loved books,
following Qū and Sòng as models.
He deeply embraced grand and florid language,
earning him fame as a master of rhetoric.
However, when examining his essential ideas,
the reason did not surpass the rhetoric.
Therefore, Yáng Zǐ considered "Chángqīng to be one whose rhetoric is beautiful but whose utility is limited."
Indeed, this statement is true!
Wáng Bāo created brilliant compositions,
achieving his effect through intricate ingenuity.
Attaching sounds and observing forms,
his works were clear and admirable.
Zǐ Yún’s intentions in writing
made his language and meaning most profound.
Observing his far-reaching and subtle scope,
and his selection of the strange and beautiful,
he exhausted his talent in deep thought,
thus his reasoning was ample and his rhetoric firm.
Huán Tán’s treatises
were praised for their richness like Yī Dùn.
Sòng Hóng recommended him,
comparing him to Xiāngrú.
However, his Rhapsodies such as Jí Líng
were shallow and lacked talent.
Thus, he was known for being skilled in admonition,
but not in beautiful literature.
Jìng Tōng had a refined fondness for rhetoric,
but he encountered difficulties in a flourishing age.
His Xiǎn Zhì and Zì Xù
were also like pearls formed from a sick oyster.
The two Bāns and two Liús
succeeded each other through generations, displaying brilliance.
Old sayings considered Gù to be superior to Biāo in writing,
and Xīn to be more refined than Xiàng in learning.
However, Wáng Mìng was clear and eloquent,
Xīn Xù was comprehensive and refined.
Jade and pearls are produced on Kūngāng,
and it is difficult for later generations to surpass the original.
Fù Yì and Cuī Yīn
shared equal brilliance.
Yuán Shí followed in their footsteps,
and was able to inherit their style.
Dù Dú and Jiǎ Kuí
also had literary renown.
Tracing their talents,
they were later followers of Cuī and Fù.
Lǐ Yóu’s Rhapsodies and inscriptions
aspired to grand composition,
but his talent and strength were sluggish,
his wings drooped and could not fly.
Mǎ Róng, a great Confucian scholar,
had comprehensive thoughts when composing on lofty subjects.
He absorbed and expressed canonical models,
with both embellishment and substance supporting each other.
Wáng Yì was knowledgeable and accomplished,
but his splendid ornamentation lacked power.
Yán Shòu continued his aspirations,
with outstanding and rare talent.
His skill in depicting objects and portraying forms,
was it not the inherited art of Méi Chéng?
Zhāng Héng was comprehensive and ample,
Cài Yōng was refined and elegant.
Their literary and historical achievements were brilliant,
looking upon each other across generations.
Thus, bamboo and cypress have different hearts but the same integrity,
and gold and jade have different qualities but are equally precious.
Liú Xiàng’s memorials and proposals
were incisive in purpose but gentle in tone.
Zhào Yī’s Rhapsodies
were elaborate in meaning but loose in form.
Kǒng Róng had vigorous spirit in writing essays,
Ní Héng had sharp thoughts in composing literary pieces;
they each had a particular excellence.
Pān Xù relied on the classics to display his talent,
thus he was peerless in drafting imperial edicts.
Wáng Lǎng expressed his aspirations with indignation,
also achieving excellence in prefaces and inscriptions.
However, before Qīngyuān,
most writers relied on their talent without much study.
After Xióng and Xiàng,
they increasingly cited books to aid their writing.
This is a major demarcation in adoption and abandonment,
their distinctions cannot be confused.
The talent of Wèi Wén [Dì],
was expansive and brilliant.
Old discussions disparaged him,
saying he was a thousand *lǐ* inferior to Zhí.
However, Zǐjiàn’s thoughts were swift and his talent outstanding,
his poetry beautiful and his prose elegant;
Zǐhuán’s deliberations were thorough, but his strength was slow,
thus he did not contend for the first flourish;
yet his *yuèfǔ* were clear and transcendent,
and his *Diǎnlùn* incisive and essential,
each employing its strengths and weaknesses,
so there was no dullness.
But popular sentiment, in its ups and downs,
unanimously echoing one opinion,
has led to Wén Dì’s talent being diminished by his high status,
and the Prince of Sī’s worth being enhanced by his difficult circumstances.

Zhòngxuān overflowed with talent,
swift yet capable of being meticulous;
his writings were often excellent in multiple aspects,
his diction rarely flawed.
If one were to select his poems and *fù*,
he would be the coronet of the Seven Masters!
Lín [Qí] and Yǔ [Yì] gained renown through official documents and memorials;
Xú Gàn marked his excellence with *fù* and essays;
Liú Zhēn’s noble sentiments collected brilliance;
Yīng Yáng, with his superior learning, excelled in prose;
Lù Cuì and Yáng Xiū
possessed considerable skill in writing notes;
Dīng Yí and Hándān [Chún],
also contained beauty in their discourse;
they are all worthy of consideration.
Liú Shào’s *Zhàodū* [Fù]
could emulate his predecessors;
Hé Yàn’s *Jǐngfú* [Fù]
shone brightly among later talents;
Xiūlián’s disposition,
was marked by *Bǎiyī*, which expressed his ambition;
Jífǔ’s literary principles,
were perfected by *Lín Dān*, achieving their brilliance;
Jī Kāng followed his own mind in composing treatises,
Ruǎn Jí gave vent to his spirit in composing poetry,
different in sound yet harmonious,
different in wings yet flying together.
Zhāng Huà’s short pieces
were sparkling, clear, and fluent;
his *Wrens* [Fù], with its allegorical meaning,
is like Hán Fēi’s *Shuō Nán*.

whose work delved deep and whose thoughts were profound;
he poured all his energy into *Sāndū* [Fù],
and stood out with his *Yǒngshǐ* [Shī],
leaving no effort spared.

his diction naturally harmonious and fluent;
his excellence was concentrated in *Xīzhēng* [Fù],
his abundance expressed in laments,
which did not come from external sources.

his diction strove for breadth,
thus his thoughts could achieve ingenuity,
but he could not control prolixity.

using knowledge to rectify disorder,
thus he could arrange his embellishments clearly and purely,
and was skillful in short pieces.

always with directness and clarity;
Zhì Yú expressed his feelings
always following rules with warmth and elegance;
their classification and distinction
had a clear order.

often contained morals and warnings;
Chángyú’s official writings
were always characterized by steadfast impartiality;
both were truly foundational talents,
not mere showy blossoms among many.
Chénggōng Zǐ’ān,
selected *fù* and was at times excellent;
Xiàhóu Xiàoruò,
was comprehensive, yet each aspect was subtle;
Cáo Chū was clear and delicate in long pieces,
Jìyīng was incisive and keen in short verses,
each had their strengths.
Mèngyáng and Jǐngyáng
had equally splendid talents,
and can be called the governments of Lǔ and Wèi,
or the writings of brothers.

Lú Chén’s emotions were manifest and his principles clear,

sufficient to crown the Revival period;
his *Jiāo Fù* was solemn and grand in its vista,

were meticulous yet unrestrained;
Wēn Tàizhēn’s notes,
followed principles and were clear and fluent;
both were excellent craftsmen with the brush.

excelled in writing history;
their aim in what they depicted
was to adhere to classical teachings;
though their approaches differed,
their literary styles were roughly similar.

thus he was outstanding but often one-sided;

thus he was orderly but lacked variety;
Yīn Zhòngwén’s unique inspiration,
Xiè Shúyuán’s leisurely sentiments,
both dissolved the structure of literary forms,
creating ethereal, floating sounds;
though a surging trend,
it greatly diluted the literary meaning.

their writings gathered like fish scales,
the era is recent and easy to understand,
so there is no need to classify them.

it can compare with the Western Capital [Cháng’ān];
the literary garden of the Jìn era,
is sufficient to rival Yè Dū;
yet the discussions of the Wèi period,
always refer to Yuánfēng as the foremost;
and the excellent discussions of the Sòng era,
also take Jiàn’ān as their standard;
why is this?

and an auspicious gathering that attracted talent?
Alas,
this is why the ancients valued the opportune time!

Talent is indeed difficult,
each nature is endowed differently.
Once literature is compiled,
a thousand years it forms brocade.
Its lingering splendor lingers,
its inherited style resonates far.
Do not say it is chaotic and mixed,
it can be clearly evaluated.
Knowing the Tune (Zhīyīn), Chapter 48

a true knower is hard to meet,

often disparage their contemporaries and admire the ancients.

and *Zǐ Xū* was newly completed,

their writings were almost equal,

and praised it as a fine piece,

comparing him to Tián Bā,
his intention is also clear.

who mistakenly wished to discuss literature,
he even claimed, "Sǐqiān, when writing his book,
consulted Dōngfāng Shuò."
At this, Huán Tán and his ilk
exchanged glances and laughed derisively.
He was truly a gambler,
who spoke carelessly and invited ridicule.
How much more so literary men,
can they speak rashly?
Thus, those whose discernment is keen and clear,
yet value the ancient and disparage the contemporary,
are the two emperors [Qín Huáng and Hàn Wǔ];
those whose talent is truly grand and noble,
yet elevate themselves and suppress others,
are Bān [Gù] and Cáo [Zhí];
those whose learning does not match their writing,
yet believe the false and mistake the true,
are Lóu Hù;
are the "jar of sauce" discussions not much to lament!
The qílín and the fènghuáng are vastly different from the roebuck and the pheasant;
pearls and jade are far superior to pebbles and stones.
The white sun sheds its light,
and clear eyes capture its form.
Yet the minister of Lǔ took a qílín for a roebuck,
and the man from Chǔ took a pheasant for a fènghuáng.
The people of Wèi mistook a night-shining pearl for a strange stone,
and the visitor from Sòng mistook a Swallow stone for a precious pearl.
When the physical form is easy to discern,
such errors are already made;
when the literary sentiment is difficult to assess,
who can say it is easy to distinguish?
Indeed, literary works are varied and mixed,
with substance and embellishment intertwined.
It is known that people have many preferences,
and no one is comprehensively discerning.
Those who are vehement will strike the beat against the sound;
those who are subtle will see the intricacies and soar high;
those with superficial wit will observe the elaborate and their hearts will leap;
those who love the extraordinary will hear the bizarre and their ears will be startled.
If it aligns with their own views, they praise and recite it;
if it differs from theirs, they hinder and discard it.
Each holds to a partial understanding,
wishing to fathom the myriad changes.
This is what is meant by "looking eastward,
one does not see the western wall."
Indeed, one only understands music after practicing a thousand tunes,
and only recognizes a weapon after observing a thousand swords.
Therefore, to achieve comprehensive illumination,
one must first cultivate extensive observation.
One should examine towering mountains to understand mounds,
and draw from vast oceans to comprehend ditches and furrows.
Be impartial towards what is light or heavy,
and unswayed by like or dislike.
Only then can one judge fairly like a balance,
and reflect literature like a mirror.
Therefore, when assessing literary sentiment,
one must first establish six criteria:
first, to observe the overall structure (wèi tǐ);
second, to observe the arrangement of words (zhì cí);
third, to observe penetration and change (tōng biàn);
fourth, to observe the unusual and the regular (qí zhèng);
fifth, to observe the facts and meaning (shì yì);
sixth, to observe the musicality (gōng shāng).
Once these methods are established,
superiority and inferiority will be evident.
Indeed, writers are moved by emotion and express it in words;
readers uncover the writing to enter into the emotion.
Following the waves to trace the source,
though hidden, it will surely become manifest.
Generations pass, and one cannot see their faces,
yet by examining their writings, one immediately perceives their hearts.
It is not that the completed work is too profound,
but rather that the capacity for discernment itself is too shallow.
If one's ambition is in mountains and rivers,
the qín expresses that sentiment.
How much more so when it is given form at the tip of a brush?
How can the principle be hidden?
Therefore, the mind's illumination of principle
is like the eye's illumination of form.
If the eye is clear, no form is indistinguishable;
if the mind is sharp, no principle is unfathomed.
However, among those with common discernment who are deluded,
the profound is discarded, and the shallow is embraced.
This is why Zhuāng Zhōu laughed at "Folding the Willows" (《折楊》),
and Sòng Yù grieved over "White Snow" (《白雪》).
Once, Qū Píng said:
"With plain and ornate intermingled,
the crowd knows not my distinct brilliance."
Recognizing the distinct belongs only to the true connoisseur.
Yáng Xióng proclaimed himself to "love profound, extensive, utterly beautiful writing."
His deeds were superficial,
which is also knowable.
Only those who deeply understand and discern the abstruse
will truly feel joy and inner delight,
like the Spring Terrace delighting the multitude,
or delicious bait stopping passing travelers.
It is said that the orchid is the nation's fragrance,
and wearing it makes its beauty even more fragrant;
writing is also the nation's splendor,
and appreciating and contemplating it makes it truly beautiful.
May discerning gentlemen
attend to it.
An encomium says:
A great bell of ten thousand catties,
Kúi and Kuàng determine its sound.
Good books fill the basket,
and subtle discernment then sets the standard.
Even the seductive tunes of Zhèng
must not be misheard.
Only this criterion exists,
which does not err from the right path.
Chapter 49: Measuring Talent (Chéng Qì)
The Book of Zhōu discusses scholars,
comparing them to timber,
emphasizing utility while also valuing literary grace.
Thus, after the rough hewing is complete, vermillion and ochre are applied;
after walls are erected, carvings and plaster are added.
However, contemporary literati
pursue embellishment and abandon substance.
Thus Wèi Wén believed that "ancient and modern literati
generally do not protect their minor conduct."
Wéi Dàn's critiques
also repeatedly denigrated various talents.
Later generations blindly followed suit,
lumping them all together.
Alas, how lamentable!
A brief look at the flaws of literati:
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú stole a wife and accepted gold;
Yáng Xióng loved wine and lacked calculation;
Jìng Tōng did not adhere to integrity;
Dù Dú's demands were insatiable;
Bān Gù flattered Dòu Xiàn to wield power;
Mǎ Róng sided with Liáng Jì and embezzled goods;
Wén Jǔ was arrogant and insolent, thus inviting execution;
Zhèng Píng was wild and foolish, leading to his demise;
Zhòng Xuān was frivolous and competitive;
Kǒng Zhāng was agitated and crude;
Dīng Yí was greedy and begged for goods;
Lù Cuì indulged in food and drink, acting shamelessly;
Pān Yuè offered strange prayers for the Empress Mǐnhuái;
Lù Jī aligned himself with Jiǎ Mì and Guō Zhāng;
Fù Xuán was rigid and narrow-minded, reviling the court;
Sūn Chǔ was stubborn and disputatious, suing the government.
Those of this sort
are all flaws and blemishes of literati.
If literary figures have such faults,
military figures should also be considered.
Among ancient generals and ministers,
there were indeed many defects:
such as Guǎn Zhòng's theft,
Wú Qǐ's greed and lewdness,
Chén Píng's blemishes,
and Jiàng Yú and Guàn Yīng's slander and jealousy.
And from these onwards,
they are countless.
Kǒng Guāng held high office
yet flattered Dǒng Xián;
how much more so for Bān Gù and Mǎ Róng, who held lowly positions!
And Pān Yuè, who was of even lower rank!
Wáng Róng, who founded a state and held high office,
yet sold official positions and was vulgar;
how much more so for Mǎ Róng and Dù Dú, who were in dire straits,
and Dīng Yí and Lù Cuì, who were impoverished!
However, Zǐ Xià did not diminish his reputation as a great scholar,
nor did Jùn Chōng get sullied by the Bamboo Grove (Zhúlín Qī Xián),
because their fame was high and criticism was reduced.
As for Qū Píng and Jiǎ Yí's loyalty and integrity,
Zōu Yǎn and Méi Chéng's astuteness,
Huáng Xiāng's pure filial piety,
and Xú Gàn's profundity and silence,
who says that literati
must necessarily have such blemishes?
Indeed, people are endowed with five talents (wǔ cái),
and their long and short points have different uses.
Unless one is a supreme sage,
it is difficult to be perfect.
However, generals and ministers, due to their elevated positions, are especially prominent,
while literati, due to their humble positions, are often criticized.
This is why great rivers surge,
while trickling streams are fragmented inch by inch.
The waxing and waning of reputation
is indeed such;
the success and failure of position
also have their reasons.
Indeed, for a scholar to be employed
is to achieve results.
Jìng Jiāng of Lǔ,
though a woman, possessed intelligence.
Yet, when her organizational skills are extended
to govern a state,
how can a man who studies literature
not be accomplished in political affairs?
Those like Yáng Xióng and Mǎ Róng
had literature but lacked substance,
which is why they ended up in humble positions.
Formerly, Yǔ Yuánguī's talent and brilliance were outstanding,
and his achievements were renowned.
Therefore, his literary accomplishments were not particularly lauded;
if he were not a high official,
he would be known purely for his literary talent.
The ways of literature and military
are both suitable.
Xì Hú diligently studied the Shū Jīng,
and was therefore appointed as commander-in-chief.
How can it be said that he loved literature but was not skilled in warfare?
Sūn Wǔ's Art of War (Bīng Jīng)
has words like pearls and jade.
How can it be said that he practiced warfare but did not understand literature?
Thus, a superior person conceals their talents,
waiting for the opportune moment to act.
In developing their career,
it is appropriate to accumulate substance to strengthen their inner self,
and to display their brilliance to adorn their outer self.
Their character should be like the *biánnán* (Chinese catalpa) and *yùzhāng* (camphor tree),
and their foundation like their trunks.
Their literary creations must serve the military and the state,
and their burdens must be to shoulder the pillars of the nation.
When impoverished, they cultivate personal virtue and leave behind writings;
when successful, they serve the times and achieve great deeds.
Such literati
are truly the men of *zǐcái* (fine timber).
An encomium says:
Behold those former cultivators,
possessing excellent literary virtue.
Their fame shone brightly in southern Chǔ,
their brilliance stirred northern Liáng.
They are carved but not made into mere utensils;
who can emulate their steadfast core?
Could they not adorn their own person?
Indeed, they also brought glory to their country.
Chapter 50: Explaining the Will
The "literary mind"
refers to the mental effort put into writing.
In ancient times, Juān Zǐ had his "Lute Mind,"
and Wáng Sūn his "Clever Mind."
How beautiful indeed are these "minds"!
Hence, the term is used here.
Classical writing,
achieved its form through embellishment and richness.
It is not merely adopting the "carved dragons" of Zōu Shì's numerous words.
Indeed, the universe is vast and boundless,
and human talents are diverse and numerous.
To stand out from the crowd,
is merely a matter of wisdom and skill.
Years and months drift by,
and the spirit does not linger.
To spread fame and achieve renown,
is merely a matter of literary creation.
Humans, whose appearance mirrors heaven and earth,
and whose nature is imbued with the five elements,
who liken their ears and eyes to the sun and moon,
and compare their voices and breaths to wind and thunder,
their transcendence over all things
is indeed spiritual.
Their form is as fragile as grass and trees,
yet their name can surpass the hardness of metal and stone.
Therefore, a superior person living in the world
cultivates virtue and establishes words.
Is it because they love to argue?
It is out of necessity!
When I was seven years old,
I dreamed of colorful clouds like brocade,
and I climbed to pluck them.
When I passed the age of thirty,
I often dreamed at night that I held vermilion-lacquered ritual vessels,
following Zhòng Ní (Confucius) on a journey south.
In the morning when I awoke,
I was delighted.
How difficult it is to see the Sage!
Was this a dream bestowed upon a humble person?
Since the beginning of humankind,
there has been none like the Master.
To expound upon the Sage's teachings,
nothing is better than annotating the Classics (*Jīng*).
However, scholars like Mǎ Rú and Zhèng Xuán
have already profoundly elaborated on them.
Even if one has a deep understanding,
it is not enough to establish a school of thought.
Only the utility of literature
is truly the branches and leaves of the classics.
The Five Rites (*wǔlǐ*) rely on it to be completed,
the Six Canons (*liùdiǎn*) depend on it to be put into practice.
Through it, rulers and ministers shine brightly,
and military and state affairs are made manifest.
Upon examining their origins,
none are not from the classics.
But as the Sages are far removed in time,
literary forms have disintegrated.
Writers love novelty,
and value words that are superficial and outlandish.
They decorate feathers and emphasize painting,
embroidering pouches and handkerchiefs.
The deviation from the root is ever greater,
and it will lead to corruption and abuse.
Indeed, the *Zhōu Shū* (Book of Zhōu) in discussing rhetoric,
values conciseness and essentiality;
Ní Fù (Confucius) in delivering his teachings,
detested heterodoxy.
The difference between rhetoric and teaching
should be embodied in conciseness.
Therefore, taking up brush and mixing ink,
I thereupon began to discuss literature.
Carefully observing the many who have discussed literature in recent times:
As for Wèi Wén's (Cáo Pī) "Discourse on the Classics,"
Chén Sī's (Cáo Zhí) "Preface to Books,"
Yīng Cháng's "Literary Discourse,"
Lù Jī's "Rhapsody on Literature,"
Zhòng Zhì's (Zhì Yú) "Classification of Styles,"
and Hóng Fàn's (Fàn Wénlǎn) "Forest of Literature."
Each illuminated a corner or crevice,
seldom observing the main thoroughfare.
Some praised or criticized the talents of their time,
some evaluated and ranked the writings of former cultivators,
some broadly presented the principles of the elegant and the common,
some concisely summarized the essence of essays and chapters.
Wèi's discourse is dense but incomplete,
Chén's preface is eloquent but inappropriate,
Yīng's discourse is flowery but superficial,
Lù's rhapsody is artful but fragmented and disordered,
the "Classification of Styles" is precise but lacks achievement,
and the "Forest of Literature" is shallow and lacking in essentials.
Moreover, the likes of Jūnshān (Huán Kān) and Gōnggàn (Wáng Chén),
and the ilk of Jífǔ (Lù Wèi) and Shìlóng (Yáo Dēng),
broadly discussed literary ideas;
they occasionally appeared,
but none were able to shake the leaves to find the root,
or observe the ripples to seek the source.
They did not recount the admonitions of ancient sages,
nor benefit the considerations of later generations.
The creation of *Wénxīn Diāolóng*
is based on the Dào,
takes the Sages as its teachers,
embodies the Classics (*Jīng*),
draws from the Apocrypha (*Wěi*),
and transforms the *Sāo* (poetry of the Chǔ state).
Its core principles of literature
are indeed comprehensive.
As for discussing literature and narrating writing,
I classify and differentiate styles,
trace origins to elucidate periods,
explain names to clarify meanings,
select writings to define chapters,
expound principles to establish systems.
From the upper chapters onwards,
the outlines are clear.
As for dissecting emotions and analyzing embellishments,
I must encompass and connect all threads,
express divine nature,
and depict stylistic force,
to embrace comprehensive understanding,
and to examine sounds and characters.
I discuss rise and fall in "Seasonal Order,"
praise and criticize in "Talent and Strategy,"
express regret in "Discerning Sounds,"
and show integrity in "Regulation and Talent."
I always hold "Explaining the Will"
to govern all chapters.
From the lower chapters onwards,
the details are apparent.
Arranging principles and defining names,
is made manifest in the numbers of the *Dàyì* (Great Changes).
Its literary utility
is encompassed in forty-nine chapters.
Indeed, to evaluate and order a single text is easy,
but to encompass and integrate all words is difficult.
Although I have lightly picked at the hair and deeply reached the marrow,
there may be hidden intentions and subtle sources
that seem close yet are distant,
things not covered by my words,
which are countless.
As for the writings I have classified and arranged,
some are similar to old discussions;
this is not mere imitation,
but because the nature of things dictates they cannot be different.
Some differ from previous theories;
this is not arbitrary difference,
but because reason dictates they cannot be the same.
Similarities and differences,
I disregard ancient and modern.
I dissect the flesh and separate the fibers,
solely aiming for a balanced judgment.
Reining in my reins in the field of refined literature,
and encompassing the treasury of artistic embellishment,
it is almost complete.
However, words cannot fully express ideas,
a difficulty even for ancient sages.
With knowledge confined to a small vessel,
how can one set standards?
The vast past
has already submerged my hearings;
the distant future
will surely obscure their view.
An Appreciation states:
Life has its limits,
Only wisdom is boundless.
Pursuing external things is truly difficult,
Relying on one's nature is quite easy.
To be lofty and unyielding among springs and rocks,
To ponder the meaning of texts.
If literature truly fills the heart,
My mind finds its abode.
